The aerial view of the 9.4-acre parcel of the Tradition Master Planned Unit Development at the southwest corner of Crosstown Parkway and Fairgreen Drive in Port St. The land-use map of the 9.4-acre parcel of the Tradition Master Planned Unit Development at the southwest corner of Crosstown Parkway and Fairgreen Drive in Port St. LUCIE — After months of debate and neighborhood concerns, the Port St. Lucie City Council has permanently prohibited a gas station from being built on a 9.4-acre commercial parcel at the southwest corner of Crosstown Parkway and Fairgreen Drive. The council unanimously approved the second and final reading of the 16th amendment to the Tradition Master Planned Unit Development on July 13, codifying a restriction that bars any current or future owner from developing a service station on the site. The amendment changes the parcel’s designation from residential to commercial, paving the way for retail and office development while addressing residents’ concerns about traffic and congestion. The issue has been under discussion for nearly three months after Winding River Crosstown LLC requested permission to convert what had been planned as Phase 3 of the Heritage Oaks at Tradition residential development into commercial property. While council members generally supported adding commercial uses to the rapidly growing area, several voiced concerns during the initial May 26 quasi-judicial hearing that a convenience store with gas pumps would worsen traffic along Crosstown Parkway west of Interstate 95. Vice Mayor Jolien Caraballo and other council members noted the increasing congestion along the commercial corridor and asked staff to determine whether gas stations could be eliminated as a permitted use on the parcel. The council tabled the request to allow time for that review. At the time, Councilwoman Stephanie Morgan questioned whether prohibiting a specific type of business amounted to government interference in the marketplace. “What concerns me is that on May 11 we approved two parcels changing from RGC to commercial general,” Morgan said during the May hearing. “We didn’t put any conditions on them. How can you put a condition on an applicant saying no gas stations? That would be like saying no Chick-fil-A because we’ve got enough chicken restaurants.” When the hearing resumed June 22, several Heritage Oaks residents urged the council to reject the land-use change, citing concerns about increased traffic, noise and neighborhood impacts. Instead, the council voted 4-0, with Morgan absent, to approve the commercial designation on first reading after the developer agreed to permanently relinquish the right to build a gas station. During the July 13 meeting, city planner Bridget Kean outlined the changes that formally incorporated the restriction into the Tradition MPUD documents. The updated development plan specifies that while service stations remain a permitted use elsewhere within the mixed-use area, they are prohibited on Parcel 11A. The concept plan also now includes a notation prohibiting a service station on the property, and the ordinance itself was revised to reference the city’s definition of a service station. Staff also added additional protections requested by nearby residents. Before any mass grading begins, the developer must install a fence along the southern property line to prevent construction access through Southwest Glenbrook Drive, which connects to Heritage Oaks. In addition, an architectural wall and landscape buffering must be completed along the southeastern and southern boundaries before the first building permit is issued for vertical construction. Several residents again voiced concerns about the proposal and questioned whether the process had been sufficiently transparent. Councilman Anthony Bonna defended both the public process and the final compromise. “Ultimately, we have to make decisions, and those decisions are not going to satisfy everybody,” Bonna said. “We listen and consider every resident that comes forward, but ultimately we have to make one decision.” Bonna said he believes expanding commercial development will benefit residents by broadening the city’s tax base. Lucie has long lacked commercial, which is a burden on homeowners,” he said. “We have had several hearings here at the city, so that is what transparency is: open meetings where people can come and share their opinions and be a part of the process.” Councilman David Pickett agreed, saying the city has consistently heard residents oppose additional housing. “When this was first introduced, I was very excited that they wanted to go from residential to commercial,” Pickett said. “It doesn’t matter which way we rule, there’s always going to be somebody in opposition. For me, going to commercial is the best possible thing for that corner.” Morgan, who had questioned the gas station restriction during the first hearing, ultimately supported the ordinance. “We have heard from so many community residents — no more housetops,” she said. “It has been transparent, there’s no denying that.” Before the vote, Mayor Shannon Martin asked staff to confirm that the prohibition would remain with the property regardless of ownership. Kean confirmed the restriction is now written directly into the Tradition MPUD documents, ensuring no future owner can develop a gas station on the parcel. The council then voted unanimously to approve the ordinance, ending months of discussion and clearing the way for commercial development while permanently removing a gas station as a future possibility. Lucie County have arrested three people in connection with the death of a 3-month-old infant, describing the case as one of the worst they’ve encountered. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office said, "Based on what I observed in my 20 years of law enforcement, this is one of the worst cases I have ever worked." The investigation began in August of last year when detectives were called to a Fort Pierce home following the infant’s death. The baby had been living with his grandfather, Robert Maxwell, and Maxwell’s girlfriend, Vikki Koon, while his mother, Nicole Maxwell, resided with a boyfriend in Vero Beach. The latest: WPBF 25 News coverage on Politics According to an arrest affidavit, Koon told deputies, "She believed a newborn should have two ounces per feeding twice a day. She said when she ran out of formula, she would fill the bottle with regular milk and add water." In the days leading up to the infant’s death, Koon and Maxwell reportedly contacted the baby’s mother and biological father, who lives out of state, via messenger, stating, "I need you to come to Florida, something's going on with the baby. I don't know what's going on but he has marks all over him." Investigators found the mobile home in poor condition. "The house was extremely hot. There was a bug infestation in the home. And the home was unsafe for walking. There wasn't an entryway that we could safely make entry into the home," Diaz said. [related id='fd1eb542-3249-4304-a049-62c61019bb7a' align='center' source=''][/related] An autopsy revealed the infant was emaciated, had a sunken abdomen, and widespread lesions consistent with severe dehydration and malnutrition. Tasha Wright, who was with Nicole Maxwell when detectives arrived to arrest her, said Maxwell claimed she wasn’t present during the events leading to the baby’s death. "She told me the whole story she wasn't there. She had dropped the baby off with her dad," Wright said. Wright expressed disbelief at the allegations, saying, "She is the sweetest person in the world." Detectives are urging the public to report any signs of child abuse. "Most of the time, something so small could end up being something so big like this case, and we could potentially save the children's lives," Diaz said. All three suspects are facing several charges, including aggravated manslaughter. Lucie County Sheriff Richard Del Toro released this statement: “The loss of a child is heartbreaking. Cases like this weigh heavily on everyone involved, from our investigators and first responders to the members of our community who mourn the death of a vulnerable child. Every child deserves the chance to grow up in a safe, loving, and nurturing home. I am incredibly proud of the relentless dedication of our investigators and all those who worked tirelessly to uncover the truth and ensure those responsible are held accountable. While justice is essential, our shared responsibility must be preventing these tragedies before they occur. Protecting children is not solely the responsibility of law enforcement or the child welfare system. It is a responsibility we all share. If you see signs that a child may be neglected, abused, or living in unsafe conditions, do not assume someone else will intervene. One phone call can be the difference between a child receiving the help they need and a life being saved. This case also reminds us that families facing difficult circumstances are not alone. Resources, support, and assistance are available. My commitment remains unwavering: to seek justice for victims, hold offenders accountable, and work alongside our community to protect our most vulnerable. By recognizing the warning signs, speaking up, and connecting families with the help they need, we can work together to prevent tragedies like this from happening again." The recently opened Port St. Lucie Police training center contains a defensive tactics training room equipped with Axon VR technology. The recently opened, 54,283-square-foot, state-of-the-art, $28.8 million police training center is on the Port St. Lucie City Hall grounds, just northwest of the police department. The 54,283-square-foot, state-of-the-art, $28.8 million police training center officially opened on July 24 on the grounds of Port St. Lucie City Hall with a ribbon-cutting for invited guests. The interior of the 54,283-square-foot, state-of-the-art, $28.8 million police training center on the Port St. Lucie City Hall grounds, just northwest of the police department. Lucie city officials who cut the ribbon for the 54,283-square-foot, state-of-the-art, $28.8 million police training center on July 24 were Mayor Shannon Martin, center, and Chief Leo Niemczyk. LUCIE – After four years of construction, the ribbon was cut on July 24 for a 54,283-square-foot, state-of-the-art, $28.8 million police training center on the Port St. Lucie City Hall grounds, just northwest of the police department. “This project is all about making sure our officers have the space, training, and resources they need to continue serving our community at the highest level,” Port St. Lucie Mayor Shannon Martin said in a Facebook posting. Lucie the safest large city in Florida takes more than dedication. It requires planning ahead and making smart investments that prepare our officers for the challenges they face every day.” Included in the three-story facility are: • A 20-lane, 9,508-square-foot indoor firearms range featuring an integrated MILO live-fire scenario system. • A 2,848-square-foot tactical shoot house with configurable rooms for realistic scenario-based training. • A MILO Virtual Simulation Theater for immersive decision-making and de-escalation exercises. • A dedicated defensive tactics training room equipped with Axon VR technology. • A multi-purpose training room designed for classroom instruction, conferences, virtual presentations, and large-scale training. • Three floors of office space supporting the Training Division and Criminal Investigations Division (CID), including 19 offices and 86 workstations. • Advanced audio/visual technology throughout the facility to support collaborative training and instruction. The facility was designed by ADG Architecture and constructed by HJ High, with specialized contributions from industry leaders including Action Target, MILO, Whelen, and numerous additional project partners, according to Port St. As of July 27, the city has a population of more than 260,000. There is a total of 455 employees in the police department with 360 sworn officers, according to city hall records. For years, officers traveled to Indian River State College in Fort Pierce for extensive training, according to Officer Brittany McNally. “By bringing much of that training in-house, this facility will reduce those recurring costs while allowing us to train more efficiently and effectively,” she said in a statement. “Equally important, the new training facility provides our officers with access to state-of-the-art technology and realistic, scenario-based training that better prepares them for the complex situations they may face in the field. From recruit training to advanced tactical instruction and continuing education, our officers will now have the resources needed to sharpen their skills throughout their careers right in our own backyard.” Once the ribbon was cut, police personnel immediately began making the move into the new facility. The WNBA has never been bigger.More people are watching. Salaries for many players are higher than ever. But mounting turmoil and discord have been a part of this transformative period that has featured a landmark collective bargaining agreement, league expansion and skyrocketing player recognition.It seems to have reached a new flashpoint, as discussions about race, gender and sexuality created headlines ahead of Saturday’s WNBA All-Star Game. Race-driven conversations resurfaced after an incident between Indiana Fever guard Caitlin Clark and Phoenix Mercury forward Alyssa Thomas, while players continued to voice frustrations with WNBA Commissioner Cathy Engelbert and leadership over what they say is a lack of protection from social media harassment and divisive remarks.“It is a moment to be celebrated without a doubt,” said Ketra Armstrong, sport management professor and director of the Center for Race and Ethnicity in Sport at the University of Michigan. “We want to celebrate what’s great. But sometimes, the progress can overshadow, still, where the perils are.”RELATED STORY | WNBA star Sophie Cunningham sparks debate after comments on transgender athletesIssues of race, gender and representation have been an undercurrent throughout the league's history. Debates over those issues have grown as women's sports have exploded. And they remain a challenge that shape the WNBA's — and most other pro sports leagues, for that matter — public and online discourse.“This is what a sports league" is, said David Berri, sports economist and economics professor at Southern Utah University. He cited the NFL’s Rooney Rule as an example. “If a sports league is going to get attention, you’re going to get attention for these things as well.”Growth has magnified broader cultural debatesContentious conversations also spread to issues of transgender athletes and harassment.WNBA veteran Brianna Turner said on social media this week that her former team, the Fever, fired a male employee last season for sexual harassment. Turner, who was with Indiana last season but now plays for Las Vegas, also said Indiana players were encouraged not to discuss the firing.Turner’s comments came as she defended transgender athletes days after Indiana forward Sophie Cunningham spoke on transgender athletes competing in women’s sports.“I got a lot of negative feedback about me hating trans. And I’m like, ‘I never once said that,’” Cunningham was quoted as saying in a story published by ESPN. “I think that I am here to extend love. But I also think with that love is truth, being honest. And I want to protect young girls in a locker room, or young girls in sport who shouldn’t have to go against biological men.”The WNBA’s conversations about race were thrust back into the spotlight after Toronto Tempo coach Sandy Brondello was suspended one game for referring to Atlanta Dream forward Angel Reese as a “protected species.”The comment, picked up by the broadcast after Reese drew a foul on Toronto player Nyara Sabally, quickly drew criticism.Brondello, a former player who has won two WNBA titles, is Australian. The “protected species” phrase is used in Australian sports to express frustration over a lack of calls against a player. However, in the U.S., the phrase suggests that someone isn’t human and could be seen as derogatory toward Black people. Brondello later apologized. Reese accepted it, saying she appreciated the league’s swift action.“It’s a much bigger platform now. Everything that happens is news,” Berri said. “There were hard fouls 10 years ago. Nobody paid any attention to that. It ends up being because of the coverage now, everything gets magnified ... I mean, this is what we wanted.”‘A lot to celebrate’ but race still mattersClark has repeatedly attempted to downplay the noise surrounding her, but she has become a springboard for projections far beyond the game itself.“It’s basketball," she said in a recent ESPN interview. "When I walk out of the locker room I shouldn’t be fearful of what the conversation is going to be. It’s emotionally exhausting. It makes your shoulders tense because people don’t want to talk about the basketball. They just want to stir it up and make something else.”The WNBA retroactively assessed Thomas a flagrant foul and suspended her one game after the veteran made contact with her fist to Clark’s throat in a June 24 matchup.RELATED STORY | WNBA adding six regular-season games starting in 2027The play, which Thomas has said was an accident, gained widespread attention and ignited debates over officiating, with coaches, pundits and lawmakers weighing in on whether the league needs to take action about physical play involving Clark.Thomas, who is Black and in her 12th WNBA season, said after the incident she had received death threats, part of increased online vitriol players have faced in recent years. Chelsea Gray of the Las Vegas Aces recently posted a message from a man that included a racial slur. And Engelbert this week met with a pair of player committees to discuss what more can be done to protect players from online harassment.Since she entered the league, Clark and her WNBA peers have become proxies for long-standing American issues — from race, gender and sexual orientation to who receives attention and who doesn't.“There’s a lot to celebrate,” Armstrong said, “but race still matters. A Massachusetts cyclist is turning heartbreak into hope after losing a close friend to young-onset colorectal cancer.Jay Weedall traveled to South Florida to begin a 2,600-mile bike ride from Key West to Maine, with a goal of raising $50,000 for research while honoring his friend's memory.WATCH WPTV'S COVERAGE BELOW:"A friend of mine recently passed away from young-onset rectal cancer," Weedall said.His friend, who was also named Jay, inspired Weedall to take on the cross-country ride as a tribute."I've adventured around the world with him, ridden bikes together with him, and this felt like the best way to honor him now that he's passed away," he said.Weedall's goal is to raise $50,000 for the young-onset colorectal cancer research center in honor of his friend. To prepare, he trained 200 to 300 miles a week, mapped out his route, and planned the 2,600-mile journey from Key West to Lubec, Maine."So, there was a lot of preplanning to make sure that the roads that I'm going to go on are safe and have been ridden on by cyclists and let's hope that the wind is kind to me," he said.Weedall began his journey in Key West, pedaling 155 miles to Miami on the first day. He picked up a key lesson along the way."Something I learned after day one is hydration packs, good for hydration obviously, but if you fill it up with ice it's good for keeping you cold as well," he said.On his second leg — a 163-mile ride to Vero Beach — Weedall described his daily strategy for managing the miles."Ideally, I try to beat the heat and then I'm going roughly 150 miles a day, just inching my way up the coast through pretty much every state all the way to the Pan Mass Challenge. Then I'll do the Pan Mass Challenge across Massachusetts on August 2nd. I'll continue to the Canadian border in Maine," he said.Even through the physical demands of riding hundreds of miles alone, Weedall says his thoughts stay with his friend."Even when my legs are hurting, even when the traffic is big or even when I'm a little anxious about what's going on around me, but I'm largely just thinking about my friend who doesn't get the opportunity to do this with me anymore," he said.The route takes Weedall through small coastal towns along the way."By avoiding highways, I get to experience these little coastal towns along those inlets," he said.Those who want to follow Weedall's journey can track his progress on the cycling app Strava.

For two Boca Raton brothers living with muscular dystrophy, soccer is more than a game.It’s motivation. And thanks to an unforgettable surprise from Cristiano Ronaldo and FIFA, it’s become a reminder that their dreams are still alive.WATCH BELOW:Seventeen-year-old Michael Berestovsky and his 13-year-old brother Vladimir Berestovsky grew up loving the sport and idolizing Portuguese soccer superstar Cristiano Ronaldo.Even as muscular dystrophy slowly weakened their muscles and changed their lives, their passion for soccer never faded.“Sometimes they still play despite the pain sometimes,” Michael Berestovsky said, while talking about the sport that inspires him.That resilience is something both boys connect deeply with.“I want to be like them more,” Michael Berestovsky said. “People like Ronaldo inspire me to try more and do more things to reach my goals.”For Vladimir Berestovsky, Ronaldo’s work ethic became a daily source of encouragement.“Ronaldo he inspires many people and he keeps working hard no matter what and he never gives up and it like motivates me to keep on trying every day,” Vladimir Berestovsky said.Muscular dystrophy is a genetic disorder that causes muscles to weaken and lose mass over time. Today, the boys can no longer walk on their own. The last time Michael walked was when he was 15 years old, playing soccer while wearing a Portugal jersey. During the game, he fell and broke his leg in two places.“It was very dark times, and we couldn’t see the hope,” their mother Anna Berestovsky said.Read more of our World Cup, soccer coverageBut Anna Berestovsky said giving up was never an option. A lifelong Ronaldo fan herself, Anna said she first fell in love with soccer at 16 years old after her grandfather introduced her to the sport.Over the years, she admired Ronaldo not only for his talent, but for the determination he showed both on and off the field, helping her through her own personal challenges as a teen.That same mindset became the foundation for her family.“We as a family decided that we should never give up. We should only move forward, we should look for new treatments, new physical treatments, things that help them from nutrition and exercises,” Anna said.Wanting to show how much Ronaldo had helped her sons emotionally through their condition, Anna reached out to FIFA and WPTV to share their story.What happened next became the soccer experience of a lifetime.The family received surprise tickets from friends and family to watch Portugal and Ronaldo play in Miami during the FIFA Club World Cup festivities.“Ronaldo was an inspiration for me to keep going to do my things right to pursue my goals, I was really amazed when my boys felt the same way,” Anna Berestovsky said. “The entire family has been Ronaldo fans.”For Vladimir, the atmosphere inside the stadium was unforgettable.“What was your favorite part of the games?” I asked him.“The fans they were like very loud and like cheering and chanting and doing waves,” Vladimir Berestovsky said with a smile, adding that he joined right in with the celebrations.“Of course I was for Portugal, I wanted them to win,” he said. “But when they lost I still kept wearing their jersey because I think Ronaldo is still a good player no matter if he has a world cup or not.”Then came another surprise.During the match, Ronaldo sent the boys two autographed official FIFA World Cup soccer balls.“It’s not just a signed ball, it’s a token,” Anna Berestovsky said. “It’s a token of being seen by such an amazing star. It's a dream come true."FIFA also gifted the family VIP tickets to the tournament’s third-place match. Today, the boys continue treatments that their family says help slow the progression of muscular dystrophy. Their hope is that one day they’ll be able to play soccer again.Inspired by the kindness shown to them, Michael and Vladimir Berestovsky are now paying it forward by sharing their journey on Instagram so other children and families living with muscular dystrophy know they’re not alone.“My message to Ronaldo would be thank you so much for your gift to us, it means a lot of me and my brother dealing with disability,” Michael Berestovsky said.“We will have this moment in our hearts forever,” Anna Berestovsky said. “We haven’t felt anything similar to this in a long long time. Thank you thank you thank you Ronaldo for everything.”Now, the brothers are already dreaming about the future — counting down the days until FIFA 2030, when they hope to watch Portugal play in Portugal.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Lucie review the upcoming city budget as some city council members worry about lost revenue if property taxes go away. Lucie hosted the summer budget workshop at the Port St. Lucie Community Center Thursday morning. During the workshop, City Manager Jesus Merejo told the City Council the city would lose over $48 million in property taxes over the next two years if the item passes in November. To prepare for the potential hit, the city isn't just deferring projects it's also holding the line on hiring. Lucie says it won't fund 184 requested positions, worth $28.3 million, including 25 new police officers and parks staff the city had already planned to add this year to keep up with growth at Torino Regional Park and the new BMX facility at Tradition Regional Park. Well, our costs continually rise just like everybody else. So, the only place that we can take that from is personnel. So, we'll have to reduce the size of the place, said Police Chief Leo Niemczyk when asked how this budget will impact the department. See also: Funeral held for Belle Glade father, two sons killed when pickup overturned into canal City employees also won't get a cost-of-living raise in the coming budget. On the capital side, the $7.8 million in canceled projects includes a study for a new interchange connecting Marshall Parkway to I-95, an inclusive playground at McChesney Park, and parking improvements at Riverland Paseo Park, along with construction on a new City Hall and parking garage Despite parks and recreation receiving an extra $1.34 million, most of that money is tied to new developments, such as the Torino Regional Park and the BMX facility at Tradition Regional Park. Parks and recreation officials told city councilors what a lack of new staff to keep these parks going will look like. I dare say the dirty words of deferred maintenance. But that's the reality when you don't have the people in the parks to maintain them at the level that we've been accustomed to doing, said Brad Keen, the director of the parks and recreation department. Not everything is being cut, though. The police department's budget is actually going up nearly 10%, to just under $104 million, driven mostly by a 5% contractual raise for sworn officers along with new equipment, training and technology upgrades. But the number of officers isn't growing; staffing stays flat at just over 468 positions, meaning the department is spending more to keep the officers it already has, not to add more. City leaders have flagged public safety, police, code enforcement, and emergency management as the areas most exposed if deeper cuts are eventually needed, since they already eat up 56% of the city's general fund. This is the reality of what the future is for, not just our city, but all this needs for safety if we're not able to be competitive and keep our officers, said Vice Mayor Jolien Caraballo. The proposal, known as Amendment 3, is headed to Florida voters on the November 3, 2026 ballot after the Legislature passed it during a June special session. If approved, it would raise the state's homestead exemption from $50,000 to $150,000 starting in January 2027, and to $250,000 in January 2028, while also directing lawmakers to come up with a plan to eliminate non-school property taxes on homesteaded properties eventually. Because it's a constitutional amendment, it needs at least 60% approval from voters to pass. Economists have estimated the change could cut local government revenue statewide by billions of dollars a year, which is why cities and counties across Florida, including Port St. Lucie, are already building the potential loss into their budget planning. Lucie County homeowners currently pay the highest property tax in the state, according to Florida tax data. Scott Samples with the city said the council will reconvene shortly after the November 3rd election to determine next steps, whether the proposal is passed or fails.

INDIANTOWN – A pair of Village Council members failed to gain momentum on a second stab at convincing their colleagues and staff that a pause on data center applications would not put the municipality at odds with the Florida Legislature’s recent bills aimed at controlling such developments and limiting more restrictive land uses. The Council previously sought the advice of Village Attorney Wade Vose last month on a moratorium after scores of local residents had protested the Village’s preliminary review of a data center application submitted earlier this year by Nelson Ferreira, which he actually withdrew on April 29. Indiantown civic activist Melissa Hague had spurred its members on during the June 11 Council meeting, citing examples of a few other Florida communities either implementing or proposing data center moratoriums. Wade shot that idea down, however, insisting such a move would put the municipality in direct violation of Senate Bills 180 and 484 and leave it open to potential lawsuits by property owners and developers. Hague repeated her request during the July 13 budget workshop. “I’m coming back asking for an administrative pause on data centers,” she said. “It’s already been admitted on media that we don’t know what we’re dealing with. If we don’t know, not having an administrative pause to go through the motions of finding out and looking at land development regulations is negligent. I know there’s pressure behind the scenes not to have that happen, but the people want it to happen, and that’s who you represent.” A few minutes later, Councilwoman Karen Onsager – who’d supported Hague’s request the previous month – again broached the topic, this time couching it in the milder terminology of a “pause.” “I’ve asked for an informative community meeting,” she said. “In light of that meeting, I move that the Village of Indiantown establish a 90-day administrative pause on the acceptance, processing and approval of all new applications for large-load data center development projects. During the 90-day period, I request the Village staff proceed with the informational meeting I requested, including technical experts, representatives from the South Florida Water Management District, utility providers and relevant staff so that the Council and our residents can better understand the current and projected demands on our water and electrical infrastructure.” Councilwoman Onsager emphasized more than once that her proposed pause was intended to provide the Council additional time to gather facts, evaluate data and consider potential solutions to community concerns while putting off any potential Board decisions on such applications until after the current election cycle. “To be clear, I am not proposing any amendments to our land development regulations nor am I seeking to impose additional restrictions or requirements on the application process at this time,” she added in a nod to the aforementioned legislation. “I am simply requesting sufficient time for the Council to conduct due-diligence and make informed decisions regarding future industrial development applications based on a thorough understanding of the facts and the infrastructure implications.” Rather than offering a second to Onsager’s motion, however, Councilwoman Vernestine Palmer wanted to negotiate the length of that pause with her colleague. “I think the administrative pause should be more than 90 days,” she said. “I think we should have at least a 12-to-18-month administrative pause so we can get all the information concerning it. No one is saying we’re against it or for it; we just want to know what’s going on so we can make an informed decision and [ensure] the LDRs have some safeguards in it for us.” That failed to sway Onsager, who knew her motion was already going against Vose’s prior legal advice. “I asked for a 90-day pause because a 90-day pause does give us time to collect information, have the meeting, get some important data and not necessarily bring down problems for our community,” she explained. “We can’t afford to be sued for doing things wrong –12 to 18 months is restrictive. We’re also in the middle of an election. I think that we should vote for a stop until we can get whoever’s here seated and they can get familiar with the actual facts and then make that choice.” For her part, Councilwoman Angelina Perez, looked to Vose for advice rather than make any comments. The latter admitted nothing had changed for him since June. “It’s my legal opinion that such an administrative pause – whether it’s 90 days or 12 months – would be a violation of Senate Bill 180, which we discussed at length previously,” he said. “My legal opinion remains the same.” Vose acknowledged receiving an email from a local land use attorney that same afternoon with an ominous warning. “He does represent multiple developers within the Village,” he explained. “He emailed me precisely about this matter and advised me that SB 180 would prohibit anything along the lines of a regulation that would inhibit the process of applications for development.” After Village Manager Taryn Kryzda confirmed the industrially zoned lands within the Village allowed data centers as a permitted use, Mayor Carmine Dipaolo warned his colleagues about another risk in offending state officials. “Basically, what we’re saying to the Legislature is we don’t care about your house bill – the same Legislature that’s given us over $120 million – and we’re asking for more,” he said. “If the residents had to pay the $120 million that we’ve received, it’d be 100 years before they had clean water.” Kryzda concurred. “My experience is, when local government goes against the state or the federal government, the first thing they look to do is withhold funding,” she said. After further Board discussion, Mayor Dipaolo called for a second to Onsager’s motion, which was not forthcoming. After her motion died, Councilwoman Onsager confirmed with Kryzda that her desired community meeting would be scheduled for Saturday, Aug. Your comment has been submitted. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office is sharing new details about the investigation into the death of a three-month-old boy in Fort Pierce, including why it took nearly a year to make arrests and the conditions investigators say they found inside the mobile home where the child lived. The infant’s mother, Nicole Maxwell, her father Robert Maxwell, and his girlfriend Vikki Koon were arrested and charged with aggravated manslaughter and child abuse. Investigators say the baby died from dehydration and malnutrition last August, and the medical examiner later ruled the death a homicide. Detectives say the case was complex, requiring outside expertise and months of additional testing before they could move forward with charges. "It takes an extended amount of resources, and due to the medical examiner, who did great job in this investigation, they had to seek out outside experts to provide an examination for the child and based on results, they could take several weeks even months," said Detective Jennifer Diaz with the St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office. See also: ICE-held Lake Worth bakery owner faces up to 10 years in prison on illegal reentry charge A neighbor, Suzan, who lives across the street from the home, says she had concerns about the children’s living conditions and believes the arrests are long overdue. "It was just a blessing in disguise because now I know the kids are safe," she said. "I'm going to keep them in prayer." Suzan said two of the boys would knock on her door and she would give them food and something to drink. The kids were so hungry and starving. The child, clothes didn't ever get changed," Suzan said. I love children." Suzan said sheets of plywood covered holes in the mobile home's floor. "I've been inside the house and it was unlivable," she said. "The boards that's out there now, are the boards that was on the floor." Detective Jennifer Diaz was one of the investigators who worked on the case. She described the horrific conditions inside the mobile home. "The house was extremely hot," she said. "There was a bug infestation in the home, lack of food in the home, and the home was unsafe for walking." Investigators said on Aug. 20, 2025, the three-month old was rushed to the hospital after the boy's grandfather messaged the mother saying the child was sick but it was too late. "This was one that I think was very hard," Diaz said. "The way the child ended one of their last days of life was probably the saddest for me." Investigators say Maxwell’s four other children also needed medical attention at the time and are now in foster care. The sheriff’s office says child protective services had previously been called to the home and is reminding the public to report any suspected child abuse or neglect. Sheriff Richard Del Toro sent a statement following the arrests that reads in part: While justice is essential, our shared responsibility must be preventing these tragedies before they occur. Protecting children is not solely the responsibility of law enforcement or the child welfare system. It is a responsibility we all share. If you see signs that a child may be neglected, abused, or living in unsafe conditions, do not assume someone else will intervene. One phone call can be the difference between a child receiving the help they need and a life being saved. This case also reminds us that families facing difficult circumstances are not alone. Resources, support, and assistance are available. My commitment remains unwavering: to seek justice for victims, hold offenders accountable, and work alongside our community to protect our most vulnerable. By recognizing the warning signs, speaking up, and connecting families with the help they need, we can work together to prevent tragedies like this from happening again.

VERO BEACH — For families struggling to find affordable housing, a set of house keys can unlock more than a front door. It can offer stability, dignity and a chance to begin again. That mission drives Indian River Habitat for Humanity. As affordable housing becomes harder to find, many working families are finding homeownership out of reach. For them, Habitat is more than a homebuilder—it is a partner in creating lasting stability. President and CEO Trevor Loomis said the housing landscape has shifted sharply in recent years. Rising costs have outpaced incomes, making homeownership difficult even for families with steady jobs. Some households are doubling up with relatives, while others commute from neighboring counties because they can no longer afford to live where they work. Habitat’s work begins long before construction ends. Loomis said families accepted into the program spend months preparing for homeownership. Through financial education, housing counseling and sweat equity, they build the skills and foundation needed for long-term success. “The house is just part of the equation. What we’re really about is empowerment and opportunity,” Loomis said. For staff, those efforts are reflected in the families they serve. Loomis recalled a father whose life changed after his wife died from cancer. Medical bills, lost income and the loss of their rental home left him and his two children searching for stability. With support from the Samaritan Center, Habitat helped the family regain its financial footing and achieve homeownership. Communications and Advocacy Manager Daniella Dominique has seen similar transformations. “For many of these children, it’s the first room they’ve ever had that’s truly their own. Watching them imagine how they’ll decorate it is something I’ll never forget,” Dominique said. Dominique said those moments are possible because of community support. More than 60 staff members, nearly 720 volunteers, churches, businesses and nonprofit partners contribute to Habitat’s mission. She highlighted partnerships with United Way, United Against Poverty, Hope for Families and the Samaritan Center, which help families access resources throughout their journey. Looking ahead, Loomis said Habitat plans to build more than 170 homes by 2032, including neighborhoods for seniors, veterans and working families across Indian River County. For each family, receiving the keys marks a new beginning—a chance to put down roots and move forward with confidence. For Indian River Habitat for Humanity, the goal remains helping families build a foundation for the future. AI data centers could soon face new federal requirements under legislation backed by Florida Republican U.S. Byron Donalds that aims to prevent rising electricity demand from increasing utility bills for everyday customers.The proposal comes as the rapid expansion of hyperscale AI data centers raises concerns nationwide about strain on the power grid and water resources. The Electric Power Research Institute estimates data centers could consume up to 9% of all U.S. electricity generation by 2030, a sharp increase from current levels.WATCH WPTV'S COVERAGE BELOW:The Trump administration recently announced the “Ratepayer Protection Pledge,” a voluntary agreement involving major technology companies, utilities and state leaders intended to keep the cost of powering new AI facilities from being passed on to residential and commercial utility customers.Donalds’ legislation would move beyond voluntary commitments by creating federal requirements for large-scale AI data centers.Donalds introduced H.R. 9777, known as the “Protecting Ratepayers Act,” which would require hyperscale AI data centers to provide their own power generation and water resources instead of relying on public utilities.Supporters of the proposal say it could help shield customers in Florida and across the country from future utility rate increases tied to growing energy demand from artificial intelligence infrastructure.A spokesperson for Donalds provided WPTV with a statement saying, ““Byron Donalds has been consistent: no ratepayer or environmental protections means no data centers. Byron is legislating and leading on this issue, while Democrat David Jolly is reacting with cheap talk like the washed up MSNBC analyst he is ,” said communications director Gates McGavick.”The legislation comes as companies race to build AI infrastructure capable of supporting growing demand for generative AI systems and cloud computing.The Trump administration’s voluntary Ratepayer Protection Pledge has been signed by several major technology companies, including Amazon, Google, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, Oracle and xAI.Utilities and state leaders have also joined the initiative, according to the administration.The pledge is designed to reassure customers that the expansion of AI-related infrastructure will not automatically lead to higher electricity costs for households and small businesses.Mehran Basiratmand, director of innovations and programs at Florida Atlantic University, said the proposed legislation could address some of the biggest public concerns surrounding AI data centers.Basiratmand previously served as chairperson of the policy board for what he described as the state’s largest data center.“I think it’s clearly a move in the right direction,” Basiratmand told WPTV's Michael Hoffman.He said requiring companies to generate their own power could encourage investment in alternative energy solutions rather than placing added pressure on public infrastructure.“I think as we set up the threshold, law is clearly going to force companies to look at alternative sources,” Basiratmand said. “I do not think it’s going to shift companies to go overseas because we already see significant pushback in many countries on that as well.”Basiratmand added that the proposal could ultimately benefit communities beyond the United States by encouraging more sustainable approaches to powering AI technology.AI companies are rapidly expanding data center construction nationwide as demand grows for artificial intelligence tools, cloud computing and digital services. Utility regulators and lawmakers in several states have increasingly debated whether residential customers could eventually absorb infrastructure costs tied to those projects.Florida leaders have also focused heavily on energy reliability and growth as the state continues to add residents and businesses.WPTV will continue tracking the progress of the Protecting Ratepayers Act through Congress.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. By: Emma Romano Posted PALM BEACH COUNTY, Fla. — Palm Beach County Fire Rescue rescued a cat and a hamster from a house fire Monday night in unincorporated Palm Beach County. Crews responded around 9 p.m. to the 5000 block of Basil Avenue for a reported structure fire, arriving within 3 minutes to find a single-story home with smoke and flames coming from the building. The homeowner told firefighters everyone inside had safely escaped, but one cat was still missing. While some crews attacked the fire, others searched the home and found the black cat hiding inside. Firefighters brought the cat to a waiting rescue unit, where it was given oxygen before being reunited with its owner. Firefighters also safely removed a hamster that was still inside its cage. The fire was quickly brought under control. No injuries were reported, and fire officials determined the fire was accidental.

Lucie County commissioners split evenly on when to schedule a referendum to renew the county's half-cent infrastructure sales tax, voting unanimously to postpone the decision until August 4. The voter-approved tax expires in December 2028 after its 10-year authorization. Commissioners must decide whether to ask voters to extend it in 2026 or wait until 2028. If they wait and voters approve it then, it would be considered a new tax rather than a continuation. Before the commission's discussion on July 21, three Port St. Lucie officials urged the board to place the referendum on the 2026 ballot. Lucie Public Works Director Colt Schwerdt said the tax has funded road, sidewalk, stormwater and water-quality improvements that have benefited city residents. Utility Systems Director Kevin Matyjaszek said there is a direct correlation between infrastructure and quality of life. Communications Director Sarah Prohaska read a letter from Kenneth Kroll, chairman of both the county and Port St. Lucie Sales Tax Oversight committees, who urged commissioners to act this year. Commissioner James Clasby opposed placing the measure on the 2026 ballot, saying he did not want it on the same ballot as Amendment 3 and the School Board tax. Commissioner Erin Lowry agreed, saying many residents are struggling financially and may reject the measure simply because it includes the word tax. Chairwoman Jamie Fowler argued the county would have two opportunities if the measure were placed on the 2026 ballot. Commissioner Cathy Townsend agreed and moved to keep the referendum on the 2026 ballot, but the motion failed on a 2-2 vote. With Vice Chairman Larry Leet absent and the commission deadlocked, members voted 4-0 to continue the item until August 4, when Leet is expected to return and cast the deciding vote. Deputy County Administrator Mayte Santamaria reminded commissioners they had already approved an ordinance in March scheduling the referendum for November 2026. Keeping that date requires no action, while delaying it until 2028 would require rescinding the ordinance and adopting a new one. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office is sharing new details about the investigation into the death of a three-month-old boy in Fort Pierce, including why it took nearly a year to make arrests and the conditions investigators say they found inside the mobile home where the child lived. The infant’s mother, Nicole Maxwell, her father Robert Maxwell, and his girlfriend Vikki Koon were arrested and charged with aggravated manslaughter and child abuse. Investigators say the baby died from dehydration and malnutrition last August, and the medical examiner later ruled the death a homicide. Detectives say the case was complex, requiring outside expertise and months of additional testing before they could move forward with charges. "It takes an extended amount of resources, and due to the medical examiner, who did great job in this investigation, they had to seek out outside experts to provide an examination for the child and based on results, they could take several weeks even months," said Detective Jennifer Diaz with the St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office. See also: ICE-held Lake Worth bakery owner faces up to 10 years in prison on illegal reentry charge A neighbor, Suzan, who lives across the street from the home, says she had concerns about the children’s living conditions and believes the arrests are long overdue. "It was just a blessing in disguise because now I know the kids are safe," she said. "I'm going to keep them in prayer." Suzan said two of the boys would knock on her door and she would give them food and something to drink. The kids were so hungry and starving. The child, clothes didn't ever get changed," Suzan said. I love children." Suzan said sheets of plywood covered holes in the mobile home's floor. "I've been inside the house and it was unlivable," she said. "The boards that's out there now, are the boards that was on the floor." Detective Jennifer Diaz was one of the investigators who worked on the case. She described the horrific conditions inside the mobile home. "The house was extremely hot," she said. "There was a bug infestation in the home, lack of food in the home, and the home was unsafe for walking." Investigators said on Aug. 20, 2025, the three-month old was rushed to the hospital after the boy's grandfather messaged the mother saying the child was sick but it was too late. "This was one that I think was very hard," Diaz said. "The way the child ended one of their last days of life was probably the saddest for me." Investigators say Maxwell’s four other children also needed medical attention at the time and are now in foster care. The sheriff’s office says child protective services had previously been called to the home and is reminding the public to report any suspected child abuse or neglect. Sheriff Richard Del Toro sent a statement following the arrests that reads in part: While justice is essential, our shared responsibility must be preventing these tragedies before they occur. Protecting children is not solely the responsibility of law enforcement or the child welfare system. It is a responsibility we all share. If you see signs that a child may be neglected, abused, or living in unsafe conditions, do not assume someone else will intervene. One phone call can be the difference between a child receiving the help they need and a life being saved. This case also reminds us that families facing difficult circumstances are not alone. Resources, support, and assistance are available. My commitment remains unwavering: to seek justice for victims, hold offenders accountable, and work alongside our community to protect our most vulnerable. By recognizing the warning signs, speaking up, and connecting families with the help they need, we can work together to prevent tragedies like this from happening again.

A suspected drunk driver fled Port St. Lucie police at nearly 80 mph in a 45 mph zone before he and his passenger abandoned their car and ran, with one suspect later found hiding on the roof of an occupied home. A reported hazing incident involving electric shocks at the St. Lucie County Fire District has resulted in the termination of three firefighters and the suspension of two others, prompting widespread debate and calls for reinstatement. Michael Jenkins, a 32-year veteran of the fire district, addressed the St. Lucie County Fire Board last week, voicing his support for the fired firefighters. [related id='aacb275c-7c82-4810-aae3-915d5124b946' align='center' source=''][/related] "I have guys calling me from all over the country right now. I had a Navy SEAL I talked to yesterday. They want to come to the fire board meeting next time and speak in defense of these guys," Jenkins said. The fire district released video footage showing firefighters administering electric shocks to newer employees, which they described as hazing. Two of the terminated firefighters, Chris Baldwin and Jordon Hutchinson, denied the allegations, claiming the actions were not hazing. It's about bringing the family together. No one was coerced into their involvement," Baldwin said. [related id='84b3bf42-2af1-44e8-8bcf-9dc1ae494db2' align='center' source=''][/related] Hutchinson agrees. "It was guys joking around at the station. There was no ill intent whatsoever in it. Every supposed victim and witness said the same thing," Hutchinson added. The fire district's lawyer, Kim Sabol presented a timeline of complaints that led to independent investigations over the past year and a half. "Starting in January of 2025, we received one, two, three, four complaints from January to June," Sabol said. The fire chief followed the recommendations outlined in the investigation report. "Based on his findings and the tie into our rules and regulations and collective bargaining agreement, the discipline that was implemented we feel was appropriate in this case," Sabol said. [related id='dd70389e-88b4-4883-a942-85c2ff2aeb18' align='center' source=''][/related] Jenkins argued that the situation has been misunderstood and pledged to continue advocating for the firefighters' reinstatement. "I think this is a lot of miscommunications, a lot of stuff taken out of context. Lucie County doesn't need this. Taxpayers don't need this. We need to give them guys their jobs back," Jenkins said. Union representatives are expected to address the matter later this week. A 3-month-old died from dehydration and malnutrition after living in a home with boarded windows, exposed electrical wiring and cockroaches, according to court documents and investigators with the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office. The infant's mother, Nicole Maxwell, grandfather, Robert Maxwell and the grandfather's girlfriend, Vikki Koon, now face charges of aggravated manslaughter of a child and aggravated child abuse. WATCH BELOW: 'One of the worst cases': Detective outlines arrest of 3 in baby's death "In my 20 years of law enforcement, this is one of the worst cases I've ever worked," St Lucie County Sheriff’s Office Detective Jennifer Diaz said. The investigation began in August 2025 when investigators responded to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital after the 3-month-old was brought in deceased by Robert Maxwell and Koon. The medical examiner determined the child died from dehydration and malnutrition. Court documents describe the infant's "ribs more prominent than its stomach." "I can tell you the facts of this case don't even paint a picture clear to what we saw at the hospital," Diaz said. Diaz said the child lived primarily with Maxwell and Koon while the child's mother, Nicole Maxwell, lived at her boyfriend's home. Investigators said the child's father lived in Virginia. According to court documents, Koon primarily fed the infant only twice a day and admitted to investigators that when she ran out of formula, she fed the child "watered-down milk with bay cereal mixed in." Other children of Nicole Maxwell were also living in the home, which court documents describe as having windows boarded shut, exposed electrical wiring and live and dead cockroaches throughout. "The living conditions at this time were environmental hazards," Diaz said. A neighbor named Suzan, said she witnessed the conditions firsthand. "It just looked unlivable," Suzan said. Suzan said she would often see one of the other children walking around the neighborhood. "They would come and ask for water, you know. I see the child be thirsty. I mean, not bathe, same clothes every day," Suzan said. Suzan said she is heartbroken thinking about the infant who lived only a few feet away. "Nobody should suffer or go hungry, and especially for a child that didn't ask to come here," Suzan said. Diaz said the Department of Children and Families had been involved with the family before. Nicole Maxwell's other children who were living inside the mobile home are now in foster care. All three suspects faces charges of aggravated manslaughter of a child and aggravated child abuse. "The baby finally got justice," Suzan said. Diaz said emphasized the importance of reporting suspicious activity to protect children. "These tips are so instrumental to keeping our children safe," Diaz said. This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. hero.body:
Three people were arrested Friday, nearly a year after a 3-month-old child died in St. Lucie County. Nicole Maxwell, 27, the child's mother, Robert Maxwell, 61, the child's grandfather, and Vikki Koon, 38, Robert Maxwell's girlfriend, face charges in the case according to the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office.

Deputies, detectives and crime scene investigators responded to Lawnwood Regional Medical Center on Aug. 20, 2025, after the 3-month-old was brought to the emergency room by the child's grandparents. The sheriff's office said medical personnel notified them that the child had been pronounced deceased and exhibited injuries and conditions consistent with possible neglect. The Medical Examiner determined the child's manner of death to be homicide, with the cause of death attributed to dehydration and malnutrition.

Each suspect faces charges of aggravated manslaughter of a child and aggravated child abuse. Bond was set at $1.5 million for each defendant.

Sheriff Richard Del Toro said in a statement that the death of a child is a tragedy that affects the entire community. He commended Detective Corporal Jennifer Diaz for her leadership and thanked the detectives, crime scene investigators, professional support staff, the Medical Examiner's Office and the State Attorneys whose commitment and teamwork led to the arrests.

cards.headline: 100 animals rescued in Martin County hoarding case west of Hobe Sound
cards.teaser: Authorities have rescued 100 animals from a property west of Hobe Sound in what the Martin County Sheriff's Office is calling the worst animal hoarding case it has ever encountered.
cards.body:
Authorities removed 80 cats and 12 dogs from the property on Monday. The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast has since taken in three more cats and five more dogs, bringing the total to 83 cats and 17 dogs. Staff discovered 12 microchips among the animals, 11 in the cats and one in a dog. Only two of those microchips were registered. Investigators traced one chip to its owner, but that person died last year.

Dozens of hopeful pet owners lined up outside the Humane Society Friday morning, hoping to be reunited with their missing animals. Sarah Fisher, spokesperson for the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast, said about 80 people came through between 10 a.m. and 2 p.m., hoping to identify their pets. She said every single one of them left in tears because the organization did not make a single identification.

The Humane Society said this will not be the last chance for people to reclaim their pets. More identification days are planned, and the organization is asking anyone who believes they may have an animal there to submit photos and descriptions to help make a match. Once every effort has been made to reunite the animals with their owners, the Humane Society will begin the adoption process.

hero.headline: Single-family home prices rise across Treasure Coast after two years of declines
hero.body:
Single-family home prices are rising across the Treasure Coast, with every county in the region seeing an increase in median home sale prices. The increases come after price drops from 2023 to 2025.

Martin County median home sale prices are up 1.1% since 2025, sitting at $655,000. St. Lucie County is seeing the highest increase in the region, up 2.3% since June 2025 with a median sale price of $399,000. Indian River County has seen an increase of 1.8%, with a median sales price of $400,000.

Kelley Decowski, an award-winning realtor at REMAX in Stuart, said the increases are being driven by low supply and high demand. Decowski said inventory is low on the Treasure Coast, though the market is currently balanced for both buyers and sellers. Buyers need to be realistic with their offers and come in pre-approved before they go looking at homes. Sellers need to price their homes realistically and present a well-maintained product.

For some Martin County homeowners, the rising prices are reshaping long-term plans. Cara Collins, who bought her home before the COVID-19 pandemic when prices were significantly lower, said she has no plans to sell. Collins said current prices are higher than she would hope for, and that the market has changed what would be possible for her family today. Condos and townhomes show a different trend, with prices dropping in Martin and St. Lucie counties and increasing by less than a percent in Indian River County.

hero.headline: Big Taste of Martin County food and spirits fundraiser returns to Stuart in October
hero.body:
Big Brothers Big Sisters of Palm Beach and Martin Counties will host Big Taste of Martin County on Oct. 6 at Atlantic Aviation in Stuart. The annual fundraiser brings together local restaurants, chefs and community partners to support mentoring programs for children across the Treasure Coast.

Guests can sample food, wine and beer from area businesses while participating restaurants compete for Big Taste awards and local bragging rights. Spritz Stuart plans to feature several menu items during the event, including a Tuscan salmon dish, a smash burger and a specialty cocktail called the Fig & Flame.

Big Brothers Big Sisters of Palm Beach and Martin Counties said the event helps fund mentorship opportunities for children who are currently waiting to be matched with a mentor, known as a Big. The nonprofit serves children and families throughout Palm Beach and Martin counties through one-on-one mentoring relationships designed to support academic achievement, confidence and personal growth.

Community members can support the mission by purchasing tickets, attending the event or volunteering to become a mentor. More information about the event and mentorship opportunities is available through Big Brothers Big Sisters of Palm Beach and Martin Counties.

hero.headline: Florida spiny lobster mini season opens Wednesday with strict two-day harvest window
hero.body:
Florida's spiny lobster sport season returns Wednesday, July 29 through Thursday, July 30, offering recreational divers and snorkelers a two-day opportunity to harvest the prized crustaceans. The annual event occurs on the last consecutive Wednesday and Thursday of July each year and is open to both Florida residents and non-residents. The Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission enforces strict bag limits that vary by location, with Monroe County and Biscayne National Park restricted to 6 lobsters per person per day, while the rest of Florida waters allow 12 lobsters per person per day. Possession limits on the water equal the daily bag limit, while off-water possession on July 29 equals the daily bag limit and doubles on July 30 to either 12 or 24 depending on location.

All harvested spiny lobsters must meet Florida's minimum size requirement, with carapace length exceeding 3 inches when measured in water. Possession and use of an approved measuring device is mandatory at all times, and all measurements must be taken while the lobster is still in the water. Night diving is prohibited in Monroe County during the sport season only, with the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission defining diving as swimming at or below the water surface. This restriction applies exclusively to Monroe County waters during the July 29-30 sport season.

Several areas remain completely off-limits to lobster harvesting, including John Pennekamp Coral Reef State Park, Everglades National Park, Dry Tortugas National Park, Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary no-take zones, Biscayne Bay/Card Sound Lobster Sanctuary, and five Coral Reef Protection Areas in Biscayne National Park. Popular diving destinations open to harvesting include Florida Keys locations outside prohibited areas, Miami-Dade County waters, Broward County reefs, and Palm Beach County diving spots. The 2026 mini season attracts thousands of recreational harvesters to these coastal locations.

Participants must possess a valid Florida saltwater fishing license, spiny lobster permit if required, approved measuring gauge, dive flag and proper safety equipment, and a cooler with ice for proper storage. According to the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission, spiny lobster mini season generates significant economic activity for coastal communities while supporting conservation efforts. The strict regulations, including size limits and seasonal restrictions, help maintain healthy lobster populations for both recreational and commercial harvesting.

cards.headline: Florida credit card holders take 12 months to pay off debt, ranking 30th nationwide
cards.teaser: Florida ranks in the middle of states for credit card payoff times, with residents carrying an average of $3,087 in debt and paying nearly $350 in interest charges.
cards.body:
Florida credit card holders are taking about a year to pay off their debt, according to a WalletHub study that placed the state 30th among states where it takes the longest to eliminate credit card balances. The typical Florida cardholder carries $3,087 in credit card debt and pays nearly $350 in interest charges while working to pay it off. The analysis found it takes the average Floridian 12 months to become debt-free from their credit cards.

The findings come as Americans nationwide are struggling with mounting credit card debt, with experts projecting total U.S. credit card debt will reach approximately $100 billion this year. For Florida families already dealing with rising costs of living, the data highlights the growing financial pressure many households face when managing everyday expenses on credit.

hero.headline: 100 animals rescued in worst hoarding case Martin County has ever seen, owners search for missing pets
hero.body:
Authorities have rescued 100 animals from a property west of Hobe Sound in what the Martin County Sheriff's Office is calling the worst animal hoarding case it has ever encountered. On Monday, authorities removed 80 cats and 12 dogs from the property. The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast has since taken in three more cats and 5 more dogs, bringing the total to 83 cats and 17 dogs.

Staff discovered 12 microchips among the animals, 11 in the cats and one in a dog. Only two of those microchips were registered. Investigators traced one chip to its owner, but that person died last year.

Dozens of hopeful pet owners lined up outside the Humane Society Friday morning, hoping to be reunited with their missing animals. Sarah Fisher, spokesperson for the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast, said about 80 people came through between 10 a.m. and 2 p.m., hoping to identify their pets. Every single one of them left in tears. The organization did not make a single identification.

The Humane Society said this will not be the last chance for people to reclaim their pets. More identification days are planned, and the organization is asking anyone who believes they may have an animal there to submit photos and descriptions to help make a match. Once every effort has been made to reunite the animals with their owners, the Humane Society will begin the adoption process.

hero.headline: Treasure Coast home prices rise after two-year decline, with St. Lucie County up 2.3%
hero.body:
Single-family home prices are rising across the Treasure Coast after dropping from 2023 to 2025. Martin County median home sale prices are up 1.1% since 2025, sitting at $655,000. St. Lucie County is seeing the highest increase in the region, up 2.3% since June 2025 with a median sale price of $399,000. Indian River County has seen an increase of 1.8%, with a median sales price of $400,000.

Kelley Decowski, an award-winning realtor at REMAX in Stuart, said the increases are being driven by low supply and high demand. Decowski said buyers should start making decisions now because there are no signs that the prices are going to come back down and they are probably going to continue to increase. She said inventory is low on the Treasure Coast, though the market is currently balanced for both buyers and sellers.

Decowski said buyers need to be realistic with their offers and need to come in pre-approved before they go looking at homes. Sellers need to price their homes realistically and need to present a well-maintained product. For some Martin County homeowners, the rising prices are reshaping long-term plans.

Cara Collins, who bought her home before the COVID-19 pandemic when prices were significantly lower, said she has no plans to sell. Collins said this is going to be her family home as long as the market is still as high as it is. She said current prices are higher than she would hope for and that the market has changed what would be possible for her family today. Collins said she would not be able to be a stay-at-home mom and be able to afford a home for her kids if they would be buying now. Condo and townhome prices have dropped in Martin and St. Lucie counties and increased by less than a percent in Indian River County.

cards.headline: 100 animals rescued from Martin County hoarding case as owners search for missing pets
cards.teaser: Authorities have rescued 100 animals from a property west of Hobe Sound in what the Martin County Sheriff's Office is calling the worst animal hoarding case it has ever encountered.
cards.body:
Authorities removed 80 cats and 12 dogs from the property on Monday. The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast has since taken in three more cats and 5 more dogs, bringing the total to 83 cats and 17 dogs. Staff discovered 12 microchips among the animals, 11 in the cats and one in a dog. Only two of those microchips were registered. Investigators traced one chip to its owner, but that person died last year.

Dozens of hopeful pet owners lined up outside the Humane Society Friday morning, hoping to be reunited with their missing animals. Sarah Fisher, spokesperson for the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast, said about 80 people came through between 10 a.m. and 2 p.m., hoping to identify their pets. Unfortunately, every single one of them left in tears. They did not make a single identification.

The Humane Society said this will not be the last chance for people to reclaim their pets. More identification days are planned, and the organization is asking anyone who believes they may have an animal there to submit photos and descriptions to help make a match. Once every effort has been made to reunite the animals with their owners, the Humane Society will begin the adoption process.

cards.headline: 100 animals rescued in Martin County's worst hoarding case, owners search for missing pets
cards.body:
Authorities have rescued 100 animals from a property west of Hobe Sound in what the Martin County Sheriff's Office is calling the worst animal hoarding case it has ever encountered. On Monday, authorities removed 80 cats and 12 dogs from the property. The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast has since taken in three more cats and 5 more dogs, bringing the total to 83 cats and 17 dogs.

Staff discovered 12 microchips among the animals, 11 in the cats and one in a dog. Only two of those microchips were registered. Investigators traced one chip to its owner, but that person died last year.

Dozens of hopeful pet owners lined up outside the Humane Society Friday morning, hoping to be reunited with their missing animals. About 80 people came through between 10 a.m. and 2 p.m., hoping to identify their pets, according to Sarah Fisher, spokesperson for the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast. Every single one of them left in tears, as the organization did not make a single identification.

The Humane Society said more identification days are planned, and the organization is asking anyone who believes they may have an animal there to submit photos and descriptions to help make a match. Once every effort has been made to reunite the animals with their owners, the Humane Society will begin the adoption process.

hero.headline: Three arrested in St. Lucie County death of 3-month-old who died from dehydration and malnutrition
hero.body:
Three people were arrested Friday, nearly a year after a 3-month-old child died in St. Lucie County. The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office announced the arrests in a Facebook post. Those facing charges are Nicole Maxwell, 27, the child's mother, Robert Maxwell, 61, the child's grandfather, and Vikki Koon, 38, who is Robert Maxwell's girlfriend.

Deputies, detectives and crime scene investigators with the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office responded to Lawnwood Regional Medical Center on Aug. 20, 2025, after the 3-month-old was brought to the emergency room by the child's grandparents. The sheriff's office said they were notified by medical personnel that the child had been pronounced deceased and exhibited injuries and conditions consistent with possible neglect. The Medical Examiner determined the child's manner of death to be homicide, with the cause of death attributed to dehydration and malnutrition.

Each suspect faces charges of aggravated manslaughter of a child and aggravated child abuse. Bond was set at $1.5 million for each defendant.

Sheriff Richard Del Toro said in a statement that the death of a child is a tragedy that affects the entire community. He commended Detective Corporal Jennifer Diaz for her leadership and thanked the detectives, crime scene investigators, professional support staff, the Medical Examiner's Office, and the State Attorneys whose commitment and teamwork led to the arrests.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County sees highest home price increase on Treasure Coast, up 2.3% to $399,000
cards.teaser: Single-family home prices are rising across the Treasure Coast after drops from 2023 to 2025. St. Lucie County is seeing the highest increase in the region.
cards.body:
St. Lucie County is seeing the highest increase in the region, up 2.3% since June 2025 with a median sale price of $399,000. Martin County median home sale prices are up 1.1% since 2025, sitting at $655,000. Indian River County has seen an increase of 1.8%, with a median sales price of $400,000.

Kelley Decowski, an award-winning realtor at REMAX in Stuart, said the increases are being driven by low supply and high demand. Decowski said buyers should start making decisions now because there are no signs that the prices are going to come back down. Decowski said inventory is low on the Treasure Coast, though the market is currently balanced for both buyers and sellers.

Prices have dropped for condos and townhomes in Martin and St. Lucie counties and increased by less than a percent in Indian River County.

hero.headline: Florida spiny lobster mini season opens Wednesday for two-day harvest
hero.teaser: The annual spiny lobster sport season runs July 29-30, offering recreational divers and snorkelers two days to harvest the prized crustaceans under strict size and bag limits.
hero.body:
Florida's spiny lobster sport season runs Wednesday, July 29 through Thursday, July 30. The annual event occurs on the last consecutive Wednesday and Thursday of July each year, welcoming both Florida residents and non-residents to harvest spiny lobsters.

Bag limits vary by location. Monroe County and Biscayne National Park allow 6 lobsters per person per day, while the rest of Florida waters allow 12 lobsters per person per day. Possession limits off the water on July 29 equal the daily bag limit, but on July 30, harvesters may possess double the daily bag limit. All harvested spiny lobsters must have a carapace length exceeding 3 inches when measured in water, and possession of an approved measuring device is mandatory at all times.

Night diving is prohibited in Monroe County during the sport season only. Several areas remain closed to harvesting, including John Pennekamp Coral Reef State Park, Everglades National Park, Dry Tortugas National Park, Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary no-take zones, Biscayne Bay/Card Sound Lobster Sanctuary, and five Coral Reef Protection Areas in Biscayne National Park. The Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission enforces the regulations to maintain healthy lobster populations for both recreational and commercial harvesting.

cards.headline: Florida credit card holders take 12 months to pay off debt, ranking middle nationwide
cards.teaser: Florida ranks 30th among states where it takes the longest to eliminate credit card balances, with the typical cardholder carrying $3,087 in debt.
cards.body:
Florida credit card holders are taking about a year to pay off their debt, according to a new WalletHub analysis that places the state 30th among states where it takes the longest to eliminate credit card balances. The typical Florida cardholder carries $3,087 in credit card debt and pays nearly $350 in interest charges while working to pay it off.

The analysis found it takes the average Floridian 12 months to become debt-free from their credit cards. Experts project total U.S. credit card debt will reach approximately $100 billion this year. For Florida families already dealing with rising costs of living, the data highlights the growing financial pressure many households face when managing everyday expenses on credit.
