cards.headline: Health insurers reverse denials after media scrutiny, raising questions about approval process
cards.teaser: Florida patients denied coverage for cancer treatments, surgeries, and medications have seen denials reversed only after journalists began investigating their cases, with insurers offering no explanation for the sudden changes.
cards.body:
Since 2025, Florida patients denied insurance coverage for doctor-recommended procedures have had those denials reversed only after media scrutiny, with no explanation from insurers. Madeline Rogers of Zephyrhills was denied coverage for colon surgery three times, Mary Barnes, a breast cancer patient in St. Pete, was forced to halt chemotherapy treatments, and Broxley Bunt of West Palm Beach was denied coverage for surgery to remove a brain tumor. In each case, the denial was reversed only after reporting began.

United Healthcare reversed coverage for Barnes' breast cancer chemotherapy treatments after originally claiming her doctor-recommended treatments, which included immunotherapy, do not meet national cancer guidelines. The company then changed the designation to medically necessary. Dr. Bill Hennessey, a physician turned patient advocate, said denials are reversed when patients are correct and complain. Hennessey attributed the reversals to the power of the press, stating insurers do not want negative public relations.

Federal data recently analyzed by KFF found most health insurance claims are ultimately approved, but the data does not show how many claims are denied first since insurers only report the final outcome. Most patients who are denied never appeal. A spokesperson for AHIP, the nation's largest health insurance trade group, provided a statement but offered no specific explanation for why denials are reversed after media contact.
cards.article_text: HEALTH INSURANCE DENIALS AND "THE POWER OF THE PRESS"Since 2025, we've been investigating the cases of Florida patients denied insurance coverage for doctor-recommended procedures, including cancer treatments, medications and life-saving surgeries.In case after case, those denials were reversed only after we started asking questions, with no explanation from insurers.Watch report from Katie LagroneMadeline Rogers of Zephyrhills was denied coverage for colon surgery three times. Mary Barnes, a breast cancer patient in St. Pete, was forced to halt her chemotherapy treatments and Broxley Bunt of West Palm Beach was diagnosed with a brain tumor when he was denied coverage for surgery to get it removed.These are just a few of the stories we've shared as part of our ongoing, award-winning "Patient No More" series.DENIALS GET REVERSED WITH LITTLE TO NO EXPLANATIONBut in each case, the denial was reversed only after our reporting began — and even then, the insurance company offered no explanation for the sudden change."I was shocked. I was floored to hear from them so quickly," Rogers said after learning the $150,000 colon surgery would be covered after Investigative Reporter Kylie McGiven contacted Oscar Health about the denial."It's a relief, but why the hell do you have to go through this to get them to do what they're supposed to do to begin with?" Mary Barnes questioned after Investigative Reporter Katie LaGrone told her United Healthcare would, in fact, cover her breast cancer chemotherapy treatments after they originally denied it.United originally claimed her doctor-recommended treatments, which included immunotherapy treatments, do not meet "national cancer guidelines" but then changed the designation to "medically necessary."REASONS FOR A DENIAL AND A SUBSEQUENT APPROVALDr. Bill Hennessey is a physician turned patient advocate who helps people appeal insurance denials and negotiate medical bills.He says most denials fall into three categories:Cost of care is too highA treatment isn't ‘medically necessary'Or a treatment is ‘experimental'When asked under what conditions most insurance companies reverse their denials, Hennessey was direct."It'll happen if, number one, you're right and number two, you complain," Hennessey said.As for why several denial cases we investigated ended up being reversed with no explanation, Hennessey summed it up like this: "Well, it's one of two things. You're either a miracle worker like Jesus, or you are correct. It is the power of the press. They don't want the negative public relations," Hennessey said.Federal data recently analyzed by KFF, the leading health policy organization in the U.S., found most health insurance claims are ultimately approved — but the data doesn't show how many claims are denied first, since insurers only report the final outcome.That's significant because most patients who are denied never appeal.Broxley Bunt was initially denied coverage for surgery to remove a meningioma brain tumor because his surgeon was out of network. His insurer, Florida Blue, reversed the denial after Reporter LaGrone started interviewing him from his hospital room where he underwent the surgery anyway."I don't think I could have done it on my own," Bunt said in response to the sudden reversal.Mark Armstrong recently got his blood cancer medication covered after his insurer, Oscar Health, wanted him to pay thousands of dollars up front as part of a "co-pay accumulator" policy."I HONESTLY BELIEVE IT'S BECAUSE YOU REACHED OUT TO THEM"But, according to a federal court ruling, Armstrong should have been exempt from this policy since the medication did not have a generic equivalent. LaGrone questioned Oscar about the exemption, and only then did the insurer make his medication available at no cost.His wife, Michele, believes the media scrutiny made all the difference."I honestly believe it's because you reached out to them. I think they're scared," she said.Patient Mary Barnes echoed that sentiment after her denial for chemotherapy treatment was reversed following our phone calls to her insurer."I really believe that if you wouldn't be doing what you're doing, they would still be denying me," Barnes said.HEALTH INSURANCE INDUSTRY RESPONDS (SORT OF?)In response to questions about how the health insurance industry responds to public scrutiny, a spokesperson for AHIP, the nation's largest health insurance trade group, responded with the following statement:Hennessey said patients must continue to fight and speak up."We just got to fight and fight and fight and publicize and publicize and talk to people like you. This is what I call a twisted sister moment. We're not going to take it anymore," Hennessey said.WHAT TO DO IF YOU'RE DENIEDIf you are denied a treatment your doctor recommends, don't assume the answer is final. Appeal the decision, ask questions and don't be afraid to take your story public by contacting the media or taking your story to social media. Hennessay shares advice on how to challenge a health insurance denial:Make sure to get all your records and itemized bills. Look for inaccuracies and point them out to your insurer.Have your in-network physician document that your care is medically necessary. Be willing to pay them for the time they take to put this in writing.Appeal your denial and submit your doctor's letter with your appeal.Emphasize your clinical situation and the worst-case scenario for your health if you don't get the procedure or treatment your doctor is recommendingIf your insurer engages in a peer-to-peer review, make sure the doctor your insurer is using for this review has the same specialty needed for your care. So, if your condition requires a neurosurgeon, then the insurance company should have a neurosurgeon reviewing the case with your neurosurgeon.Finally, go public with your denial. Tell your story on social media and your local news station. Get your message and your denial out there!CONTACT ME! hero.headline: Three arrested in St. Lucie County death of 3-month-old who died from dehydration and malnutrition
hero.body:
Three people were arrested Friday, nearly a year after a 3-month-old child died in St. Lucie County. Nicole Maxwell, 27, the child's mother, Robert Maxwell, 61, the child's grandfather, and Vikki Koon, 38, who is Robert Maxwell's girlfriend, each face charges of aggravated manslaughter of a child and aggravated child abuse. Bond was set at $1.5 million for each defendant.

Deputies, detectives and crime scene investigators with the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office responded to Lawnwood Regional Medical Center on Aug. 20, 2025, after the 3-month-old was brought to the emergency room by the child's grandparents. The sheriff's office said they were notified by medical personnel that the child had been pronounced deceased and exhibited injuries and conditions consistent with possible neglect. The Medical Examiner determined the child's manner of death to be homicide, with the cause of death attributed to dehydration and malnutrition.

Sheriff Richard Del Toro said the death of a child is a tragedy that affects the entire community. He commended Detective Corporal Jennifer Diaz for her leadership and thanked the detectives, crime scene investigators, professional support staff, the Medical Examiner's Office, and the State Attorneys whose commitment and teamwork led to the arrests.

The sheriff's office said its responsibility is to pursue the truth, protect those who cannot protect themselves, and hold those responsible accountable. The investigation spanned nearly 12 months before the arrests were made Friday.

cards.headline: 100 animals rescued in Martin County hoarding case west of Hobe Sound, dozens search for missing pets
cards.teaser: Authorities have rescued 100 animals from a property west of Hobe Sound in what the Martin County Sheriff's Office is calling the worst animal hoarding case it has ever encountered. Dozens of hopeful pet owners lined up outside the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast Friday morning hoping to be reunited with their missing animals.
cards.body:
The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast has taken in 83 cats and 17 dogs from the property. Staff discovered 12 microchips among the animals, with 11 in cats and one in a dog. Only two of those microchips were registered. Investigators traced one chip to its owner, but that person died last year.

At 10 o'clock Friday morning, a line wrapped around the Humane Society building. About 80 people came through between 10 a.m. and 2 p.m., hoping to identify their pets, said Sarah Fisher, spokesperson for the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast. Every single one of them left in tears because the organization did not make a single identification.

The Humane Society said this will not be the last chance for people to reclaim their pets. More identification days are planned, and the organization is asking anyone who believes they may have an animal there to submit photos and descriptions to help make a match. Once every effort has been made to reunite the animals with their owners, the Humane Society will begin the adoption process.

hero.headline: Indian River County home prices rise 1.8% as Treasure Coast housing market rebounds
hero.body:
Single-family home prices are rising across the Treasure Coast after price drops from 2023 to 2025. Indian River County has seen an increase of 1.8%, with a median sales price of $400,000. Martin County median home sale prices are up 1.1% since 2025, sitting at $655,000. St. Lucie County is seeing the highest increase in the region, up 2.3% since June 2025 with a median sale price of $399,000.

Kelley Decowski, an award-winning realtor at REMAX in Stuart, said the increases are being driven by low supply and high demand. Decowski said buyers should start making decisions now because there are no signs that the prices are going to come back down. Decowski said inventory is low on the Treasure Coast, though the market is currently balanced for both buyers and sellers.

Decowski said buyers need to be realistic with their offers and come in pre-approved before they go looking at homes. Sellers need to price their homes realistically and present a well-maintained product, Decowski said. Cara Collins, who bought her Martin County home before the COVID-19 pandemic when prices were significantly lower, said she has no plans to sell. Collins said this is going to be her family home as long as the market's still as high as it is.

Condo and townhome prices have dropped in Martin and St. Lucie counties and only increased by less than a percent in Indian River County. Collins said she wouldn't be able to be a stay-at-home mom and be able to afford a home for her kids if her family would be buying now. Decowski said that means buyers need to come in pre-approved before they go looking at homes, and sellers need to price their homes realistically.

hero.headline: Big Taste of Martin County returns Oct. 6 in Stuart to support youth mentoring programs
hero.body:
Big Brothers Big Sisters of Palm Beach and Martin Counties will host Big Taste of Martin County on Oct. 6 at Atlantic Aviation in Stuart. The annual fundraiser brings together local restaurants, chefs and community partners to support mentoring programs for children across the Treasure Coast.

Guests can sample food, wine and beer from area businesses while participating restaurants compete for Big Taste awards and local bragging rights. Spritz Stuart plans to feature several menu items during the event promotion, including a Tuscan salmon dish, a smash burger and a specialty cocktail called the Fig & Flame.

Big Brothers Big Sisters of Palm Beach and Martin Counties said the event helps fund mentorship opportunities for children who are currently waiting to be matched with a mentor, known as a Big. The nonprofit serves children and families throughout Palm Beach and Martin counties through one-on-one mentoring relationships designed to support academic achievement, confidence and personal growth.

Community members can support the mission by purchasing tickets, attending the event or volunteering to become a mentor. More information about the event and mentorship opportunities is available through Big Brothers Big Sisters of Palm Beach and Martin Counties.

hero.headline: Treasure Coast home prices rise across all three counties as inventory remains low
hero.body:
Single-family home prices are rising across the Treasure Coast, with every county in the region seeing an increase in median home sale prices. The increases come after price drops from 2023 to 2025.

St. Lucie County is seeing the highest increase in the region, up 2.3% since June 2025 with a median sale price of $399,000. Indian River County has seen an increase of 1.8%, with a median sales price of $400,000. Martin County median home sale prices are up 1.1% since 2025, sitting at $655,000.

Kelley Decowski, an award-winning realtor at REMAX in Stuart, said the increases are being driven by low supply and high demand. Decowski said buyers should start making decisions now because there are no signs that the prices are going to come back down. Decowski said inventory is low on the Treasure Coast, though the market is currently balanced for both buyers and sellers. That means buyers need to be realistic with their offers and come in pre-approved before they go looking at homes, while sellers need to price their homes realistically and present a well-maintained product.

For some Martin County homeowners, the rising prices are reshaping long-term plans. Cara Collins, who bought her home before the COVID-19 pandemic when prices were significantly lower, said she has no plans to sell. Collins said current prices are higher than she would hope for, and that the market has changed what would be possible for her family today. She said she would not be able to be a stay-at-home mom and be able to afford a home for her kids if buying now. Condo and townhome prices have dropped in Martin and St. Lucie counties and only increased by less than a percent in Indian River County.

hero.headline: 3 arrested in death of 3-month-old in St. Lucie County who died from dehydration, malnutrition
hero.body:
Three people were arrested Friday, nearly a year after a 3-month-old child died in St. Lucie County. Nicole Maxwell, 27, the child's mother, Robert Maxwell, 61, the child's grandfather, and Vikki Koon, 38, who is Robert Maxwell's girlfriend, face charges in the case.

Deputies, detectives and crime scene investigators with the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office responded to Lawnwood Regional Medical Center on Aug. 20, 2025, after the 3-month-old was brought to the emergency room by the child's grandparents. The sheriff's office said they were notified by medical personnel that the child had been pronounced deceased and exhibited injuries and conditions consistent with possible neglect. The Medical Examiner determined the child's manner of death to be homicide, with the cause of death attributed to dehydration and malnutrition.

Each suspect faces charges of aggravated manslaughter of a child and aggravated child abuse. Bond was set at $1.5 million for each defendant.

Sheriff Richard Del Toro said in a statement the death of a child is a tragedy that affects the entire community. He commended Detective Corporal Jennifer Diaz for her leadership and thanked the detectives, crime scene investigators, professional support staff, the Medical Examiner's Office, and the State Attorneys whose commitment and teamwork led to the arrests.

cards.headline: 100 animals rescued in worst hoarding case Martin County has seen, owners search for missing pets
cards.teaser: Authorities have rescued 100 animals from a property west of Hobe Sound in what the Martin County Sheriff's Office is calling the worst animal hoarding case it has ever encountered. Dozens of hopeful pet owners lined up outside the Humane Society Friday morning hoping to be reunited with their missing animals.
cards.body:
Authorities have rescued 100 animals from a property west of Hobe Sound in what the Martin County Sheriff's Office is calling the worst animal hoarding case it has ever encountered. On Monday, authorities removed 80 cats and 12 dogs from the property. The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast has since taken in three more cats and 5 more dogs, bringing the total to 83 cats and 17 dogs.

Staff discovered 12 microchips among the animals, 11 in the cats and one in a dog. Only two of those microchips were registered. Investigators traced one chip to its owner, but that person died last year.

Dozens of hopeful pet owners lined up outside the Humane Society Friday morning, hoping to be reunited with their missing animals. Sarah Fisher, spokesperson for the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast, said about 80 people came through between 10 a.m. and 2 p.m., hoping to identify their pets. She said every single one of them left in tears, and that they did not make a single identification. The Humane Society said this will not be the last chance for people to reclaim their pets, and more identification days are planned.

hero.headline: Big Taste of Martin County food and spirits fundraiser returns to Stuart in October
hero.body:
Big Brothers Big Sisters of Palm Beach and Martin Counties will host Big Taste of Martin County on Oct. 6 at Atlantic Aviation in Stuart. The annual fundraiser brings together local restaurants, chefs and community partners to support mentoring programs for children across the Treasure Coast.

Guests can sample food, wine and beer from area businesses while participating restaurants compete for Big Taste awards and local bragging rights. Spritz Stuart plans to feature several menu items during the event, including a Tuscan salmon dish, a smash burger and a specialty cocktail called the Fig & Flame.

Organizers say the event helps fund mentorship opportunities for children who are currently waiting to be matched with a mentor, known as a Big. Big Brothers Big Sisters of Palm Beach and Martin Counties serves children and families throughout Palm Beach and Martin counties through one-on-one mentoring relationships designed to support academic achievement, confidence and personal growth.

Community members can support the mission by purchasing tickets, attending the event or volunteering to become a mentor. More information about the event and mentorship opportunities is available through Big Brothers Big Sisters of Palm Beach and Martin Counties.

hero.headline: Florida spiny lobster mini season opens Wednesday with strict bag limits and prohibited zones
hero.teaser: Florida's spiny lobster sport season runs July 29-30, with different bag limits depending on location and strict regulations for recreational harvesters.
hero.body:
Florida's spiny lobster sport season returns Wednesday, July 29 through Thursday, July 30. The annual event occurs on the last consecutive Wednesday and Thursday of July each year, welcoming both Florida residents and non-residents. Bag limits vary by location, with Monroe County and Biscayne National Park allowing 6 lobsters per person per day, while the rest of Florida waters allow 12 lobsters per person per day. On the water, possession limits equal the daily bag limit. Off the water July 29, limits equal the daily bag limit, while off the water July 30, limits double to 12 or 24 depending on location.

All harvested spiny lobsters must meet Florida's minimum size requirement, with carapace length exceeding 3 inches when measured in water. Possession and use of an approved measuring device is mandatory at all times, and all measurements must be taken while the lobster is still in the water. Night diving is prohibited in Monroe County during sport season only, with the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission defining diving as swimming at or below the water surface.

Several areas are closed to lobster harvesting, including John Pennekamp Coral Reef State Park, Everglades National Park, Dry Tortugas National Park, Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary no-take zones, Biscayne Bay/Card Sound Lobster Sanctuary, and five Coral Reef Protection Areas in Biscayne National Park. Required equipment includes a valid Florida saltwater fishing license, spiny lobster permit, approved measuring gauge, dive flag and proper safety equipment, and a cooler with ice for proper storage.

cards.headline: Florida residents take 12 months on average to pay off credit card debt, new study finds
cards.teaser: Florida ranks 30th among states for longest credit card payoff times, with the typical cardholder carrying $3,087 in debt.
cards.body:
Florida credit card holders are taking about a year to pay off their debt, according to a new analysis from WalletHub that ranks the Sunshine State 30th among states where it takes the longest to eliminate credit card balances. The typical Florida cardholder carries $3,087 in credit card debt and pays nearly $350 in interest charges while working to pay it off.

hero.headline: Indian River County home prices rise 1.8% as Treasure Coast housing market rebounds
hero.body:

Martin County median home sale prices increased 1.1% to $655,000, while St. Lucie County is seeing the highest increase in the region at 2.3%, with a median sale price of $399,000.

Kelley Decowski, an award-winning realtor at REMAX in Stuart, said the increases are being driven by low supply and high demand. Decowski said buyers should start making decisions now because there are no signs that prices are coming back down and they will probably continue to increase. Inventory is low on the Treasure Coast, though the market is currently balanced for both buyers and sellers.

Decowski said buyers need to be realistic with their offers and come in pre-approved before they go looking at homes. Sellers need to price their homes realistically and present a well-maintained product. For some Martin County homeowners, the rising prices are reshaping long-term plans. Cara Collins, who bought her home before the COVID-19 pandemic when prices were significantly lower, said she has no plans to sell.

Collins said current prices are higher than she would hope for, and that the market has changed what would be possible for her family today. She would not be able to be a stay-at-home mom and afford a home for her kids if buying now. Condos and townhomes tell a different story, with prices dropping in Martin and St. Lucie counties and increasing by less than a percent in Indian River County.

hero.headline: Big Taste of Martin County returns to Stuart in October to support youth mentoring
hero.body:
Big Brothers Big Sisters of Palm Beach and Martin Counties is preparing for the return of Big Taste of Martin County, a food and spirits event scheduled for Oct. 6 at Atlantic Aviation in Stuart. The annual fundraiser brings together local restaurants, chefs and community partners to support mentoring programs for children across the Treasure Coast.

Guests can sample food, wine and beer from area businesses while participating restaurants compete for Big Taste awards and local bragging rights. Spritz Stuart plans to feature several menu items during the event promotion, including a Tuscan salmon dish, a smash burger and a specialty cocktail called the Fig & Flame.

The event helps fund mentorship opportunities for children who are currently waiting to be matched with a mentor, known as a Big. Big Brothers Big Sisters of Palm Beach and Martin Counties serves children and families throughout Palm Beach and Martin counties through one-on-one mentoring relationships designed to support academic achievement, confidence and personal growth.

Community members can support the mission by purchasing tickets, attending the event or volunteering to become a mentor. More information about the event and mentorship opportunities is available through Big Brothers Big Sisters of Palm Beach and Martin Counties.

hero.headline: 3 arrested in St. Lucie County after 3-month-old dies from dehydration and malnutrition
hero.body:
Three people were arrested Friday in St. Lucie County, nearly a year after a 3-month-old child died from dehydration and malnutrition. Nicole Maxwell, 27, the child's mother, Robert Maxwell, 61, the child's grandfather, and Vikki Koon, 38, Robert Maxwell's girlfriend, each face charges of aggravated manslaughter of a child and aggravated child abuse. Bond was set at $1.5 million for each defendant.

Deputies, detectives and crime scene investigators with the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office responded to Lawnwood Regional Medical Center on Aug. 20, 2025, after the child's grandparents brought the 3-month-old to the emergency room. Medical personnel notified the sheriff's office that the child had been pronounced deceased and exhibited injuries and conditions consistent with possible neglect.

The Medical Examiner determined the child's manner of death to be homicide, with the cause of death attributed to dehydration and malnutrition. The case required nearly a year of investigation before arrests were made.

Sheriff Richard Del Toro commended Detective Corporal Jennifer Diaz for her leadership in the investigation. Del Toro said the death of a child is a tragedy that affects the entire community and thanked the detectives, crime scene investigators, professional support staff, the Medical Examiner's Office and the State Attorneys whose commitment and teamwork led to the arrests.

hero.headline: Florida spiny lobster mini season opens July 29-30 with strict bag limits, prohibited zones
hero.teaser: Florida's two-day spiny lobster sport season returns Wednesday and Thursday with bag limits of 6 or 12 lobsters per person depending on location.
hero.body:
Florida's spiny lobster sport season runs Wednesday, July 29 through Thursday, July 30, offering recreational divers and snorkelers a two-day opportunity to harvest the crustaceans. The annual event occurs on the last consecutive Wednesday and Thursday of July each year, welcoming both Florida residents and non-residents. Monroe County and Biscayne National Park have a daily bag limit of 6 lobsters per person per day, while the rest of Florida waters allow 12 lobsters per person per day.

All harvested spiny lobsters must have a carapace length exceeding 3 inches when measured in water. Possession and use of an approved measuring device is mandatory at all times, and all measurements must be taken while the lobster is still in the water. Night diving is prohibited in Monroe County during sport season only, with the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission defining diving as swimming at or below the water surface.

Several areas remain closed to lobster harvesting, including John Pennekamp Coral Reef State Park, Everglades National Park, Dry Tortugas National Park, Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary no-take zones, Biscayne Bay/Card Sound Lobster Sanctuary, and five Coral Reef Protection Areas in Biscayne National Park. Harvesters must have a valid Florida saltwater fishing license, a spiny lobster permit if required, an approved measuring gauge, dive flag and proper safety equipment, and a cooler with ice for proper storage.

hero.headline: Martin County home prices rise to $655,000 as Treasure Coast housing market climbs
hero.body:
Single-family home prices are rising across the Treasure Coast after dropping from 2023 to 2025. Martin County median home sale prices increased 1.1% since 2025 to $655,000. Kelley Decowski, an award-winning realtor at REMAX in Stuart, said the increases are being driven by low supply and high demand. Decowski said buyers should start making decisions now because there are no signs that prices will come back down. Inventory is low on the Treasure Coast, though the market is currently balanced for both buyers and sellers.

Decowski said buyers need to be realistic with their offers and come in pre-approved before looking at homes. Sellers need to price their homes realistically and present a well-maintained product. The good news for buyers is that the market is not seeing huge jumps in prices, Decowski said.

For some Martin County homeowners, the rising prices are reshaping long-term plans. Cara Collins, who bought her home before the COVID-19 pandemic when prices were significantly lower, said she has no plans to sell. Collins said she wouldn't be able to be a stay-at-home mom and afford a home for her kids if buying now. Prices for condos and townhomes have dropped in Martin and St. Lucie counties and increased by less than a percent in Indian River County.

hero.headline: Big Taste of Martin County returns to Stuart airport to support youth mentoring programs
hero.body:
Big Brothers Big Sisters of Palm Beach and Martin Counties is preparing for the return of Big Taste of Martin County, a food and spirits event scheduled for Oct. 6 at Atlantic Aviation in Stuart. The annual fundraiser brings together local restaurants, chefs and community partners to support mentoring programs for children across the Treasure Coast.

Guests can sample food, wine and beer from area businesses while participating restaurants compete for Big Taste awards. Spritz Stuart plans to feature several menu items during the event promotion, including a Tuscan salmon dish, a smash burger and a specialty cocktail called the Fig & Flame.

According to Big Brothers Big Sisters of Palm Beach and Martin Counties, the event helps fund mentorship opportunities for children who are currently waiting to be matched with a mentor, known as a Big. The nonprofit serves children and families throughout Palm Beach and Martin counties through one-on-one mentoring relationships designed to support academic achievement, confidence and personal growth.

Community members can support the mission by purchasing tickets, attending the event or volunteering to become a mentor. More information about the event and mentorship opportunities is available through Big Brothers Big Sisters of Palm Beach and Martin Counties.

cards.headline: P1 Motor Club building private racetrack resort community on 650 acres off Okeechobee Road in St. Lucie County
cards.teaser: A new private racetrack resort community is under construction in St. Lucie County, featuring 10 miles of racing circuits designed for street cars, race cars and go-karts.
cards.body:
P1 Motor Club is being built on 650 acres off Okeechobee Road, replacing fairways with racing circuits and welcoming its first drivers this fall. The club features 10 miles of racing circuits designed for street cars, race cars and go-karts. Chris DuPlessis, Director of Fun for P1 Motor Club, said the club is designed for drivers of all ages and skill levels, from kids as young as 8 years old driving go-karts to grandparents driving on track.

The first track under construction is the 3-mile Treasure Coast Track, set to open in October. Over the next six months, crews will continue work on additional circuits, including the flagship 4.5-mile P1 International Circuit. Membership comes with a $192,000 initiation fee and $12,000 in yearly dues. The club already has 260 members.

Construction on a clubhouse and homes for up to 125 residents is scheduled to begin in 2027. The development will also include condos and customizable garages with living spaces situated directly along the tracks. Developers say they want to preserve the character of the region by planting trees, creating lakes, and incorporating natural landscaping throughout the property. P1 Motor Club is expected to be fully completed by 2028.

cards.headline: Martin County Fire Rescue faces $16.5 million loss if property tax reform passes in November
cards.teaser: Martin County Fire Rescue could lose $16.5 million if voters approve property tax reform in November, forcing the department to consider closing stations or eliminating 116 firefighters.
cards.body:
County commissioners are set to discuss what those changes could mean for the fire department in a commission meeting Tuesday. Rick Sterl, president of the Martin County Firefighters Association, IAFF Local 2959, said most of the department's funding comes from the ad-valorem and general fund.

The proposed reform would increase the homestead exemption over two years. Martin County Fire Rescue's presentation outlines two stark options: cut services or cut staff. Cutting services would mean closing fire stations, ending hazmat, dive and technical rescue operations, grounding the critical care helicopter, and using firefighting equipment past its lifespan. Cutting staff would mean eliminating 116 firefighters over two years, roughly 1 in 3 of the firefighters in the department. Sterl said any reductions is going to possibly change the outcome of the level of care and the response time.

Residents in Martin County offered mixed reactions. Joe Vessichio said he does not believe the cuts will happen. Lisa Freitas, owner of Lisa Gay Fashions, said she is concerned about what cuts could mean for public safety. Fire rescue argues no version of the proposal allows the department to remain whole.

cards.headline: Martin County condo and townhome prices drop while single-family homes rise

cards.body:

The good news for buyers is that they are not seeing huge jumps in prices, Decowski said. However, Decowski said buyers should start making decisions now because there are no signs that the prices are going to come back down.

hero.headline: $16,000 Reward Offered as Murder Suspect Isabelle Johnson Remains at Large in Florida
hero.body:
The Walton County Sheriff's Office has announced a $16,000 reward for information leading to the arrest of Isabelle Johnson, 38, who is wanted on an open count of murder in connection with the death of Jason Coulthart. One month after Coulthart's remains were found buried on a Freeport property, investigators released new identifying details Friday in hopes of locating Johnson, who they believe has altered her appearance by cutting and dyeing her hair to avoid capture. The sheriff's office stated that Johnson is believed to have a rose or floral tattoo on her left hand extending from below her thumb toward her index finger, a tattoo on her right ankle, and a large scorpion tattoo stretching from her left buttock down her left thigh.

Coulthart, 43, was reported missing on May 24. His remains were discovered June 25 in a shallow grave on a property off Sunset Lane in Freeport after information developed during a Niceville Police Department missing persons investigation. Authorities later confirmed the remains belonged to Coulthart through DNA testing. The homicide investigation has already resulted in five arrests of individuals accused of helping Johnson evade law enforcement. Bobbi Wagstaff, 31, Martin Leaverton, 63, Sandra Leaverton, 63, Michael Ray White, 74, and Kathleen Morris, 59, have been charged with providing Johnson with shelter, transportation, supplies, cell phones or other assistance after Coulthart's death.

Investigators say Johnson is known to use multiple aliases, including Harley, Jessica Elaine Bowman, Jessica Elaine Thrush, Jessica Elaine Thrash, Jessica Dowdy, and possibly Denise. According to the sheriff's office, she often gains assistance by telling people she is fleeing domestic violence or facing other personal hardships. The Walton County Sheriff's Office emphasized that every lead is pursued, every tip is investigated, and that someone knows where she is.

The reward consists of $11,000 from Emerald Coast Crime Stoppers and the Florida Sheriffs Association Criminal Apprehension Assistance Program, with an additional $5,000 from the U.S. Marshals Task Force under separate reward guidelines. Anyone with information about Johnson's whereabouts is asked to contact the Walton County Sheriff's Office at 850-892-8111. Anonymous tips can be submitted through Emerald Coast Crime Stoppers by calling 850-863-TIPS (8477), online through Emerald Coast Crime Stoppers, or through the P3 Tips mobile app.

cards.headline: Martin County Fire Rescue faces $16.5M loss if property tax reform passes in November
cards.teaser: Martin County Fire Rescue could lose $16.5 million if voters approve property tax reform in November, forcing the department to choose between cutting services or eliminating 116 firefighters.
cards.body:
Martin County Fire Rescue could lose $16.5 million if voters approve property tax reform in November. County commissioners are set to discuss what those changes could mean for the fire department in a commission meeting Tuesday. Rick Sterl, president of the Martin County Firefighters Association, IAFF Local 2959, said most of the department's funding comes from the ad-valorem and general fund.

The proposed reform would increase the homestead exemption over two years. Martin County Fire Rescue's presentation outlines two options: cut services or cut staff. Cutting services would mean closing fire stations, ending hazmat, dive and technical rescue operations, grounding the critical care helicopter, and using firefighting equipment past its lifespan. Cutting staff would mean eliminating 116 firefighters over two years, roughly 1 in 3 of the firefighters in their department.

Sterl said any reductions is going to possibly change the outcome of the level of care and the response time. Fire rescue argues no version of the proposal allows the department to remain whole. Residents in Martin County offered mixed reactions. Joe Vessichio said he does not believe the cuts will happen. Lisa Freitas, owner of Lisa Gay Fashions, said she is concerned about what cuts could mean for public safety.

hero.headline: Treasure Coast single-family home prices rise after two-year decline
hero.body:
Single-family home prices are rising across the Treasure Coast after drops from 2023 to 2025. Martin County median home sale prices are up 1.1% since 2025, sitting at $655,000. St. Lucie County is seeing the highest increase in the region, up 2.3% since June 2025 with a median sale price of $399,000. Indian River County has seen an increase of 1.8%, with a median sales price of $400,000.

Kelley Decowski, an award-winning realtor at REMAX in Stuart, said the increases are being driven by low supply and high demand. Decowski said buyers should start making decisions now because there are no signs that the prices are going to come back down. Inventory is low on the Treasure Coast, though the market is currently balanced for both buyers and sellers.

For some Martin County homeowners, the rising prices are reshaping long-term plans. Cara Collins, who bought her home before the COVID-19 pandemic when prices were significantly lower, said she has no plans to sell. Collins said she would not be able to be a stay-at-home mom and afford a home for her kids if her family were buying now.

Condos and townhomes show a different trend. Prices have dropped in Martin and St. Lucie counties and only increased by less than a percent in Indian River County.

cards.headline: P1 Motor Club building private racetrack resort on 650 acres in St. Lucie County
cards.teaser: A new private racetrack resort community is under construction off Okeechobee Road in St. Lucie County, featuring 10 miles of racing circuits and welcoming its first drivers this fall.
cards.body:
P1 Motor Club is being built on 650 acres off Okeechobee Road, featuring 10 miles of racing circuits designed for street cars, race cars and go-karts. Chris DuPlessis, Director of Fun for P1 Motor Club, said the club is designed for drivers of all ages and skill levels, from 8-year-old kids driving go-karts to grandparents driving on track.

The first track under construction is the 3-mile Treasure Coast Track, set to open in October. Over the next six months, crews will continue work on additional circuits, including the flagship 4.5-mile P1 International Circuit. Membership comes with a $192,000 initiation fee and $12,000 in yearly dues. The club already has 260 members.

Construction on a clubhouse and homes for up to 125 residents is scheduled to begin in 2027. The development will also include condos and customizable garages with living spaces situated directly along the tracks. P1 Motor Club is expected to be fully completed by 2028.

cards.headline: Families reunited with pets after 92 animals rescued from Hobe Sound property
cards.teaser: Families were reunited with their pets Wednesday at the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast after animals were rescued from a Martin County property the sheriff described as the worst hoarding case it has ever seen.
cards.body:
The pets, 80 cats and 12 dogs, were rescued from a property located in the 11500 block of Southwest Meadowlark Circle, west of Hobe Sound, on Monday. Investigators said the home belongs to 77-year-old Gail Giustino. Sheriff John Budensiek said Wednesday was emotional for families who had feared they would never see their animals again.

Linh Nguyen had been searching for her cat Patchy since January. She said she cried so much when she lost him and there were many nights when she could not sleep. She said she was praying to God and asking for a miracle, and when she saw the news on Monday night, she had a very strong feeling. The sheriff's office said a microchip made the reunion possible.

Lori Tucker, the shelter's director of operations, said it is important that the animals are reunited with the correct owners. Anyone who believes their pet may be among those rescued is asked to first file a lost pet report with the Martin County Sheriff's Office. From there, an appointment can be made with the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast.

hero.body:
Single-family home prices are rising across the Treasure Coast after drops from 2023 to 2025. Martin County median home sale prices are up 1.1% since 2025, sitting at $655,000. St. Lucie County is seeing the highest increase in the region, up 2.3% since June 2025 with a median sale price of $399,000. Indian River County has seen an increase of 1.8%, with a median sales price of $400,000.

Kelley Decowski, an award-winning realtor at REMAX in Stuart, said the increases are being driven by low supply and high demand. Decowski said buyers should start making decisions now because there are no signs that the prices are going to come back down. Inventory is low on the Treasure Coast, though the market is currently balanced for both buyers and sellers.

Cara Collins, who bought her Martin County home before the COVID-19 pandemic when prices were significantly lower, said she has no plans to sell. Collins said current prices are higher than she would hope for, and that the market has changed what would be possible for her family today. She said she would not be able to be a stay-at-home mom and be able to afford a home for her kids if buying now.

Condos and townhomes show different trends. Prices have dropped in Martin and St. Lucie counties and only increased by less than a percent in Indian River County. Decowski said buyers need to come in pre-approved before they go looking at homes, and sellers need to price their homes realistically and present a well-maintained product.

hero.headline: Big Taste of Martin County returns to Stuart in October to support youth mentoring programs
hero.body:
Big Brothers Big Sisters of Palm Beach and Martin Counties will host the Big Taste of Martin County on Oct. 6 at Atlantic Aviation in Stuart. The annual fundraiser brings together local restaurants, chefs and community partners to support mentoring programs for children across the Treasure Coast.

Guests can sample food, wine and beer from area businesses while participating restaurants compete for Big Taste awards and local bragging rights. Spritz Stuart plans to feature several menu items during the event, including a Tuscan salmon dish, a smash burger and a specialty cocktail called the Fig & Flame.

Big Brothers Big Sisters of Palm Beach and Martin Counties said the event helps fund mentorship opportunities for children who are currently waiting to be matched with a mentor, known as a Big. The nonprofit serves children and families throughout Palm Beach and Martin counties through one-on-one mentoring relationships designed to support academic achievement, confidence and personal growth.

Community members can support the mission by purchasing tickets, attending the event or volunteering to become a mentor. More information about the event and mentorship opportunities is available through Big Brothers Big Sisters of Palm Beach and Martin Counties.

hero.headline: Florida governor's race heats up as Donalds challenges Jolly to debates, residency lawsuit threatens Fishback ballot spot
hero.body:
Republican front-runner Byron Donalds challenged leading Democratic candidate David Jolly to three general-election debates this fall, even as Donalds continues facing three opponents for the GOP nomination ahead of Florida's Aug. 18 primary. Jolly, a former Republican congressman now running as a Democrat, initially told Donalds to survive his own primary first but later said he would meet Donalds on the debate stage. The exchange gave Donalds' Republican opponents another opportunity to criticize the front-runner for looking beyond them. Donalds has not debated his primary rivals while maintaining sizable advantages in polling, fundraising and endorsements. A recent Cygnal survey showed Donalds at 43%, compared with 12% for businessman James Fishback, 11% for Lt. Jay Collins and 2% for former Florida House Speaker Paul Renner. A separate University of North Florida poll showed Donalds leading Jolly 46% to 41% among likely midterm voters, with a margin of error of 3.8 percentage points.

Fishback spent much of Tuesday defending his place on the Republican primary ballot during a one-day hearing in Leon County. Collins is asking a judge to disqualify Fishback, arguing his Washington, D.C., voting, tax, mortgage and homestead records show he failed to meet the Florida Constitution's requirement that a governor reside in the state for the preceding seven years. Collins' attorneys presented records showing Fishback registered and voted in Washington in 2020, listed D.C. addresses on tax documents and signed mortgage paperwork identifying a condominium there as his principal residence. Fishback acknowledged voting in Washington but testified that he never intended to abandon Florida as his permanent home. Fishback said he arrived at a polling place with his Florida driver's license and did not understand that he was registering as a Washington voter. He also said he did not closely read mortgage documents identifying the condominium as his primary residence.

Circuit Judge David Frank ordered both sides to submit proposed rulings by Friday and said he expects to issue a decision by 5 p.m. The ruling could determine whether Fishback remains on the Aug. 18 ballot. Meanwhile, Gov. Ron DeSantis led a state business-development mission through England and Scotland, where he opened Florida's pavilion at the Farnborough International Airshow and announced that Relativity Space plans to expand its operations at Cape Canaveral. The company plans an additional production facility for its Terran R rocket, along with expanded testing and launch infrastructure at Kennedy Space Center and Cape Canaveral Space Force Station. State officials say the project could create thousands of jobs by 2034, and Relativity Space is eligible for up to $134 million through Florida's Spaceport Improvement Program.

A new UNF poll showed the state's proposed property-tax amendment may be popular enough to pass, depending on how it is described to voters. The proposal would raise the homestead exemption for non-school property taxes from $50,000 to $150,000 in 2027 and then to $250,000 in 2028. The survey initially found 61% support after respondents were told the amendment would reserve property-tax revenue for core public services, narrowly above the 60% approval required for a constitutional amendment. Support fell 16 points, however, after respondents were told the proposal is estimated to create an approximately $11.8 billion municipal budget shortfall over two years. Three lawsuits challenging the amendment's ballot title and summary argue phrases promising to protect small businesses, ensure fairness and preserve core services amount to political advertising instead of a neutral description. A hearing on the ballot-language challenges is scheduled for July 29 in Leon County.

cards.headline: Jellyfish Museum in Pompano Beach showcases medical research advances from ancient sea creatures
cards.teaser: Researchers at the Jellyfish Museum in Pompano Beach have developed an antidote for the potentially fatal sting of box jellyfish and are exploring medical applications including tumor reduction and hemorrhage treatment.
cards.body:
The Jellyfish Museum in Pompano Beach houses thousands of jellyfish in all sizes and shapes, offering visitors a window into some of the ocean's most ethereal and elusive creatures. Researchers at the museum have developed an antidote for the box jellyfish sting, which can kill its prey in 3 to 5 minutes. Museum educator Naphtalie Jeanty, who holds degrees in archaeology and anthropology, said the antidote could represent a breakthrough in treating the potentially fatal stings.

Medical advances at the museum extend beyond antidotes. Collagen harvested from flame jellies has been found to help stop hemorrhages and may appear in bandages in the future. Research into the Japanese sea nettle yielded promising results when a part of the jellyfish was found to shrink tumors in mouse cancer studies, with human cancer treatment as the possible next step.

Jellyfish have been moving through the world's oceans for over 500 million years, predating dinosaurs, trees and fish. Moon jellies can regenerate after being split in half, creating two different versions of themselves. Jellyfish also perform symmetrization, the ability to reorganize their bodies for balance. Some jellyfish scrub out microplastics from the seas, while polka-dotted jellies native to a lake on the island of Palau in the South Pacific work to keep that lake alive. Comb jellies bend light to create a rainbow effect where the light hits them, making it look like lights are running through their bodies.
cards.article_text: And for Naphtalie Jeanty, they were an unexpected career turn she never saw coming.These ocean creatures are an explosion of color and mesmerizing movement that greets visitors at the Jellyfish Museum in Pompano Beach, where thousands of jellyfish in all sizes and shapes offer a window into some of the ocean's most ethereal and elusive creatures.WATCH BELOW: The Jellyfish Museum: Where ancient creatures reveal modern miracles"Even the most inconsequential creature that we can think of is more consequential than we know," Jeanty said.Jeanty holds degrees in both archaeology and anthropology and found her way to the museum through a passion for teaching about flora and fauna."My degree is in archaeology and anthropology, and I've been doing teaching about flora and fauna and after-school programs, so when it's jellyfish museum I was like what you gotta be kidding me," Jeanty said.Seemingly simple sea creatures, jellyfish are quite remarkable.Moon jellies, for example, can regenerate after being split in half."These guys, if you split them in half - the moon jellies will actually create two different versions of themselves and will continue on," Jeanty said.Jellyfish also perform something called symmetrization — the ability to reorganize their bodies for balance."They'll reorganize their bodies for balance — so can you imagine - getting a limb cut off and then suddenly just like there's 45 arms and suddenly there's three and maybe this works better for you?" Jeanty said.When asked whether jellyfish are adaptable, Jeanty did not hesitate."I think that's like the No. 1 thing that they are adaptable," Jeanty said.Jellyfish are also vital to ocean ecosystems.Polka-dotted jellies on display at the museum are native to a lake on the island of Palau in the South Pacific, where they play a critical role."They actually work to keep this lake they live in alive," Jeanty said.Their contributions extend far beyond a single lake."They provide nutrients, they move nutrients, all throughout the ocean, they take out excess ones that don't need to be there," Jeanty said. "It gives people this idea of, oh, like the jellyfish have purpose in the waters."Some jellyfish even scrub out microplastics — among the smallest particles of pollution found in our seas. Others, like those with long, lacy arms, provide transportation for crabs."The crabs will sort of use them as a school bus, like when they're ready to get off they hop off," Jeanty said.Comb jellies add another layer of wonder, bending light to create a stunning optical illusion."They give off this rainbow sort of effect where the light hits them, and then it looks like lights are running through their bodies — which is kind of fascinating," Jeanty said.Jellyfish have been gracefully moving through the world's oceans for over 500 million years, making them some of the oldest living species on Earth — predating dinosaurs, trees and even fish.Despite the name, jellyfish are not technically fish at all."They just got the name ... I think a lot of the world is starting to describe them as just jellies," Jeanty said. "But they are not fish; they don't have the same anatomy."As for predators, jellyfish face threats from sea turtles, birds, fish, other jellyfish, humans, and even sharks.Some jellyfish are completely harmless, but others can be deadly. The box jellyfish can kill its prey in 3 to 5 minutes. Researchers at the museum have developed an antidote for its potentially fatal sting."I think it's going to be a breakthrough," Jeanty said.Other medical advances involve collagen harvested from flame jellies."The collagen has been apparently found to help stop hemorrhages, so we might find that you'll see that collagen in like bandages in the future," Jeanty said.Research into the Japanese sea nettle has also yielded promising results."There's a part of them also that was found to shrink tumors in a mouse cancer, and then so the next step would be possibly human cancer," Jeanty said.Many beachgoers once thought of jellyfish as little more than a nuisance.But a visit to the museum offers a different perspective."You realize that they're an integral part of the whole ecosystem of the oceans," Jeanty said. "And that makes them amazing."This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. hero.headline: St. Lucie County commissioners deadlock on infrastructure sales tax referendum timing
hero.body:
St. Lucie County commissioners split 2-2 on July 21 over whether to ask voters in November 2026 or November 2028 to renew the county's half-cent infrastructure sales tax, which expires in December 2028 after its 10-year authorization. With Vice Chairman Larry Leet absent, the board voted unanimously to postpone the decision until its Aug. 4 meeting, when Leet is expected to return and cast the deciding vote.

Three Port St. Lucie officials urged commissioners to place the referendum on the 2026 ballot before the vote. Public Works Director Colt Schwerdt said the tax has funded road, sidewalk, stormwater and water-quality improvements that have benefited city residents. Utility Systems Director Kevin Matyjaszek said theres a direct correlation between infrastructure and quality of life and that not allowing residents to vote on extending the sales tax is a disservice. Communications Director Sarah Prohaska read a letter from Kenneth Kroll, chairman of both the county and Port St. Lucie Sales Tax Oversight committees, who said approving the referendum in 2026 would provide certainty for long-range planning and ensure continued investment in transportation, stormwater, public safety and environmental projects.

Commissioner James Clasby opposed the 2026 ballot placement, saying he didn't want the measure competing with Amendment 3 and a School Board tax on the same ballot. Commissioner Erin Lowry agreed, saying many residents are struggling financially and may reject the measure simply because it includes the word tax. Chairwoman Jamie Fowler and Commissioner Cathy Townsend argued the county would have two opportunities if the measure were placed on the 2026 ballot. Townsend moved to keep the referendum on the 2026 ballot, but the motion failed 2-2. Clasby's motion to delay it until 2028 also failed 2-2.

Deputy County Administrator Mayte Santamaria reminded commissioners they had already approved an ordinance in March scheduling the referendum for November 2026. Keeping that date requires no action, while delaying it until 2028 would require rescinding the ordinance and adopting a new one. If voters approve the referendum in 2028 instead of 2026, it would be treated as a new infrastructure sales tax rather than a continuation.
hero.article_text: Lucie County Commissioners, from left: Erin Lowry, James Clasby, Cathy Townsend, Larry Leet and Jamie Fowler. FORT PIERCE — With Vice Chairman Larry Leet absent and the remaining four St. Lucie County commissioners split evenly on when to schedule a referendum to renew the county’s half-cent infrastructure sales tax, the board voted unanimously July 21 to postpone the decision until its Aug. The voter-approved tax expires in December 2028 after its 10-year authorization. Commissioners must decide whether to ask voters to extend it in 2026 or wait until 2028. If they wait and voters approve it then, it would be considered a new tax rather than a continuation. Before the commission’s discussion, three Port St. Lucie officials urged the board to place the referendum on the 2026 ballot. Lucie Public Works Director Colt Schwerdt said the tax has funded road, sidewalk, stormwater and water-quality improvements that have benefited city residents. “Our request is to let the residents decide whether or not to continue the sales tax referendum,” Schwerdt said. “Providing for the sales tax referendum provides for long-term planning. We’d like you to continue allowing us to make needed progress on infrastructure projects throughout the county.” Utility Systems Director Kevin Matyjaszek echoed that message. “There’s a direct correlation between infrastructure and quality of life,” he said. “Not allowing residents to vote on extending this sales tax is a disservice. They’re already going to the polls, so let them decide.” Communications Director Sarah Prohaska read a letter from Kenneth Kroll, chairman of both the county and Port St. Lucie Sales Tax Oversight committees, who urged commissioners to act this year. Kroll said approving the referendum in 2026 would provide certainty for long-range planning, allow time for public education and ensure continued investment in transportation, stormwater, public safety and environmental projects. Deputy County Administrator Mayte Santamaria reminded commissioners they had already approved an ordinance in March scheduling the referendum for November 2026. Keeping that date requires no action, while delaying it until 2028 would require rescinding the ordinance and adopting a new one. Chairwoman Jamie Fowler asked whether a failed 2026 referendum could be brought back in 2028. Santamaria said it could, although it would be treated as a new infrastructure sales tax rather than a continuation. Commissioner James Clasby opposed placing the measure on the 2026 ballot. “I don’t want it on the 2026 ballot because there’s Amendment 3 on it and there’s the School Board tax,” he said. “I don’t think it’s a smart idea to put a tax on a ballot where people are being asked to basically eliminate taxes.” Commissioner Erin Lowry agreed, saying many residents are struggling financially and may reject the measure simply because it includes the word “tax.” “I don’t feel people understand it’s a continuation and not a new tax,” Lowry said. “It’s not that we don’t support it — we just want a better opportunity to make sure that it continues.” Fowler argued the county would have two opportunities if the measure were placed on the 2026 ballot. “If I get two chances to win, I’m going to take two chances over one,” she said. “If we wait until 2028 and it doesn’t pass, we’re done.” Commissioner Cathy Townsend agreed and moved to keep the referendum on the 2026 ballot, but the motion failed on a 2-2 vote. Clasby’s motion to delay it until 2028 also failed 2-2. With the commission deadlocked, members voted 4-0 to continue the item until Aug. 4, when Leet is expected to return and cast the deciding vote. Your comment has been submitted. cards.headline: Port St. Lucie cuts property tax rate for 11th consecutive year
cards.teaser: Port St. Lucie City Council approved a property tax rate of 4.8750 for fiscal year 2026-27, down from 4.9750 in the current year, continuing an 11-year streak of annual millage reductions.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie City Council approved a property tax millage rate of 4.8750 for fiscal year 2026-27 at the annual Summer Workshop held July 22-23, a decrease from 4.9750 in fiscal year 2025-26. The budget will be adopted by City Council in September, with public hearings taking place Sept. 3 and Sept. 17. The fiscal year 2026-27 budget goes into effect Oct. 1.

Since 2016, the City has reduced its millage rate by 25 percent, saving the average homeowner nearly $2,000 over a 10-year period. Port St. Lucie has the third lowest municipal tax rate out of Florida's 20 largest cities. The property tax reduction maintains Port St. Lucie's record of steadily reducing its millage rate while managing historic population growth, investing in essential infrastructure and improving public safety.

Residents can learn more about the City's budget, millage rate history and financial planning at CityofPSL.com/budget.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie police find suspect hiding on roof after 80 mph chase
hero.teaser: A suspected drunk driver fled Port St. Lucie police at nearly 80 mph before abandoning his car and running, with one suspect later found hiding on the roof of an occupied home.
hero.body:
Port St. Lucie police officers attempted to stop a white Acura after observing multiple traffic violations and signs of impaired driving. Instead of pulling over, the driver accelerated to nearly 80 mph in a 45 mph zone on Southwest Becker Road. Police said the driver and passenger weaved in and out of traffic, ignored traffic signs and signals, then abandoned the vehicle in a residential driveway near Southwest Idol Avenue before fleeing on foot.

A nearby resident called 911 after seeing the two men run from the scene. Police deployed a K-9 and a drone while officers established a perimeter. Both suspects were located, including one who was found hiding on the roof of an occupied home. The suspects were identified as Joseph Gary Harris, 42, and Bryan Shawn Baker, 46. Harris was charged with fleeing and eluding law enforcement, burglary of an occupied dwelling, resisting an officer without violence and loitering or prowling. Baker was charged with resisting an officer without violence and loitering or prowling.

cards.headline: Armed robbery at Wells Fargo ATM in Fort Pierce forces victim to withdraw cash
cards.teaser: A man using a Wells Fargo ATM in Fort Pierce was forced to withdraw cash at gunpoint Sunday night after two men approached him, one displaying a concealed firearm.
cards.body:
The Fort Pierce Police Department said the robbery happened Sunday at about 8:38 p.m. when two men approached the victim at the Wells Fargo ATM. One of the men displayed a gun concealed in his waistband before forcing the victim to withdraw an unknown amount of cash. The two suspects then fled the scene on foot.

Officers with the Fort Pierce Police Department responded to the scene, established a perimeter and used a K-9 and drone to search for the suspects. The suspects were not located. Police described the suspects as two men in their early 20s, about 5 feet 10 inches tall and weighing about 170 pounds. The armed suspect was last seen wearing jeans and a gray hooded sweatshirt.

cards.headline: 3 arrested in St. Lucie County after 3-month-old dies from dehydration and malnutrition
cards.body:
Three people face charges of aggravated manslaughter of a child and aggravated child abuse after a 3-month-old died from dehydration and malnutrition in Fort Pierce, according to the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office. Nicole Maxwell, the infant's mother, Robert Maxwell, the grandfather, and Vikki Koon, the grandfather's girlfriend, were arrested Monday. St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office Detective Jennifer Diaz said the case is one of the worst she has encountered in 20 years of law enforcement.

The investigation began in August 2025 when investigators responded to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital after Robert Maxwell and Koon brought the 3-month-old in deceased. The medical examiner determined the child died from dehydration and malnutrition. Court documents describe the infant's ribs as more prominent than its stomach. Koon told investigators she primarily fed the infant only twice a day and admitted that when she ran out of formula, she fed the child watered-down milk with baby cereal mixed in.

The child lived primarily with Maxwell and Koon in a Fort Pierce mobile home while Nicole Maxwell lived at her boyfriend's home. Court documents describe the home as having windows boarded shut, exposed electrical wiring and live and dead cockroaches throughout. Detective Diaz said the house was extremely hot with a bug infestation and was unsafe for walking. A neighbor named Suzan said she witnessed the conditions firsthand and described the home as unlivable. She said other children in the home would come to her door asking for water and appeared thirsty, unwashed and wearing the same clothes every day.

Nicole Maxwell's other children who were living inside the mobile home are now in foster care. The Department of Children and Families had been involved with the family before the infant's death. Sheriff Richard Del Toro said protecting children is a shared responsibility and urged the public to report any signs that a child may be neglected, abused or living in unsafe conditions. Detective Diaz said tips are instrumental to keeping children safe.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie opens $28.8 million police training facility
cards.teaser: Port St. Lucie cut the ribbon on a 54,283-square-foot, state-of-the-art police training center on July 24 after four years of construction.
cards.body:
The three-story facility on the Port St. Lucie City Hall grounds includes a 20-lane indoor firearms range, a tactical shoot house with configurable rooms for scenario-based training, a MILO Virtual Simulation Theater for immersive decision-making exercises and a defensive tactics training room equipped with Axon VR technology. The facility also includes three floors of office space supporting the Training Division and Criminal Investigations Division, including 19 offices and 86 workstations.

Port St. Lucie Mayor Shannon Martin said the project ensures officers have the space, training and resources needed to continue serving the community at the highest level. Officer Brittany McNally said officers previously traveled to Indian River State College in Fort Pierce for extensive training. By bringing much of that training in-house, the facility will reduce recurring costs while allowing the department to train more efficiently and effectively. The facility was designed by ADG Architecture and constructed by HJ High. Police personnel immediately began making the move into the new facility after the ribbon-cutting ceremony.
cards.article_text: The recently opened Port St. Lucie Police training center contains a defensive tactics training room equipped with Axon VR technology. The recently opened, 54,283-square-foot, state-of-the-art, $28.8 million police training center is on the Port St. Lucie City Hall grounds, just northwest of the police department. The 54,283-square-foot, state-of-the-art, $28.8 million police training center officially opened on July 24 on the grounds of Port St. Lucie City Hall with a ribbon-cutting for invited guests. The interior of the 54,283-square-foot, state-of-the-art, $28.8 million police training center on the Port St. Lucie City Hall grounds, just northwest of the police department. Lucie city officials who cut the ribbon for the 54,283-square-foot, state-of-the-art, $28.8 million police training center on July 24 were Mayor Shannon Martin, center, and Chief Leo Niemczyk. LUCIE – After four years of construction, the ribbon was cut on July 24 for a 54,283-square-foot, state-of-the-art, $28.8 million police training center on the Port St. Lucie City Hall grounds, just northwest of the police department. “This project is all about making sure our officers have the space, training, and resources they need to continue serving our community at the highest level,” Port St. Lucie Mayor Shannon Martin said in a Facebook posting. Lucie the safest large city in Florida takes more than dedication. It requires planning ahead and making smart investments that prepare our officers for the challenges they face every day.” Included in the three-story facility are: • A 20-lane, 9,508-square-foot indoor firearms range featuring an integrated MILO live-fire scenario system. • A 2,848-square-foot tactical shoot house with configurable rooms for realistic scenario-based training. • A MILO Virtual Simulation Theater for immersive decision-making and de-escalation exercises. • A dedicated defensive tactics training room equipped with Axon VR technology. • A multi-purpose training room designed for classroom instruction, conferences, virtual presentations, and large-scale training. • Three floors of office space supporting the Training Division and Criminal Investigations Division (CID), including 19 offices and 86 workstations. • Advanced audio/visual technology throughout the facility to support collaborative training and instruction. The facility was designed by ADG Architecture and constructed by HJ High, with specialized contributions from industry leaders including Action Target, MILO, Whelen, and numerous additional project partners, according to Port St. As of July 27, the city has a population of more than 260,000. There is a total of 455 employees in the police department with 360 sworn officers, according to city hall records. For years, officers traveled to Indian River State College in Fort Pierce for extensive training, according to Officer Brittany McNally. “By bringing much of that training in-house, this facility will reduce those recurring costs while allowing us to train more efficiently and effectively,” she said in a statement. “Equally important, the new training facility provides our officers with access to state-of-the-art technology and realistic, scenario-based training that better prepares them for the complex situations they may face in the field. From recruit training to advanced tactical instruction and continuing education, our officers will now have the resources needed to sharpen their skills throughout their careers right in our own backyard.” Once the ribbon was cut, police personnel immediately began making the move into the new facility.
