hero.headline: Port St. Lucie bans gas station at Tradition development site after months of resident concerns
hero.body:
The Port St. Lucie City Council unanimously approved a permanent ban on gas stations at a 9.4-acre commercial parcel at the southwest corner of Crosstown Parkway and Fairgreen Drive. The council voted July 13 to finalize the 16th amendment to the Tradition Master Planned Unit Development, ending nearly three months of debate that began when Winding River Crosstown LLC requested permission to convert the site from residential to commercial use.

The amendment changes the parcel designation from residential to commercial while permanently prohibiting any current or future owner from developing a service station on the property. The restriction was added after Vice Mayor Jolien Caraballo and other council members raised concerns during a May 26 hearing that a convenience store with gas pumps would worsen traffic along Crosstown Parkway west of Interstate 95. The council initially tabled the request to allow staff time to review whether gas stations could be eliminated as a permitted use.

Several Heritage Oaks residents urged the council during a June 22 hearing to reject the land-use change, citing concerns about increased traffic, noise and neighborhood impacts. The developer agreed to permanently relinquish the right to build a gas station, and the council voted 4-0 to approve the commercial designation on first reading. City planner Bridget Kean said the restriction is now written directly into the Tradition MPUD documents, ensuring no future owner can develop a gas station on the parcel.

Councilman Anthony Bonna defended the decision at the July 13 meeting, saying expanding commercial development will benefit residents by broadening the city's tax base. Bonna said Port St. Lucie has long lacked commercial development, which places a burden on homeowners. Before any mass grading begins, the developer must install a fence along the southern property line to prevent construction access through Southwest Glenbrook Drive. An architectural wall and landscape buffering must be completed along the southeastern and southern boundaries before the first building permit is issued for vertical construction.
hero.article_text: The aerial view of the 9.4-acre parcel of the Tradition Master Planned Unit Development at the southwest corner of Crosstown Parkway and Fairgreen Drive in Port St. The land-use map of the 9.4-acre parcel of the Tradition Master Planned Unit Development at the southwest corner of Crosstown Parkway and Fairgreen Drive in Port St. LUCIE — After months of debate and neighborhood concerns, the Port St. Lucie City Council has permanently prohibited a gas station from being built on a 9.4-acre commercial parcel at the southwest corner of Crosstown Parkway and Fairgreen Drive. The council unanimously approved the second and final reading of the 16th amendment to the Tradition Master Planned Unit Development on July 13, codifying a restriction that bars any current or future owner from developing a service station on the site. The amendment changes the parcel’s designation from residential to commercial, paving the way for retail and office development while addressing residents’ concerns about traffic and congestion. The issue has been under discussion for nearly three months after Winding River Crosstown LLC requested permission to convert what had been planned as Phase 3 of the Heritage Oaks at Tradition residential development into commercial property. While council members generally supported adding commercial uses to the rapidly growing area, several voiced concerns during the initial May 26 quasi-judicial hearing that a convenience store with gas pumps would worsen traffic along Crosstown Parkway west of Interstate 95. Vice Mayor Jolien Caraballo and other council members noted the increasing congestion along the commercial corridor and asked staff to determine whether gas stations could be eliminated as a permitted use on the parcel. The council tabled the request to allow time for that review. At the time, Councilwoman Stephanie Morgan questioned whether prohibiting a specific type of business amounted to government interference in the marketplace. “What concerns me is that on May 11 we approved two parcels changing from RGC to commercial general,” Morgan said during the May hearing. “We didn’t put any conditions on them. How can you put a condition on an applicant saying no gas stations? That would be like saying no Chick-fil-A because we’ve got enough chicken restaurants.” When the hearing resumed June 22, several Heritage Oaks residents urged the council to reject the land-use change, citing concerns about increased traffic, noise and neighborhood impacts. Instead, the council voted 4-0, with Morgan absent, to approve the commercial designation on first reading after the developer agreed to permanently relinquish the right to build a gas station. During the July 13 meeting, city planner Bridget Kean outlined the changes that formally incorporated the restriction into the Tradition MPUD documents. The updated development plan specifies that while service stations remain a permitted use elsewhere within the mixed-use area, they are prohibited on Parcel 11A. The concept plan also now includes a notation prohibiting a service station on the property, and the ordinance itself was revised to reference the city’s definition of a service station. Staff also added additional protections requested by nearby residents. Before any mass grading begins, the developer must install a fence along the southern property line to prevent construction access through Southwest Glenbrook Drive, which connects to Heritage Oaks. In addition, an architectural wall and landscape buffering must be completed along the southeastern and southern boundaries before the first building permit is issued for vertical construction. Several residents again voiced concerns about the proposal and questioned whether the process had been sufficiently transparent. Councilman Anthony Bonna defended both the public process and the final compromise. “Ultimately, we have to make decisions, and those decisions are not going to satisfy everybody,” Bonna said. “We listen and consider every resident that comes forward, but ultimately we have to make one decision.” Bonna said he believes expanding commercial development will benefit residents by broadening the city’s tax base. Lucie has long lacked commercial, which is a burden on homeowners,” he said. “We have had several hearings here at the city, so that is what transparency is: open meetings where people can come and share their opinions and be a part of the process.” Councilman David Pickett agreed, saying the city has consistently heard residents oppose additional housing. “When this was first introduced, I was very excited that they wanted to go from residential to commercial,” Pickett said. “It doesn’t matter which way we rule, there’s always going to be somebody in opposition. For me, going to commercial is the best possible thing for that corner.” Morgan, who had questioned the gas station restriction during the first hearing, ultimately supported the ordinance. “We have heard from so many community residents — no more housetops,” she said. “It has been transparent, there’s no denying that.” Before the vote, Mayor Shannon Martin asked staff to confirm that the prohibition would remain with the property regardless of ownership. Kean confirmed the restriction is now written directly into the Tradition MPUD documents, ensuring no future owner can develop a gas station on the parcel. The council then voted unanimously to approve the ordinance, ending months of discussion and clearing the way for commercial development while permanently removing a gas station as a future possibility. hero.headline: Vero Beach Museum of Art opens new Jill Nathanson exhibition
hero.teaser: More than 20 works by artist Jill Nathanson are now on display at the Vero Beach Museum of Art in an exhibition running through February.
hero.body:
The Jill Nathanson: Chromatic Phrases exhibition opened July 25 at Vero Beach Museum of Art, 3001 Riverside Drive, Vero Beach. The show features more than 20 works by the artist and runs through February.

Admission is free to members, veterans and active duty military personnel with valid identification. Non-member adults pay $12, seniors 65 and older pay $11, and students with identification pay $5.

The museum is also showing James Prosek: At Work in Holmes Gallery through October 25, consisting of projects that define the artist's first 30 years of artmaking. Another exhibition, American Made, runs through August 16 in Holmes and Titelman Galleries, featuring more than 80 works by artists including Benjamin West, Sarah Miriam Peale, Edward Moran, John Singer Sargent, Mary Cassatt, Robert Henri and Charles Alston.

hero.headline: Big Taste of Martin County returns to Stuart in October to support youth mentoring programs
hero.body:
Big Brothers Big Sisters of Palm Beach and Martin Counties is preparing for the return of Big Taste of Martin County, a food and spirits event scheduled for Oct. 6 at Atlantic Aviation in Stuart. The annual fundraiser brings together local restaurants, chefs and community partners to support mentoring programs for children across the Treasure Coast.

Guests can sample food, wine and beer from area businesses while participating restaurants compete for Big Taste awards and local bragging rights. Spritz Stuart plans to feature several menu items during the event, including a Tuscan salmon dish, a smash burger and a specialty cocktail called the Fig & Flame.

According to Big Brothers Big Sisters of Palm Beach and Martin Counties, the event helps fund mentorship opportunities for children who are currently waiting to be matched with a mentor, known as a Big. The nonprofit serves children and families throughout Palm Beach and Martin counties through one-on-one mentoring relationships designed to support academic achievement, confidence and personal growth.

Community members can support the mission by purchasing tickets, attending the event or volunteering to become a mentor. More information about the event and mentorship opportunities is available through Big Brothers Big Sisters of Palm Beach and Martin Counties.

cards.headline: Recycled fishing line becomes friendship bracelets at Vero Beach Museum of Art
cards.teaser: Coastal Connections and the Vero Beach Museum of Art will transform discarded fishing line into friendship bracelets during a free Second Saturday program beginning at 10 a.m. Aug. 8.
cards.body:
Discarded fishing line will find new purpose as friendship bracelets when art and marine conservation come together at the Vero Beach Museum of Art. The museum and Coastal Connections will team up for a free Second Saturday program beginning at 10 a.m. Aug. 8, with hands-on activities, gallery tours and lessons about protecting local marine life.

Coastal Connections will lead a hands-on activity in the Laura and Bill Buck Atrium, where visitors can make friendship bracelets using recycled fishing line collected from local waterways. Participants also can learn about the organizations Fishing Line Recycling Program. The museum has adopted the fishing line recycling tube at the Riverside Park boat ramp.

Kendra Bergman, founder and executive director of Coastal Connections, said the partnership with the museum is a great example of how the organization is working with the community to introduce everyone to marine conservation and environmental protection in unique ways. Second Saturday includes free museum admission throughout the day. Coastal Connections was founded in 2017 with a mission of advancing the survival of sea turtles by educating and connecting people to the environment.
cards.article_text: Recycled fishing line is transformed into a friendship bracelet during a hands-on activity presented by Coastal Connections at the Vero Beach Museum of Art. VERO BEACH — Discarded fishing line will find new purpose as friendship bracelets when art and marine conservation come together at the Vero Beach Museum of Art. The museum and Coastal Connections will team up for a free Second Saturday program beginning at 10 a.m. 8, with hands-on activities, gallery tours and lessons about protecting local marine life. Activities also include docent-led mini-tours, studio art projects and opportunities to learn about protecting local marine life. Coastal Connections will lead a hands-on activity in the Laura and Bill Buck Atrium, where visitors can make friendship bracelets using recycled fishing line collected from local waterways. Participants also can learn about the organization’s Fishing Line Recycling Program. The museum has adopted the fishing line recycling tube at the Riverside Park boat ramp. to 1 p.m., families can take short, docent-led gallery tours through the Museum Studios family program. Visitors can then participate in “Nature in Layers,” an art activity for children connected to the museum’s exhibitions. Guests also can tour the museum’s summer exhibitions throughout the day. “James Prosek: At Work” is on view in the Holmes Gallery, while “Jill Nathanson: Chromatic Phrases” is displayed in the Schumann and Titelman galleries. “Our partnership with VBMA is a great example of how we are working with our community to introduce everyone to marine conservation and environmental protection in unique ways,” explained Kendra Bergman, founder and executive director of Coastal Connections. “Collaborations like these are key to meeting our mission and watching one of the greatest conservation success stories unfold within our lifetime.” Second Saturday includes free museum admission throughout the day. Additional programs may include performances, lectures, films and other arts and humanities offerings on select Saturdays. Coastal Connections was founded in 2017 with a mission of advancing the survival of sea turtles by educating and connecting people to the environment. hero.headline: Judge rules James Fishback can remain on Florida governor ballot after residency challenge
hero.body:
Republican gubernatorial candidate James Fishback will remain on Florida's Aug. 18 primary ballot after Leon County Circuit Judge David Frank rejected Lt. Gov. Jay Collins' challenge to his residency qualifications. Frank ruled Monday that Collins did not present enough evidence to overcome Florida's legal presumptions favoring continued residency and candidate access to the ballot. The judge wrote that the court will not be deciding the race between the lieutenant governor and Fishback, adding that decision will be in the sound hands of the voters. The final order denies Collins' request to remove Fishback, declares that the Department of State properly certified his candidacy and says Fishback shall remain qualified for the Republican nomination for governor.

Collins sued Fishback in June, arguing the candidate failed to meet the Florida Constitution's requirement that a governor reside in the state for the seven years preceding the election. During an expedited hearing last week, Collins' attorneys presented voter registration, mortgage, tax and homestead records they argued showed Fishback established legal residency in Washington, D.C., between 2019 and 2022. Fishback voted in Washington during the 2020 presidential election, filed D.C. resident income tax returns and signed mortgage paperwork describing a condominium there as his principal residence. Property tax records also showed the condominium received a D.C. homestead deduction. A forensic document examiner testified it was probable Fishback signed the disputed voter registration form.

Frank acknowledged those records could carry consequences outside the Florida candidacy case, writing that it may be true the various election and financial filings could result in regulatory, maybe even more severe legal, repercussions for Fishback under Washington, D.C. law. But the judge found they did not prove Fishback intended to abandon Florida as his permanent home. Fishback testified for several hours that he never intended to move his legal domicile from Florida. He acknowledged signing mortgage paperwork identifying the Washington condominium as his primary residence but said he rushed through the documents without reading them closely. He also characterized his 2020 D.C. vote as an inadvertent registration during the pandemic, saying he was staying with his parents and wanted to vote for President Donald Trump. Frank found Fishback credible on the central issue of intent, stating that despite defendant stating at various points his residence was in Washington, D.C., defendant never had an actual subjective intent to move his permanent residency from Florida.

Fishback's campaign called the ruling a victory for the Constitution and for every Floridian who believes elections should be decided by voters. Collins' attorney Mark Meuser criticized the ruling and argued the court improperly accepted Fishback's explanation that he did not understand the legal significance of his Washington filings. Meuser did not indicate whether Collins plans to appeal the ruling. Unless an appellate court intervenes, Fishback will remain on the Aug. 18 Republican primary ballot alongside Collins, U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds and former House Speaker Paul Renner.

cards.headline: Florida families say Medicaid abruptly stopped covering autism therapy without explanation
cards.teaser: Palm Beach County parents say their children lost access to Applied Behavioral Analysis after Medicaid stopped covering the therapy. Florida's health agency has not explained why.
cards.body:
Palm Beach County parents say their children lost access to Applied Behavioral Analysis after Medicaid abruptly stopped covering it. The Cleveland Clinic describes ABA as a research based behavior therapy for people with autism and other developmental disorders, adding that many studies have proven the effectiveness of ABA. Families connected to Reflection Services ABA Therapy in Lake Worth say they received notice that Medicaid would no longer cover their children's treatment. Daura Mabel Sanchez Cano de Fundora said her son David is classified by his neurologist as level one on the autism spectrum. She described how his vocabulary has been increasingly amazing and he can understand what is happening. Myrian Suarez, a mother of two boys with autism, said ABA gave her son tools to manage his emotions.

Since the therapy stopped, families described dangerous regressions in their children's behavior. Talia Quiroz said she has bites all over her body. Suarez described bruised arms from her son's pinching. Melissa Moran, a registered behavior technician at Reflection Services ABA Therapy, acknowledged the cost of the services but warned of societal repercussions. She said parents may not go to work, affecting the economy, and that some kids have unsafe behaviors including physical aggression and self injurious behaviors that may put themselves and other kids at risk.

Reports of Medicaid cuts to ABA therapy have surfaced in states across the country. The Health and Human Services Office of the Inspector General audited Medicaid spending on ABA in Maine, Michigan, Wisconsin and Colorado, identifying roughly $197.9 million in what it considers improper payments among the four states. A separate audit in Nebraska found yearly Medicaid spending on ABA therapy multiplied 18 times over across a five year period. U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert Kennedy Jr. said during a news conference last week that the administration is not sending Medicaid and Medicare dollars out the door until it has confidence they are being spent lawfully and appropriately.

She described the progress he had made through ABA."His vocabulary have been increasingly amazing. He can understand what is happening," Sanchez Cano de Fundora said. "How you can deny a service that can decide the life of those children and those parents?"Myrian Suarez, a mother of two boys with autism, described the daily demands of caring for her children without adequate support."I have to do everything for them: feed them, bathe them, help them get dressed, comb their hair — everything, everything, everything," Suarez said.She said ABA gave her son tools to manage his emotions."His therapist gives him tools so he can channel the frustration he feels," Suarez said.Talia Quiroz said her daughter Salma was diagnosed with autism at 2 and a half years old. She described the progress Salma made through ABA therapy."She can learn. In fact, things that years before we're not thinking that will be possible," Quiroz said.Since the therapy stopped, Quiroz said she has experienced dangerous regressions in her daughter's behavior."I cannot show, but I have bites all over me," Quiroz said.Suarez described similar physical consequences."I have bruised arms from (one of my son's) pinching," Suarez said.She also described the role ABA support plays in her son's school day."The ABA registered behavior technician at school helps Dagito stay seated and complete his tasks, but she is also protecting Dagito from other children who are like him and protecting the other children from how Dagito is," Suarez said."It just hurts-- not just as a family, but it hurts thinking in the future," Quiroz said. The chance to be able to grow up and be part of this society."Reports of Medicaid cuts to ABA therapy have surfaced in states across the country.The Health and Human Services Office of the Inspector General audited Medicaid spending on ABA in Maine, Michigan, Wisconsin, and Colorado. "(But) the things that may happen in society if they don't have ABA — those are really important. WATCH BELOW: Florida families fight Medicaid cuts to autism therapy The therapy at the center of the dispute is Applied Behavioral Analysis, or ABA. The Cleveland Clinic describes it as 'a research-based behavior therapy for people with autism and other developmental disorders,' adding that 'many studies have proven the effectiveness of ABA.' Families connected to Reflection Services ABA Therapy in Lake Worth say they received notice that Medicaid would no longer cover their children's treatment. For many, the loss has been immediate and painful. 'It's like a dark hole. Like you don't know what to do,' Daura Mabel Sanchez Cano de Fundora said. Her son David, she said, is classified by his neurologist as level one on the autism spectrum. She described the progress he had made through ABA. 'His vocabulary have been increasingly amazing. He can make sentences. He can understand what is happening,' Sanchez Cano de Fundora said. 'How you can deny a service that can decide the life of those children and those parents?' 'I have to do everything for them: feed them, bathe them, help them get dressed, comb their hair everything, everything, everything,' Suarez said. She said ABA gave her son tools to manage his emotions. 'His therapist gives him tools so he can channel the frustration he feels,' Suarez said. cards.headline: Byron Donalds challenges David Jolly to Florida governor debates before primary concludes
cards.teaser: Republican front runner Byron Donalds challenged leading Democratic candidate David Jolly to three general election debates this fall, even as Donalds continues facing three opponents for the GOP nomination.
cards.body:
Republican gubernatorial front runner Byron Donalds challenged leading Democratic candidate David Jolly to three general election debates this fall with less than a month remaining before Florida's Aug. 18 primary. Donalds continues facing three opponents for the GOP nomination. Donalds said when the time comes for these debates, his vision is one for a free Florida that puts the people of Florida first, protects the Florida dream, expands Florida's economies and makes sure Florida remains number one in all of America. Jolly, a former Republican congressman now running as a Democrat, initially responded by telling Donalds to survive his own primary first. During a later CNN appearance, however, he said he would gladly meet Donalds on the debate stage a dozen times, adding that Donalds should get through his Republican primary first.

The exchange gave Donalds' Republican opponents another opportunity to criticize the front runner for looking beyond them. Lt. Gov. Jay Collins, former Florida House Speaker Paul Renner and businessman James Fishback have not received debate invitations from Donalds. Donalds has not debated his primary rivals while maintaining sizable advantages in polling, fundraising and endorsements. A recent Cygnal survey showed Donalds at 43 percent, compared with 12 percent for Fishback, 11 percent for Collins and 2 percent for Renner, although nearly one third of voters remained undecided.

A separate University of North Florida poll offered an early look at the possible general election matchup. Donalds led Jolly 46 percent to 41 percent among likely midterm voters, with a margin of error of 3.8 percentage points. The poll surveyed 848 likely midterm voters from July 8 through July 17.

cards.headline: Poll shows Florida property tax amendment support drops after voters learn of budget impact
cards.teaser: A University of North Florida poll found 61 percent initial support for Florida's proposed property tax amendment. Support fell to 45 percent after respondents were told the proposal is estimated to create an approximately $11.8 billion municipal budget shortfall over two years.
cards.body:
A new poll showed Florida's proposed property tax amendment may be popular enough to pass depending on how it is described to voters. The proposal would raise the homestead exemption for non school property taxes from $50,000 to $150,000 in 2027 and then to $250,000 in 2028. It would also lower the annual assessment growth cap for non homestead properties from 10 percent to 5 percent and restrict how local governments spend remaining property tax revenue. The University of North Florida survey initially found 61 percent support after respondents were told the amendment would reserve property tax revenue for core public services. That is narrowly above the 60 percent approval required for a constitutional amendment.

Support fell 16 points after respondents were told the proposal is estimated to create an approximately $11.8 billion municipal budget shortfall over two years. With that information, 45 percent supported the amendment and 47 percent opposed it. The poll surveyed 848 likely midterm voters from July 8 through July 17. Those results add significance to three lawsuits challenging the amendment's ballot title and summary. Plaintiffs argue phrases promising to protect small businesses, ensure fairness and preserve core services amount to political advertising instead of a neutral description of the proposal.

The challengers are not asking a judge to remove the amendment from the November ballot. If the language is found defective, state law would require Attorney General James Uthmeier to rewrite what voters see. A hearing on the ballot language challenges is scheduled for July 29 in Leon County. The cases could be consolidated ahead of that hearing.

cards.headline: Boston cyclist rides 2,600 miles from Key West to Maine to honor friend lost to colorectal cancer
cards.teaser: Jay Weedall traveled to South Florida to begin a 2,600 mile bike ride from Key West to Maine, with a goal of raising $50,000 for research while honoring his friend's memory.
cards.body:
Boston cyclist Jay Weedall traveled to South Florida to begin a 2,600 mile bike ride from Key West to Maine after losing a close friend to young onset colorectal cancer. Weedall said a friend of his recently passed away from young onset rectal cancer. The death of his friend, who was also named Jay, inspired Weedall to honor his memory by riding his bike across the country. Weedall said he has adventured around the world with his friend, ridden bikes together with him, and this felt like the best way to honor him now that he has passed away. His goal is to raise $50,000 for the Young Onset Colorectal Cancer Research Center in honor of the friend he lost to the disease. To prepare, Weedall trained 200 to 300 miles a week, mapped out his route and planned for the long journey ahead.

Weedall began his journey in Key West, pedaling 155 miles to Miami on day one. He set off on his second leg a 163 mile ride to Vero Beach. Weedall said he tries to beat the heat and is going roughly 150 miles a day just niching his way up the coast through pretty much every state all the way to the Pan Mass Challenge. He will do the Pan Mass Challenge across Massachusetts on August 2 and continue to the Canadian border in Maine. By avoiding highways, Weedall says the route offers something unexpected, allowing him to experience little coastal towns along the inlets.

Weedall said even when his legs are hurting, even when the traffic is big or even when he is a little anxious about what is going on around him, he is largely just thinking about his friend who does not get the opportunity to do this with him anymore. Fans can follow Weedall's journey on the cycling app Strava.

cards.headline: Jellyfish Museum in Pompano Beach showcases medical breakthroughs from ancient sea creatures
cards.teaser: Researchers at the Jellyfish Museum in Pompano Beach have developed an antidote for the potentially fatal sting of the box jellyfish. Other medical advances include collagen harvested from flame jellies that has been found to help stop hemorrhages.
cards.body:
The Jellyfish Museum in Pompano Beach houses thousands of jellyfish in all sizes and shapes, offering a window into some of the ocean's most ethereal and elusive creatures. Naphtalie Jeanty, who holds degrees in both archaeology and anthropology, found her way to the museum through a passion for teaching about flora and fauna. Jellyfish have been gracefully moving through the world's oceans for over 500 million years, making them some of the oldest living species on Earth, predating dinosaurs, trees and even fish. Despite the name, jellyfish are not technically fish at all. Jeanty said a lot of the world is starting to describe them as just jellies, and they do not have the same anatomy as fish.

Researchers at the museum have developed an antidote for the potentially fatal sting of the box jellyfish, which can kill its prey in 3 to 5 minutes. Jeanty said she thinks it is going to be a breakthrough. Other medical advances involve collagen harvested from flame jellies. The collagen has been apparently found to help stop hemorrhages, so it might be found in bandages in the future. Research into the Japanese sea nettle has also yielded promising results. There is a part of them that was found to shrink tumors in a mouse cancer, and the next step would be possibly human cancer.

Jellyfish also perform something called symmetrization, the ability to reorganize their bodies for balance. Moon jellies can regenerate after being split in half, creating two different versions of themselves. Some jellyfish even scrub out microplastics, among the smallest particles of pollution found in seas. Polka dotted jellies on display at the museum are native to a lake on the island of Palau in the South Pacific, where they work to keep the lake alive. Jeanty said they provide nutrients and move nutrients all throughout the ocean, taking out excess ones that do not need to be there.

hero.headline: Indiantown Council rejects second attempt to pause data center applications
hero.body:
The Indiantown Village Council on Monday declined to implement a 90-day pause on data center applications despite renewed pressure from residents and two council members. Councilwoman Karen Onsager proposed the pause to allow time for the council to study infrastructure demands on water and electrical systems before making decisions on data center projects. She requested a community informational meeting with technical experts, representatives from the South Florida Water Management District, and utility providers before any votes on future applications.

Councilwoman Vernestine Palmer said she supported a longer pause of 12 to 18 months to gather information and update land development regulations with safeguards. Indiantown civic activist Melissa Hague told the council during the July 13 budget workshop that refusing to pause applications was negligent when officials admitted they did not fully understand data center impacts. Nelson Ferreira had submitted a data center application earlier this year but withdrew it on April 29 after scores of residents protested during preliminary review.

Village Attorney Wade Vose warned that any pause would violate Senate Bills 180 and 484 and expose the municipality to lawsuits from property owners and developers. Vose said a local land use attorney who represents multiple developers in the village emailed him the same afternoon warning that SB 180 prohibits any regulation that would inhibit development applications. Village Manager Taryn Kryzda confirmed that data centers are a permitted use on industrially zoned lands within the village.

Mayor Carmine Dipaolo warned that defying the Legislature could jeopardize state funding after Indiantown received over $120 million in recent years. Kryzda said local governments that go against state or federal government typically face withheld funding. Onsager's motion died after no council member offered a second. The community informational meeting Onsager requested will be held Saturday, Aug. 2.
hero.article_text: INDIANTOWN – A pair of Village Council members failed to gain momentum on a second stab at convincing their colleagues and staff that a pause on data center applications would not put the municipality at odds with the Florida Legislature’s recent bills aimed at controlling such developments and limiting more restrictive land uses. The Council previously sought the advice of Village Attorney Wade Vose last month on a moratorium after scores of local residents had protested the Village’s preliminary review of a data center application submitted earlier this year by Nelson Ferreira, which he actually withdrew on April 29. Indiantown civic activist Melissa Hague had spurred its members on during the June 11 Council meeting, citing examples of a few other Florida communities either implementing or proposing data center moratoriums. Wade shot that idea down, however, insisting such a move would put the municipality in direct violation of Senate Bills 180 and 484 and leave it open to potential lawsuits by property owners and developers. Hague repeated her request during the July 13 budget workshop. “I’m coming back asking for an administrative pause on data centers,” she said. “It’s already been admitted on media that we don’t know what we’re dealing with. If we don’t know, not having an administrative pause to go through the motions of finding out and looking at land development regulations is negligent. I know there’s pressure behind the scenes not to have that happen, but the people want it to happen, and that’s who you represent.” A few minutes later, Councilwoman Karen Onsager – who’d supported Hague’s request the previous month – again broached the topic, this time couching it in the milder terminology of a “pause.” “I’ve asked for an informative community meeting,” she said. “In light of that meeting, I move that the Village of Indiantown establish a 90-day administrative pause on the acceptance, processing and approval of all new applications for large-load data center development projects. During the 90-day period, I request the Village staff proceed with the informational meeting I requested, including technical experts, representatives from the South Florida Water Management District, utility providers and relevant staff so that the Council and our residents can better understand the current and projected demands on our water and electrical infrastructure.” Councilwoman Onsager emphasized more than once that her proposed pause was intended to provide the Council additional time to gather facts, evaluate data and consider potential solutions to community concerns while putting off any potential Board decisions on such applications until after the current election cycle. “To be clear, I am not proposing any amendments to our land development regulations nor am I seeking to impose additional restrictions or requirements on the application process at this time,” she added in a nod to the aforementioned legislation. “I am simply requesting sufficient time for the Council to conduct due-diligence and make informed decisions regarding future industrial development applications based on a thorough understanding of the facts and the infrastructure implications.” Rather than offering a second to Onsager’s motion, however, Councilwoman Vernestine Palmer wanted to negotiate the length of that pause with her colleague. “I think the administrative pause should be more than 90 days,” she said. “I think we should have at least a 12-to-18-month administrative pause so we can get all the information concerning it. No one is saying we’re against it or for it; we just want to know what’s going on so we can make an informed decision and [ensure] the LDRs have some safeguards in it for us.” That failed to sway Onsager, who knew her motion was already going against Vose’s prior legal advice. “I asked for a 90-day pause because a 90-day pause does give us time to collect information, have the meeting, get some important data and not necessarily bring down problems for our community,” she explained. “We can’t afford to be sued for doing things wrong –12 to 18 months is restrictive. We’re also in the middle of an election. I think that we should vote for a stop until we can get whoever’s here seated and they can get familiar with the actual facts and then make that choice.” For her part, Councilwoman Angelina Perez, looked to Vose for advice rather than make any comments. The latter admitted nothing had changed for him since June. “It’s my legal opinion that such an administrative pause – whether it’s 90 days or 12 months – would be a violation of Senate Bill 180, which we discussed at length previously,” he said. “My legal opinion remains the same.” Vose acknowledged receiving an email from a local land use attorney that same afternoon with an ominous warning. “He does represent multiple developers within the Village,” he explained. “He emailed me precisely about this matter and advised me that SB 180 would prohibit anything along the lines of a regulation that would inhibit the process of applications for development.” After Village Manager Taryn Kryzda confirmed the industrially zoned lands within the Village allowed data centers as a permitted use, Mayor Carmine Dipaolo warned his colleagues about another risk in offending state officials. “Basically, what we’re saying to the Legislature is we don’t care about your house bill – the same Legislature that’s given us over $120 million – and we’re asking for more,” he said. “If the residents had to pay the $120 million that we’ve received, it’d be 100 years before they had clean water.” Kryzda concurred. “My experience is, when local government goes against the state or the federal government, the first thing they look to do is withhold funding,” she said. After further Board discussion, Mayor Dipaolo called for a second to Onsager’s motion, which was not forthcoming. hero.headline: Three arrested in Fort Pierce after 3-month-old dies from dehydration and malnutrition
hero.body:
Three people are facing charges of aggravated manslaughter of a child and aggravated child abuse after a 3-month-old died from dehydration and malnutrition in Fort Pierce. The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office arrested Nicole Maxwell, her father Robert Maxwell, and his girlfriend Vikki Koon following an investigation that began in August 2025 when the infant was brought to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital deceased.

The medical examiner determined the child died from dehydration and malnutrition. Court documents describe the infant's ribs as more prominent than its stomach. Detective Jennifer Diaz with the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office said the child lived primarily with Robert Maxwell and Koon in a Fort Pierce mobile home while Nicole Maxwell lived at her boyfriend's home in Vero Beach. According to court documents, Koon fed the infant only twice a day and admitted that when she ran out of formula, she fed the child watered-down milk with bay cereal mixed in.

The mobile home had windows boarded shut, exposed electrical wiring, and live and dead cockroaches throughout. Detective Diaz described the house as extremely hot with a bug infestation and unsafe for walking. A neighbor named Suzan said she witnessed the conditions firsthand and would see other children from the home walking around the neighborhood asking for water. Nicole Maxwell's other children who were living inside the mobile home are now in foster care.

Detective Diaz said the Department of Children and Families had been involved with the family before. Sheriff Richard Del Toro emphasized the shared responsibility of protecting children, stating that if you see signs that a child may be neglected, abused, or living in unsafe conditions, do not assume someone else will intervene. Detective Diaz stressed the importance of reporting suspicious activity to protect children.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie Police open $28.8 million training facility with indoor firearms range
cards.teaser: Port St. Lucie Police cut the ribbon on a three-story, 54,283-square-foot training center on the City Hall grounds after four years of construction.
cards.body:
The new police training center officially opened on July 24 with a ribbon-cutting attended by Mayor Shannon Martin and Chief Leo Niemczyk. The facility includes a 20-lane, 9,508-square-foot indoor firearms range featuring an integrated MILO live-fire scenario system, a 2,848-square-foot tactical shoot house with configurable rooms, and a MILO Virtual Simulation Theater for decision-making and de-escalation exercises.

The three-story building houses a defensive tactics training room equipped with Axon VR technology, a multi-purpose training room for classroom instruction, and three floors of office space supporting the Training Division and Criminal Investigations Division with 19 offices and 86 workstations. The facility was designed by ADG Architecture and constructed by HJ High.

Officer Brittany McNally said that for years, officers traveled to Indian River State College in Fort Pierce for extensive training. By bringing training in-house, the facility will reduce recurring costs while allowing officers to train more efficiently. Police personnel immediately began moving into the new facility after the ribbon cutting.

The recently opened, 54,283-square-foot, state-of-the-art, $28.8 million police training center is on the Port St. Lucie City Hall grounds, just northwest of the police department. The 54,283-square-foot, state-of-the-art, $28.8 million police training center officially opened on July 24 on the grounds of Port St. Lucie City Hall with a ribbon-cutting for invited guests. Lucie city officials who cut the ribbon for the 54,283-square-foot, state-of-the-art, $28.8 million police training center on July 24 were Mayor Shannon Martin, center, and Chief Leo Niemczyk. LUCIE – After four years of construction, the ribbon was cut on July 24 for a 54,283-square-foot, state-of-the-art, $28.8 million police training center on the Port St. Lucie City Hall grounds, just northwest of the police department. “This project is all about making sure our officers have the space, training, and resources they need to continue serving our community at the highest level,” Port St. Lucie Mayor Shannon Martin said in a Facebook posting. Lucie the safest large city in Florida takes more than dedication. It requires planning ahead and making smart investments that prepare our officers for the challenges they face every day.” Included in the three-story facility are: • A 20-lane, 9,508-square-foot indoor firearms range featuring an integrated MILO live-fire scenario system. • A 2,848-square-foot tactical shoot house with configurable rooms for realistic scenario-based training. • A MILO Virtual Simulation Theater for immersive decision-making and de-escalation exercises. • A dedicated defensive tactics training room equipped with Axon VR technology. • A multi-purpose training room designed for classroom instruction, conferences, virtual presentations, and large-scale training. • Three floors of office space supporting the Training Division and Criminal Investigations Division (CID), including 19 offices and 86 workstations. • Advanced audio/visual technology throughout the facility to support collaborative training and instruction. The facility was designed by ADG Architecture and constructed by HJ High, with specialized contributions from industry leaders including Action Target, MILO, Whelen, and numerous additional project partners, according to Port St. As of July 27, the city has a population of more than 260,000. There is a total of 455 employees in the police department with 360 sworn officers, according to city hall records. For years, officers traveled to Indian River State College in Fort Pierce for extensive training, according to Officer Brittany McNally. “By bringing much of that training in-house, this facility will reduce those recurring costs while allowing us to train more efficiently and effectively,” she said in a statement. “Equally important, the new training facility provides our officers with access to state-of-the-art technology and realistic, scenario-based training that better prepares them for the complex situations they may face in the field. From recruit training to advanced tactical instruction and continuing education, our officers will now have the resources needed to sharpen their skills throughout their careers right in our own backyard.” Once the ribbon was cut, police personnel immediately began making the move into the new facility. Because of safety and confidentiality concerns, the facility is not open to the general public. Your comment has been submitted. Reported There was a problem reporting this. cards.headline: Port St. Lucie cuts property tax rate for 11th consecutive year
cards.teaser: City Council approved a property tax millage rate of 4.8750 for the 2026-27 fiscal year, down from 4.9750 in the current year.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie City Council agreed to lower the city's millage rate for the 11th consecutive year at the annual Summer Workshop held July 22-23. The budget will be adopted by City Council in September, with public hearings taking place in September, and goes into effect in October.

Since 2016, the city has reduced its millage rate by 25 percent, saving the average homeowner nearly $2,000 over a 10-year period. Port St. Lucie has the third lowest municipal tax rate out of Florida's 20 largest cities. The property tax reduction maintains the city's record of steadily reducing its millage rate while managing historic population growth, investing in essential infrastructure, and improving public safety.

cards.body:
The Fort Pierce Police Department said the robbery happened Sunday at about 8:38 p.m. when two men approached a victim using the ATM. One of the men displayed a gun concealed in his waistband before forcing the victim to withdraw an unknown amount of cash.

Officers responded to the scene, established a perimeter, and used a K-9 and drone to search for the suspects. The suspects were not located. Police described them as two men in their early 20s, about 5 feet 10 inches tall and weighing about 170 pounds. The armed suspect was last seen wearing jeans and a gray hooded sweatshirt.

cards.headline: Two suspects arrested after 80 mph chase in Port St. Lucie, one found hiding on roof
cards.teaser: A driver fled police at nearly 80 mph in a 45 mph zone on Southwest Becker Road before abandoning the vehicle and fleeing on foot with a passenger.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie Police attempted to stop a white Acura after observing multiple traffic violations and signs of impaired driving. The driver accelerated to nearly 80 mph in a 45 mph zone on Southwest Becker Road, weaving in and out of traffic and ignoring traffic signs and signals. The driver and passenger abandoned the vehicle in a residential driveway near Southwest Idol Avenue before fleeing on foot.

A nearby resident called 911 after seeing the two men run from the scene. Police deployed a K-9 and a drone while officers established a perimeter. Both suspects were located, including one who was found hiding on the roof of an occupied home.

The suspects were identified as Joseph Gary Harris, 42, and Bryan Shawn Baker, 46. Harris was charged with fleeing and eluding law enforcement, burglary of an occupied dwelling, resisting an officer without violence, and loitering or prowling. Baker was charged with resisting an officer without violence and loitering or prowling.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County corrections deputy sentenced to probation after road rage incident
cards.teaser: Devin Mills, 57, was sentenced to two years of probation after pleading no contest to burglary of a conveyance charge related to an off-duty incident on Southwest Tulip Boulevard in Port St. Lucie.
cards.body:
According to court documents in St. Lucie County, Mills was sentenced on Thursday, July 16, to two years of probation and must pay court costs. He pleaded no contest to burglary of a conveyance charge on June 29. Florida Department of Corrections database records indicate Mills' probation is supervised by its Fort Pierce Circuit office and expires on July 15, 2028.

Court documents note Mills' probation will automatically terminate after one year if he completes conditions of probation, which include a mental health evaluation and if needed, treatment, along with no contact with the victims or victims' families during the probation. Mills was accused of confronting two 18-year-olds in a vehicle during a road rage incident on the 100 block of Southwest Tulip Boulevard in Port St. Lucie. A video recording by the teenagers showed Mills reaching into the open passenger side of the teens' vehicle, grabbing one of the teens' arms to take the cellphone that was recording the incident away.

After his no-contest plea, the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office said Mills remained on unpaid administrative leave pending an internal investigation. A spokesperson for the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office said on Thursday, July 23 that Mills' employment status is pending the completion of an internal affairs investigation.

cards.headline: P1 Motor Club building private racetrack resort on 650 acres in St. Lucie County
cards.teaser: The new private racetrack resort community is under construction on 650 acres off Okeechobee Road, featuring 10 miles of racing circuits and set to welcome its first drivers this fall.
cards.body:
P1 Motor Club is designed for drivers of all ages and skill levels, with tracks for street cars, race cars, and go-karts. Chris DuPlessis, Director of Fun for P1 Motor Club, said kids as young as 8 years old can drive go-karts. The first track under construction is the 3-mile Treasure Coast Track, set to open in October. Over the next six months, crews will continue work on additional circuits, including the flagship 4.5-mile P1 International Circuit.

Membership comes with a $192,000 initiation fee and $12,000 in yearly dues. The club already has 260 members. Construction on a clubhouse and homes for up to 125 residents is scheduled to begin in 2027. The development will also include condos and customizable garages with living spaces situated directly along the tracks.

Developers say they want to preserve the character of the region by planting trees, creating lakes, and incorporating natural landscaping throughout the property. P1 Motor Club is expected to be fully completed by 2028.

hero.headline: Boston cyclist passes through Vero Beach on 2,600-mile ride honoring friend lost to cancer
hero.teaser: Jay Weedall stopped in Vero Beach during his second day of cycling from Key West to Maine to raise $50,000 for young-onset colorectal cancer research.
hero.body:
Jay Weedall, a Boston cyclist, traveled to South Florida to begin a 2,600-mile bike ride from Key West to Maine with a goal of raising $50,000 for the Young Onset Colorectal Cancer Research Center. The ride honors his close friend, also named Jay, who recently died from young-onset rectal cancer. The two had adventured around the world together and ridden bikes together.

Weedall rode 155 miles from Key West to Miami on his first day. On his second day, he rode 163 miles to Vero Beach. He is riding roughly 150 miles each day, avoiding highways to experience small coastal towns along the inlets. Weedall trained 200 to 300 miles a week to prepare for the journey.

Weedall will complete the Pan Mass Challenge across Massachusetts on August 2 and continue to the Canadian border in Maine. He said even when his legs hurt or traffic is heavy, he thinks about his friend who no longer has the opportunity to ride with him. Fans can follow his journey on the cycling app Strava.

To prepare, Weedall trained 200 to 300 miles a week, mapped out his route, and planned for the long journey ahead."So, there was a lot of preplanning to make sure that the roads that I'm going to go on are safe and have been ridden on by cyclists and let's hope that the wind is kind to me," Weedall said.Weedall began his journey in Key West, pedaling 155 miles to Miami on day one."Something I learned after day one is hydration packs, good for hydration obviously but if you fill it up with ice it's good for keeping you cold as well," Weedall said.I caught up with him the next morning as he set off on his second leg — a 163-mile ride to Vero Beach."Ideally, I try to beat the heat and then I'm going roughly 150 miles a day just niching my way up the coast through pretty much every state all the way to the Pan Mass Challenge. Then I'll do the Pan Mass Challenge across Massachusetts on August 2nd. I'll continue to the Canadian border in Maine," Weedall said.By avoiding highways, Weedall says the route offers something unexpected."By avoiding highways, I get to experience these little coastal towns along those inlets," Weedall said.When you're riding hundreds of miles alone, Weedall says, you have plenty of time to think."Even when my legs are hurting, even when the traffic is big or even when I'm a little anxious about what's going on around me, but I'm largely just thinking about my friend who doesn't get the opportunity to do this with me anymore," Weedall said.Every pedal stroke is a tribute to his friend — and, he hopes, a step toward a cure.Fans can follow Weedall's journey on the cycling app Strava.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. cards.headline: Indian River County firefighter Geoffrey Lang dies following personal tragedy at Sebastian home
cards.body:
Indian River County Fire Rescue is mourning the loss of Firefighter/Paramedic Geoffrey Lang, who died Saturday following what officials described as a personal tragedy at his Sebastian home. Lang was 35 years old and is survived by his wife, two children and his parents.

Lang joined Indian River County Fire Rescue in 2015 and served the community for more than a decade. He worked out of Station 9 at 13550 Roseland Road in Sebastian. County officials said he was known for his professionalism, compassion and dedication to serving others.

Fire Chief David Johnson said Lang's absence will be deeply felt throughout the department. County Administrator John A. said the county's thoughts are with Lang's family, friends and fellow firefighters during this difficult time. County Commission Chairman Deryl Loar extended condolences on behalf of the Board of County Commissioners and emphasized the county's commitment to supporting the mental health and well-being of first responders and their families.

Indian River County Fire Rescue asked the public to respect the privacy of Lang's family, friends and colleagues as they grieve. Officials said memorial service information will be released when it becomes available. Multiple agencies across Indian River County, including the Sebastian Police Department, Vero Beach Police Department and Indian River County Sheriff's Office, expressed condolences to Lang's family and colleagues.

hero.headline: St. Lucie County commissioners deadlock on infrastructure tax renewal, postpone decision
hero.body:
St. Lucie County commissioners split evenly on when to schedule a referendum to renew the county's half-cent infrastructure sales tax, voting unanimously to postpone the decision until August 4. The voter-approved tax expires in December 2028 after its 10-year authorization. Commissioners must decide whether to ask voters to extend it in 2026 or wait until 2028. If they wait and voters approve it then, it would be considered a new tax rather than a continuation.

Before the commission's discussion on July 21, three Port St. Lucie officials urged the board to place the referendum on the 2026 ballot. Port St. Lucie Public Works Director Colt Schwerdt said the tax has funded road, sidewalk, stormwater and water-quality improvements that have benefited city residents. Utility Systems Director Kevin Matyjaszek said there is a direct correlation between infrastructure and quality of life. Communications Director Sarah Prohaska read a letter from Kenneth Kroll, chairman of both the county and Port St. Lucie Sales Tax Oversight committees, who urged commissioners to act this year.

Commissioner James Clasby opposed placing the measure on the 2026 ballot, saying he did not want it on the same ballot as Amendment 3 and the School Board tax. Commissioner Erin Lowry agreed, saying many residents are struggling financially and may reject the measure simply because it includes the word tax. Chairwoman Jamie Fowler argued the county would have two opportunities if the measure were placed on the 2026 ballot. Commissioner Cathy Townsend agreed and moved to keep the referendum on the 2026 ballot, but the motion failed on a 2-2 vote.

With Vice Chairman Larry Leet absent and the commission deadlocked, members voted 4-0 to continue the item until August 4, when Leet is expected to return and cast the deciding vote. Deputy County Administrator Mayte Santamaria reminded commissioners they had already approved an ordinance in March scheduling the referendum for November 2026. Keeping that date requires no action, while delaying it until 2028 would require rescinding the ordinance and adopting a new one.
hero.article_text: Lucie County Commissioners, from left: Erin Lowry, James Clasby, Cathy Townsend, Larry Leet and Jamie Fowler. FORT PIERCE — With Vice Chairman Larry Leet absent and the remaining four St. Lucie County commissioners split evenly on when to schedule a referendum to renew the county’s half-cent infrastructure sales tax, the board voted unanimously July 21 to postpone the decision until its Aug. The voter-approved tax expires in December 2028 after its 10-year authorization. Commissioners must decide whether to ask voters to extend it in 2026 or wait until 2028. If they wait and voters approve it then, it would be considered a new tax rather than a continuation. Before the commission’s discussion, three Port St. Lucie officials urged the board to place the referendum on the 2026 ballot. Lucie Public Works Director Colt Schwerdt said the tax has funded road, sidewalk, stormwater and water-quality improvements that have benefited city residents. “Our request is to let the residents decide whether or not to continue the sales tax referendum,” Schwerdt said. “Providing for the sales tax referendum provides for long-term planning. We’d like you to continue allowing us to make needed progress on infrastructure projects throughout the county.” Utility Systems Director Kevin Matyjaszek echoed that message. “There’s a direct correlation between infrastructure and quality of life,” he said. “Not allowing residents to vote on extending this sales tax is a disservice. They’re already going to the polls, so let them decide.” Communications Director Sarah Prohaska read a letter from Kenneth Kroll, chairman of both the county and Port St. Lucie Sales Tax Oversight committees, who urged commissioners to act this year. Kroll said approving the referendum in 2026 would provide certainty for long-range planning, allow time for public education and ensure continued investment in transportation, stormwater, public safety and environmental projects. Deputy County Administrator Mayte Santamaria reminded commissioners they had already approved an ordinance in March scheduling the referendum for November 2026. Keeping that date requires no action, while delaying it until 2028 would require rescinding the ordinance and adopting a new one. Chairwoman Jamie Fowler asked whether a failed 2026 referendum could be brought back in 2028. Santamaria said it could, although it would be treated as a new infrastructure sales tax rather than a continuation. Commissioner James Clasby opposed placing the measure on the 2026 ballot. “I don’t want it on the 2026 ballot because there’s Amendment 3 on it and there’s the School Board tax,” he said. “I don’t think it’s a smart idea to put a tax on a ballot where people are being asked to basically eliminate taxes.” Commissioner Erin Lowry agreed, saying many residents are struggling financially and may reject the measure simply because it includes the word “tax.” “I don’t feel people understand it’s a continuation and not a new tax,” Lowry said. “It’s not that we don’t support it — we just want a better opportunity to make sure that it continues.” Fowler argued the county would have two opportunities if the measure were placed on the 2026 ballot. “If I get two chances to win, I’m going to take two chances over one,” she said. “If we wait until 2028 and it doesn’t pass, we’re done.” Commissioner Cathy Townsend agreed and moved to keep the referendum on the 2026 ballot, but the motion failed on a 2-2 vote. Clasby’s motion to delay it until 2028 also failed 2-2. With the commission deadlocked, members voted 4-0 to continue the item until Aug. 4, when Leet is expected to return and cast the deciding vote. Your comment has been submitted. cards.headline: Port St. Lucie cuts property tax rate for 11th consecutive year
cards.teaser: Port St. Lucie City Council approved a property tax rate of 4.8750 for the coming fiscal year, down from 4.9750, continuing a streak of reductions that began in 2016.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie City Council approved a property tax millage rate of 4.8750 for fiscal year 2026-27 at the annual Summer Workshop held July 22-23, a decrease from 4.9750 in fiscal year 2025-26. The budget will be adopted by City Council in September, with public hearings taking place September 2 and September 16. The fiscal year 2026-27 budget goes into effect October 1.

Since 2016, the city has reduced its millage rate by 25 percent, saving the average homeowner nearly $2,000 over a 10-year period. Port St. Lucie has the third lowest municipal tax rate out of Florida's 20 largest cities. The property tax reduction maintains Port St. Lucie's record of steadily reducing its millage rate while managing historic population growth, investing in essential infrastructure and improving public safety.

cards.headline: Boston cyclist passes through Treasure Coast on 2,600-mile ride for colorectal cancer research
cards.teaser: Jay Weedall began a journey from Key West to Maine to raise $50,000 for the Young Onset Colorectal Cancer Research Center after losing a close friend to the disease.
cards.body:
A Boston cyclist is riding 2,600 miles from Key West to Maine to raise $50,000 for colorectal cancer research while honoring his friend's memory. Jay Weedall lost a close friend, also named Jay, to young-onset rectal cancer. Weedall began his journey in Key West, pedaling 155 miles to Miami on day one. The next morning he set off on his second leg, a 163-mile ride to Vero Beach.

To prepare, Weedall trained 200 to 300 miles a week, mapped out his route, and planned for the long journey ahead. Weedall is riding roughly 150 miles a day through coastal towns along inlets. He will complete the Pan Mass Challenge across Massachusetts on August 2 and continue to the Canadian border in Maine. His goal is to raise funds for the Young Onset Colorectal Cancer Research Center. Fans can follow Weedall's journey on the cycling app Strava.

To prepare, Weedall trained 200 to 300 miles a week, mapped out his route, and planned for the long journey ahead."So, there was a lot of preplanning to make sure that the roads that I'm going to go on are safe and have been ridden on by cyclists and let's hope that the wind is kind to me," Weedall said.Weedall began his journey in Key West, pedaling 155 miles to Miami on day one."Something I learned after day one is hydration packs, good for hydration obviously but if you fill it up with ice it's good for keeping you cold as well," Weedall said.I caught up with him the next morning as he set off on his second leg — a 163-mile ride to Vero Beach."Ideally, I try to beat the heat and then I'm going roughly 150 miles a day just niching my way up the coast through pretty much every state all the way to the Pan Mass Challenge. hero.headline: Port St. Lucie police open $28.8 million training facility with indoor shooting range
hero.teaser: Port St. Lucie cut the ribbon Thursday on a 54,283-square-foot police training center at City Hall, ending years of travel to Fort Pierce for officer training.
hero.body:
The three-story, $28.8 million police training center officially opened July 24 on the Port St. Lucie City Hall grounds, just northwest of the police department. The facility includes a 20-lane indoor firearms range, a tactical shoot house with configurable rooms, and a MILO Virtual Simulation Theater for decision-making exercises. The building also houses a defensive tactics training room equipped with Axon VR technology and three floors of office space for the Training Division and Criminal Investigations Division.

Mayor Shannon Martin said the project ensures officers have the space, training, and resources to continue serving the community at the highest level. For years, officers traveled to Indian River State College in Fort Pierce for extensive training. Officer Brittany McNally said bringing training in-house will reduce recurring costs while allowing more efficient training. The facility was designed by ADG Architecture and constructed by HJ High. Police personnel immediately began moving into the new facility after the ribbon-cutting.
hero.article_text: The recently opened Port St. Lucie Police training center contains a defensive tactics training room equipped with Axon VR technology. The recently opened, 54,283-square-foot, state-of-the-art, $28.8 million police training center is on the Port St. Lucie City Hall grounds, just northwest of the police department. The 54,283-square-foot, state-of-the-art, $28.8 million police training center officially opened on July 24 on the grounds of Port St. Lucie City Hall with a ribbon-cutting for invited guests. The interior of the 54,283-square-foot, state-of-the-art, $28.8 million police training center on the Port St. Lucie City Hall grounds, just northwest of the police department. Lucie city officials who cut the ribbon for the 54,283-square-foot, state-of-the-art, $28.8 million police training center on July 24 were Mayor Shannon Martin, center, and Chief Leo Niemczyk. LUCIE – After four years of construction, the ribbon was cut on July 24 for a 54,283-square-foot, state-of-the-art, $28.8 million police training center on the Port St. Lucie City Hall grounds, just northwest of the police department. “This project is all about making sure our officers have the space, training, and resources they need to continue serving our community at the highest level,” Port St. Lucie Mayor Shannon Martin said in a Facebook posting. Lucie the safest large city in Florida takes more than dedication. It requires planning ahead and making smart investments that prepare our officers for the challenges they face every day.” Included in the three-story facility are: • A 20-lane, 9,508-square-foot indoor firearms range featuring an integrated MILO live-fire scenario system. • A 2,848-square-foot tactical shoot house with configurable rooms for realistic scenario-based training. • A MILO Virtual Simulation Theater for immersive decision-making and de-escalation exercises. • A dedicated defensive tactics training room equipped with Axon VR technology. • A multi-purpose training room designed for classroom instruction, conferences, virtual presentations, and large-scale training. • Three floors of office space supporting the Training Division and Criminal Investigations Division (CID), including 19 offices and 86 workstations. • Advanced audio/visual technology throughout the facility to support collaborative training and instruction. The facility was designed by ADG Architecture and constructed by HJ High, with specialized contributions from industry leaders including Action Target, MILO, Whelen, and numerous additional project partners, according to Port St. As of July 27, the city has a population of more than 260,000. There is a total of 455 employees in the police department with 360 sworn officers, according to city hall records. For years, officers traveled to Indian River State College in Fort Pierce for extensive training, according to Officer Brittany McNally. “By bringing much of that training in-house, this facility will reduce those recurring costs while allowing us to train more efficiently and effectively,” she said in a statement. “Equally important, the new training facility provides our officers with access to state-of-the-art technology and realistic, scenario-based training that better prepares them for the complex situations they may face in the field. From recruit training to advanced tactical instruction and continuing education, our officers will now have the resources needed to sharpen their skills throughout their careers right in our own backyard.” Once the ribbon was cut, police personnel immediately began making the move into the new facility. Because of safety and confidentiality concerns, the facility is not open to the general public. Your comment has been submitted. Reported There was a problem reporting this. cards.headline: 3 arrested in St. Lucie County after 3-month-old dies from dehydration and malnutrition
cards.body:
Three people face charges of aggravated manslaughter of a child and aggravated child abuse after a 3-month-old infant died from dehydration and malnutrition in Fort Pierce, according to the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office. Nicole Maxwell, the infant's mother, her father Robert Maxwell, and his girlfriend Vikki Koon were arrested Monday following an investigation that began in August 2025 when the baby was brought to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital deceased.

The medical examiner determined the child died from dehydration and malnutrition. Court documents describe the infant's ribs as more prominent than its stomach. St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office Detective Jennifer Diaz said the child lived primarily with Robert Maxwell and Vikki Koon while Nicole Maxwell lived at her boyfriend's home. Koon admitted to investigators that she fed the infant only twice a day and when she ran out of formula, she fed the child watered-down milk with bay cereal mixed in.

Investigators described the mobile home where the child lived as having windows boarded shut, exposed electrical wiring, and live and dead cockroaches throughout. The house was extremely hot with a bug infestation and was unsafe for walking, Diaz said. A neighbor named Suzan said she witnessed the conditions firsthand and would often see other children from the home walking around the neighborhood asking for water. Suzan said the children appeared unwashed and wore the same clothes every day.

Nicole Maxwell's other children who were living inside the mobile home are now in foster care. Diaz said the Department of Children and Families had been involved with the family before. Detective Diaz called it one of the worst cases she has worked in 20 years of law enforcement and emphasized the importance of reporting suspicious activity to protect children. Sheriff Richard Del Toro said protecting children is not solely the responsibility of law enforcement or the child welfare system but a responsibility the community shares.

The investigation began in August 2025 when investigators responded to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital after the 3-month-old was brought in deceased by Robert Maxwell and Koon. The medical examiner determined the child died from dehydration and malnutrition. Court documents describe the infant's "ribs more prominent than its stomach." "I can tell you the facts of this case don't even paint a picture clear to what we saw at the hospital," Diaz said. Diaz said the child lived primarily with Maxwell and Koon while the child's mother, Nicole Maxwell, lived at her boyfriend's home. Investigators said the child's father lived in Virginia. According to court documents, Koon primarily fed the infant only twice a day and admitted to investigators that when she ran out of formula, she fed the child "watered-down milk with bay cereal mixed in." Other children of Nicole Maxwell were also living in the home, which court documents describe as having windows boarded shut, exposed electrical wiring and live and dead cockroaches throughout. "The living conditions at this time were environmental hazards," Diaz said. A neighbor named Suzan, said she witnessed the conditions firsthand. "It just looked unlivable," Suzan said. Suzan said she would often see one of the other children walking around the neighborhood. "They would come and ask for water, you know. I see the child be thirsty. I mean, not bathe, same clothes every day," Suzan said. Suzan said she is heartbroken thinking about the infant who lived only a few feet away. "Nobody should suffer or go hungry, and especially for a child that didn't ask to come here," Suzan said. Diaz said the Department of Children and Families had been involved with the family before. Nicole Maxwell's other children who were living inside the mobile home are now in foster care. All three suspects faces charges of aggravated manslaughter of a child and aggravated child abuse. "The baby finally got justice," Suzan said. Diaz said emphasized the importance of reporting suspicious activity to protect children. "These tips are so instrumental to keeping our children safe," Diaz said. This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. cards.headline: Port St. Lucie police find suspect hiding on roof after 80 mph chase
cards.teaser: A suspected drunk driver fled Port St. Lucie police at nearly 80 mph before abandoning his car and hiding on the roof of an occupied home.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie police attempted to stop a white Acura after observing multiple traffic violations and signs of impaired driving. The driver accelerated to nearly 80 mph in a 45 mph zone on Southwest Becker Road, weaving in and out of traffic and ignoring traffic signs and signals. The driver and passenger abandoned the vehicle in a residential driveway near Southwest Idol Avenue before fleeing on foot.

A nearby resident called 911 after seeing the two men run from the scene. Police deployed a K-9 and a drone while officers established a perimeter. Both suspects were located, including one who was found hiding on the roof of an occupied home. The suspects were identified as Joseph Gary Harris, 42, and Bryan Shawn Baker, 46. Harris was charged with fleeing and eluding law enforcement, burglary of an occupied dwelling, resisting an officer without violence, and loitering or prowling. Baker was charged with resisting an officer without violence and loitering or prowling.
