cards.headline: St. Lucie Sheriff details year-long investigation into Fort Pierce infant death
cards.teaser: Investigators explain why arrests in the death of a 3-month-old Fort Pierce boy took nearly a year after the child died in August 2025.
cards.body:
Detective Jennifer Diaz with the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office said the case required outside expertise and months of additional testing before charges could be filed against Nicole Maxwell, Robert Maxwell, and Vikki Koon. The medical examiner had to seek out outside experts to provide an examination for the child, and based on results, the process took several weeks and even months, Diaz said.

A neighbor named Suzan who lives across the street from the home said she had concerns about the children's living conditions and believes the arrests are long overdue. Suzan said two of the boys would knock on her door and she would give them food and something to drink because the kids were so hungry and starving. Suzan said she had been inside the house and it was unlivable, with sheets of plywood covering holes in the mobile home's floor. Investigators said on Aug. 20, 2025, the 3-month-old was rushed to the hospital after the boy's grandfather messaged the mother saying the child was sick, but it was too late.
cards.article_text: Lucie County Sheriff’s Office is sharing new details about the investigation into the death of a three-month-old boy in Fort Pierce, including why it took nearly a year to make arrests and the conditions investigators say they found inside the mobile home where the child lived. The infant’s mother, Nicole Maxwell, her father Robert Maxwell, and his girlfriend Vikki Koon were arrested and charged with aggravated manslaughter and child abuse. Investigators say the baby died from dehydration and malnutrition last August, and the medical examiner later ruled the death a homicide. Detectives say the case was complex, requiring outside expertise and months of additional testing before they could move forward with charges. "It takes an extended amount of resources, and due to the medical examiner, who did great job in this investigation, they had to seek out outside experts to provide an examination for the child and based on results, they could take several weeks even months," said Detective Jennifer Diaz with the St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office. See also: ICE-held Lake Worth bakery owner faces up to 10 years in prison on illegal reentry charge A neighbor, Suzan, who lives across the street from the home, says she had concerns about the children’s living conditions and believes the arrests are long overdue. "It was just a blessing in disguise because now I know the kids are safe," she said. "I'm going to keep them in prayer." Suzan said two of the boys would knock on her door and she would give them food and something to drink. The kids were so hungry and starving. The child, clothes didn't ever get changed," Suzan said. I love children." Suzan said sheets of plywood covered holes in the mobile home's floor. "I've been inside the house and it was unlivable," she said. "The boards that's out there now, are the boards that was on the floor." Detective Jennifer Diaz was one of the investigators who worked on the case. She described the horrific conditions inside the mobile home. "The house was extremely hot," she said. "There was a bug infestation in the home, lack of food in the home, and the home was unsafe for walking." Investigators said on Aug. 20, 2025, the three-month old was rushed to the hospital after the boy's grandfather messaged the mother saying the child was sick but it was too late. "This was one that I think was very hard," Diaz said. "The way the child ended one of their last days of life was probably the saddest for me." Investigators say Maxwell’s four other children also needed medical attention at the time and are now in foster care. The sheriff’s office says child protective services had previously been called to the home and is reminding the public to report any suspected child abuse or neglect. Sheriff Richard Del Toro sent a statement following the arrests that reads in part: While justice is essential, our shared responsibility must be preventing these tragedies before they occur. Protecting children is not solely the responsibility of law enforcement or the child welfare system. It is a responsibility we all share. If you see signs that a child may be neglected, abused, or living in unsafe conditions, do not assume someone else will intervene. One phone call can be the difference between a child receiving the help they need and a life being saved. This case also reminds us that families facing difficult circumstances are not alone. Resources, support, and assistance are available. My commitment remains unwavering: to seek justice for victims, hold offenders accountable, and work alongside our community to protect our most vulnerable. By recognizing the warning signs, speaking up, and connecting families with the help they need, we can work together to prevent tragedies like this from happening again.

cards.article_text: The recently opened Port St. Lucie Police training center contains a defensive tactics training room equipped with Axon VR technology. The recently opened, 54,283-square-foot, state-of-the-art, $28.8 million police training center is on the Port St. Lucie City Hall grounds, just northwest of the police department. The 54,283-square-foot, state-of-the-art, $28.8 million police training center officially opened on July 24 on the grounds of Port St. Lucie City Hall with a ribbon-cutting for invited guests. The interior of the 54,283-square-foot, state-of-the-art, $28.8 million police training center on the Port St. Lucie City Hall grounds, just northwest of the police department. Lucie city officials who cut the ribbon for the 54,283-square-foot, state-of-the-art, $28.8 million police training center on July 24 were Mayor Shannon Martin, center, and Chief Leo Niemczyk. LUCIE – After four years of construction, the ribbon was cut on July 24 for a 54,283-square-foot, state-of-the-art, $28.8 million police training center on the Port St. Lucie City Hall grounds, just northwest of the police department. “This project is all about making sure our officers have the space, training, and resources they need to continue serving our community at the highest level,” Port St. Lucie Mayor Shannon Martin said in a Facebook posting. Lucie the safest large city in Florida takes more than dedication. It requires planning ahead and making smart investments that prepare our officers for the challenges they face every day.” Included in the three-story facility are: • A 20-lane, 9,508-square-foot indoor firearms range featuring an integrated MILO live-fire scenario system. • A 2,848-square-foot tactical shoot house with configurable rooms for realistic scenario-based training. • A MILO Virtual Simulation Theater for immersive decision-making and de-escalation exercises. • A dedicated defensive tactics training room equipped with Axon VR technology. • A multi-purpose training room designed for classroom instruction, conferences, virtual presentations, and large-scale training. • Three floors of office space supporting the Training Division and Criminal Investigations Division (CID), including 19 offices and 86 workstations. • Advanced audio/visual technology throughout the facility to support collaborative training and instruction. The facility was designed by ADG Architecture and constructed by HJ High, with specialized contributions from industry leaders including Action Target, MILO, Whelen, and numerous additional project partners, according to Port St. As of July 27, the city has a population of more than 260,000. There is a total of 455 employees in the police department with 360 sworn officers, according to city hall records. For years, officers traveled to Indian River State College in Fort Pierce for extensive training, according to Officer Brittany McNally. “By bringing much of that training in-house, this facility will reduce those recurring costs while allowing us to train more efficiently and effectively,” she said in a statement. “Equally important, the new training facility provides our officers with access to state-of-the-art technology and realistic, scenario-based training that better prepares them for the complex situations they may face in the field. From recruit training to advanced tactical instruction and continuing education, our officers will now have the resources needed to sharpen their skills throughout their careers right in our own backyard.” Once the ribbon was cut, police personnel immediately began making the move into the new facility. Because of safety and confidentiality concerns, the facility is not open to the general public. Your comment has been submitted. Reported There was a problem reporting this. hero.headline: Port St. Lucie bans gas station on Tradition commercial site after months of resident concerns
hero.body:
The Port St. Lucie City Council unanimously approved a permanent ban on gas stations at a 9.4-acre commercial parcel at the southwest corner of Crosstown Parkway and Fairgreen Drive on July 13. The restriction came after months of debate over a request by Winding River Crosstown LLC to convert what had been planned as Phase 3 of the Heritage Oaks at Tradition residential development into commercial property. While council members supported adding commercial uses to the rapidly growing area, several voiced concerns during the initial May 26 hearing that a convenience store with gas pumps would worsen traffic along Crosstown Parkway west of Interstate 95.

The council tabled the request in May after Vice Mayor Jolien Caraballo and other council members asked staff to determine whether gas stations could be eliminated as a permitted use on the parcel. When the hearing resumed June 22, several Heritage Oaks residents urged the council to reject the land-use change, citing concerns about increased traffic, noise and neighborhood impacts. The council voted 4-0 to approve the commercial designation on first reading after the developer agreed to permanently relinquish the right to build a gas station.

The updated development plan now specifies that while service stations remain permitted elsewhere within the Tradition mixed-use area, they are prohibited on Parcel 11A. The city also added protections requested by nearby residents. Before any mass grading begins, the developer must install a fence along the southern property line to prevent construction access through Southwest Glenbrook Drive, which connects to Heritage Oaks. An architectural wall and landscape buffering must be completed along the southeastern and southern boundaries before the first building permit is issued for vertical construction.

City planner Bridget Kean confirmed the restriction is now written directly into the Tradition Master Planned Unit Development documents, ensuring no future owner can develop a gas station on the parcel. Councilman Anthony Bonna said he believes expanding commercial development will benefit residents by broadening the city's tax base. Councilman David Pickett said going to commercial is the best possible thing for that corner. The amendment changes the parcel's designation from residential to commercial, paving the way for retail and office development.
hero.article_text: The aerial view of the 9.4-acre parcel of the Tradition Master Planned Unit Development at the southwest corner of Crosstown Parkway and Fairgreen Drive in Port St. The land-use map of the 9.4-acre parcel of the Tradition Master Planned Unit Development at the southwest corner of Crosstown Parkway and Fairgreen Drive in Port St. LUCIE — After months of debate and neighborhood concerns, the Port St. Lucie City Council has permanently prohibited a gas station from being built on a 9.4-acre commercial parcel at the southwest corner of Crosstown Parkway and Fairgreen Drive. The council unanimously approved the second and final reading of the 16th amendment to the Tradition Master Planned Unit Development on July 13, codifying a restriction that bars any current or future owner from developing a service station on the site. The amendment changes the parcel’s designation from residential to commercial, paving the way for retail and office development while addressing residents’ concerns about traffic and congestion. The issue has been under discussion for nearly three months after Winding River Crosstown LLC requested permission to convert what had been planned as Phase 3 of the Heritage Oaks at Tradition residential development into commercial property. While council members generally supported adding commercial uses to the rapidly growing area, several voiced concerns during the initial May 26 quasi-judicial hearing that a convenience store with gas pumps would worsen traffic along Crosstown Parkway west of Interstate 95. Vice Mayor Jolien Caraballo and other council members noted the increasing congestion along the commercial corridor and asked staff to determine whether gas stations could be eliminated as a permitted use on the parcel. The council tabled the request to allow time for that review. At the time, Councilwoman Stephanie Morgan questioned whether prohibiting a specific type of business amounted to government interference in the marketplace. “What concerns me is that on May 11 we approved two parcels changing from RGC to commercial general,” Morgan said during the May hearing. “We didn’t put any conditions on them. How can you put a condition on an applicant saying no gas stations? That would be like saying no Chick-fil-A because we’ve got enough chicken restaurants.” When the hearing resumed June 22, several Heritage Oaks residents urged the council to reject the land-use change, citing concerns about increased traffic, noise and neighborhood impacts. Instead, the council voted 4-0, with Morgan absent, to approve the commercial designation on first reading after the developer agreed to permanently relinquish the right to build a gas station. During the July 13 meeting, city planner Bridget Kean outlined the changes that formally incorporated the restriction into the Tradition MPUD documents. The updated development plan specifies that while service stations remain a permitted use elsewhere within the mixed-use area, they are prohibited on Parcel 11A. The concept plan also now includes a notation prohibiting a service station on the property, and the ordinance itself was revised to reference the city’s definition of a service station. Staff also added additional protections requested by nearby residents. Before any mass grading begins, the developer must install a fence along the southern property line to prevent construction access through Southwest Glenbrook Drive, which connects to Heritage Oaks. In addition, an architectural wall and landscape buffering must be completed along the southeastern and southern boundaries before the first building permit is issued for vertical construction. Several residents again voiced concerns about the proposal and questioned whether the process had been sufficiently transparent. Councilman Anthony Bonna defended both the public process and the final compromise. “Ultimately, we have to make decisions, and those decisions are not going to satisfy everybody,” Bonna said. “We listen and consider every resident that comes forward, but ultimately we have to make one decision.” Bonna said he believes expanding commercial development will benefit residents by broadening the city’s tax base. Lucie has long lacked commercial, which is a burden on homeowners,” he said. “We have had several hearings here at the city, so that is what transparency is: open meetings where people can come and share their opinions and be a part of the process.” Councilman David Pickett agreed, saying the city has consistently heard residents oppose additional housing. “When this was first introduced, I was very excited that they wanted to go from residential to commercial,” Pickett said. “It doesn’t matter which way we rule, there’s always going to be somebody in opposition. For me, going to commercial is the best possible thing for that corner.” Morgan, who had questioned the gas station restriction during the first hearing, ultimately supported the ordinance. “We have heard from so many community residents — no more housetops,” she said. “It has been transparent, there’s no denying that.” Before the vote, Mayor Shannon Martin asked staff to confirm that the prohibition would remain with the property regardless of ownership. Kean confirmed the restriction is now written directly into the Tradition MPUD documents, ensuring no future owner can develop a gas station on the parcel. The council then voted unanimously to approve the ordinance, ending months of discussion and clearing the way for commercial development while permanently removing a gas station as a future possibility. cards.headline: TPS expiration leaves Haitian workers in Port St. Lucie and Fort Pierce without jobs
cards.teaser: Temporary Protected Status expired Monday for Haitian immigrants, stripping workers of jobs and disrupting schools and public services across the Treasure Coast.
cards.body:
Valentina Lorissaint said many relatives and friends are already unable to work after losing authorization tied to TPS. She said a lot of people have been scared, just wondering what the next meal they're going to eat the next day. Residents described widespread anxiety rippling through the community, with some families afraid to leave their homes or send children to school.

Chuck Ridley, director of civic engagement for the Service Employees International Union, said the union expects hundreds of workers statewide to be affected, including nearly 20 employees in the Palm Beach County School District alone. The Palm Beach County School District said 19 District employees will be separated from employment as all School District employees must be legally authorized to work in the United States. Ridley said many of the workers losing TPS protections are bus drivers, custodians, paraprofessionals, food service employees and city workers.

The Florida Healthcare Association said Haitian caregivers are valued members of the long term care workforce, serving as certified nursing assistants, nurses, dietary aides, housekeepers and other essential team members. According to the Lar Management Group, the Haitian community contributes an estimated $1.2 billion to Florida's economy. TPS allows people from countries facing war, natural disasters or other unsafe conditions to live and work temporarily in the United States. The U.S. State Department currently maintains a Level 4 Do Not Travel advisory for Haiti, citing crime, civil unrest and kidnapping.
cards.article_text: Haitian immigrants in Palm Beach County say the end of Temporary Protected Status is pushing families into crisis, stripping workers of jobs, disrupting schools and public services and forcing many to confront the possibility of deportation to a country the U.S. government warns Americans not to visit because of widespread violence and kidnappings.Inside the Tru Island Grill restaurant in Delray Beach on Monday, community members described mounting fear as TPS protections expire for many Haitians who have lived and worked in the United States for years.WATCH BELOW: TPS expiration: Workers lose jobs, kids fear for parents"It's not doing us well at all," said Valentina Lorissaint, who said many relatives and friends are already unable to work after losing authorization tied to TPS. "We have a lot of family members that are under (TPS) that can't work, that cannot pay their bills, that are struggling."TPS allows people from countries facing war, natural disasters or other unsafe conditions to live and work temporarily in the United States. Haiti has been designated for TPS because of ongoing instability, gang violence and humanitarian crises.The U.S. State Department currently maintains a Level 4 "Do Not Travel" advisory for Haiti, citing crime, civil unrest and kidnapping.Still, Lorissaint says she knows "a lot" of people who have been sent back to Haiti."They struggle. That's the reason why they try to come here, to try to survive," she said. "So it's like starting all over again."Residents described widespread anxiety rippling through the community, with some families afraid to leave their homes or send children to school."A lot of people have been scared," Lorissaint said. "Just wondering what's the next meal they're gonna eat the next day."Others said the loss of TPS is affecting people who have spent decades working and paying taxes in the United States."Some people a long time ago, they lost their job, no driver's license for driving," said Elana Dixon. You're supposed to get paperwork."Dixon said many Haitian immigrants arrived in the 1990s, built families and contributed to local communities for years. The uncertainty is also affecting U.S.-born children whose parents could face deportation."Their kids were born here … it's crazy," Lorissaint said.Labor leaders warn the effects are spreading beyond immigrant households and into the broader economy.Chuck Ridley, director of civic engagement for the Service Employees International Union, said the union expects hundreds of workers statewide to be affected, including nearly 20 employees in the Palm Beach County School District alone."We know at the school district that's almost 20 staff that's going to be impacted from what we know, but that's the tip of the iceberg," Ridley said.Ridley said many of the workers losing TPS protections are bus drivers, custodians, paraprofessionals, food service employees and city workers.WPTV reached out to the Palm Beach County School District PBCSD for comment. A spokesperson responded with the following statement:"Temporary Protected Status (TPS) is expected to expire today. Without another extension, 19 District employees will be separated from employment today, as all School District employees must be legally authorized to work in the United States. Additional details regarding federal updates are available via U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services.Furthermore, the School District of Palm Beach County does not collect or store a student's immigration status. The District has eliminated positions due to enrollment shifts and to balance the District's budget. These enrollment shifts are driven by demographic changes in our region, the rising cost of living in Palm Beach County, and the expansion of the Family Empowerment Scholarship program.""When you are not able to get the services because you don't have drivers to pick up folk, or folk who are working in cities like Delray in the public sector that can't provide the service, or you're not getting your garbage collected … there's so many areas that you don't think about," Ridley said.The healthcare system could also face staffing shortages, Ridley said, particularly in hospitals and nursing homes that rely heavily on immigrant workers. "If we talk about hospitals, it even adds onto the amount of folks who are CNAs, the folk who work in the kitchen," he said. "If we talk about nursing home, most of that staff are folks who are going to be impacted."Regarding the loss of TPS, the Florida Healthcare Association said the following:"Haitian caregivers are valued members of the long term care workforce, serving as certified nursing assistants, nurses, dietary aides, housekeepers and other essential team members. Our priority is always protecting access to quality care for Florida's growing aging population, and we know that a disruption to experienced staff could create additional challenges to our long term care centers who are focused on supporting the needs of residents, families and care teams."Community members said the economic effects are already visible in restaurants and businesses across South Florida. According to the Lar Management Group, the Haitian community contributes an estimated $1.2 billion to Florida's economy"Every immigrant .... we need them," one diner said. They pay tax."Kepler Deneville said empty workplaces and declining activity are becoming increasingly noticeable."TPS is ending. It's not good for anybody," he said. "People are losing their jobs."Ridley said many workers now fear appearing in public after losing legal protections."One, they're out of a job, and then two, they're gonna go underground," he said. hero.headline: Leon County judge rules James Fishback can remain on Florida governor ballot
hero.body:
Republican gubernatorial candidate James Fishback will remain on Florida's Aug. 18 primary ballot after a Leon County judge rejected Lt. Gov. Jay Collins' challenge to his residency qualifications. Circuit Judge David Frank ruled Monday that Collins did not present enough evidence to overcome Florida's legal presumptions favoring continued residency and candidate access to the ballot.

The final order denies Collins' request to remove Fishback, declares that the Department of State properly certified his candidacy and says Fishback shall remain qualified for the Republican nomination for governor. Collins sued Fishback in June, arguing the candidate failed to meet the Florida Constitution's requirement that a governor reside in the state for the seven years preceding the election. During an expedited hearing last week, Collins' attorneys presented voter registration, mortgage, tax and homestead records they argued showed Fishback established legal residency in Washington, D.C., between 2019 and 2022. Fishback voted in Washington during the 2020 presidential election, filed D.C. resident income tax returns and signed mortgage paperwork describing a condominium there as his principal residence.

Frank acknowledged those records could carry consequences outside the Florida candidacy case, writing that the various election and financial filings could result in regulatory or more severe legal repercussions for Fishback under Washington, D.C. law. But the judge found they did not prove Fishback intended to abandon Florida as his permanent home. Fishback testified for several hours that he never intended to move his legal domicile from Florida. He acknowledged signing mortgage paperwork identifying the Washington condominium as his primary residence but said he rushed through the documents without reading them closely. He also characterized his 2020 D.C. vote as an inadvertent registration during the pandemic, saying he was staying with his parents and wanted to vote for President Donald Trump.

Frank found Fishback credible on the central issue of intent. The judge also pointed to Fishback's Florida upbringing, family relationships, driver's license, vehicle registration, voting history and work with Incubate Debate, a statewide nonprofit operating student debate programs throughout Florida. Collins' attorney Mark Meuser criticized the ruling and argued the court improperly accepted Fishback's explanation that he did not understand the legal significance of his Washington filings. Meuser did not indicate whether Collins plans to appeal the ruling. Unless an appellate court intervenes, Fishback will remain on the Aug. 18 Republican primary ballot alongside Collins, U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds and former House Speaker Paul Renner.

cards.headline: Byron Donalds challenges David Jolly to three debates while Florida primary opponents remain unmet
cards.teaser: Republican gubernatorial front-runner Byron Donalds issued a challenge for three general election debates with Democratic candidate David Jolly despite facing three GOP primary opponents he has not debated.
cards.body:
Republican gubernatorial front-runner Byron Donalds challenged leading Democratic candidate David Jolly to three general election debates this fall, even as Donalds continues facing three opponents for the GOP nomination. Jolly, a former Republican congressman now running as a Democrat, initially responded by telling Donalds to survive his own primary first. During a later CNN appearance, however, he said he would gladly meet Donalds on the debate stage a dozen times.

The exchange gave Donalds' Republican opponents Lt. Gov. Jay Collins, former Florida House Speaker Paul Renner and businessman James Fishback another opportunity to criticize the front-runner for looking beyond them. Donalds has not debated his primary rivals while maintaining sizable advantages in polling, fundraising and endorsements. A recent Cygnal survey showed Donalds at 43 percent, compared with 12 percent for Fishback, 11 percent for Collins and 2 percent for Renner, although nearly one-third of voters remained undecided.

A separate University of North Florida poll offered an early look at the possible general election matchup. Donalds led Jolly 46 percent to 41 percent among likely midterm voters, with a margin of error of 3.8 percentage points. The Aug. 18 Florida primary is less than a month away.
cards.article_text: With less than a month remaining before Florida's Aug. 18 primary, the race for governor briefly skipped ahead to November this week.Republican front-runner Byron Donalds challenged leading Democratic candidate David Jolly to three general-election debates this fall, even as Donalds continues facing three opponents for the GOP nomination.WATCH BELOW: Florida politics recap: Governor's race heats up"There has been a lot of talk about debates," Donalds said while issuing the challenge. "When the time comes for these debates, you're going to see my vision is one for a free Florida that puts the people of Florida first, protects the Florida dream, expands our economies and makes sure that Florida remains number one in all of America."Jolly, a former Republican congressman now running as a Democrat, initially responded by telling Donalds to survive his own primary first. During a later CNN appearance, however, he said he would gladly meet Donalds on the debate stage."A dozen times," Jolly said. "Let him get through his Republican primary right now, because I'm not sure he can get through that. Let's see what he does on August 18."The exchange gave Donalds' Republican opponents — Lt. Jay Collins, former Florida House Speaker Paul Renner and businessman James Fishback — another opportunity to criticize the front-runner for looking beyond them.Donalds has not debated his primary rivals while maintaining sizable advantages in polling, fundraising and endorsements. A recent Cygnal survey showed Donalds at 43%, compared with 12% for Fishback, 11% for Collins and 2% for Renner, although nearly one-third of voters remained undecided.A separate University of North Florida poll offered an early look at the possible general-election matchup. Donalds led Jolly 46% to 41% among likely midterm voters, with a margin of error of 3.8 percentage points.While Donalds looked toward the fall, Fishback spent much of Tuesday defending his place on the Republican primary ballot.Collins is asking a Leon County judge to disqualify Fishback, arguing his Washington, D.C., voting, tax, mortgage and homestead records show he failed to meet the Florida Constitution's requirement that a governor reside in the state for the preceding seven years.During the one-day hearing, Collins' attorneys presented records showing Fishback registered and voted in Washington in 2020, listed D.C. addresses on tax documents and signed mortgage paperwork identifying a condominium there as his principal residence.Fishback acknowledged voting in Washington but testified that he never intended to abandon Florida as his permanent home. polling place with his Florida driver's license and did not understand that he was registering as a Washington voter."On Election Day, I inadvertently registered and voted in that election," Fishback testified.Fishback also said he did not closely read mortgage documents identifying the condominium as his primary residence. His defense presented corporate filings, insurance records, travel records and other documents intended to show that his legal and personal ties remained in Florida.The hearing, originally expected to last two days, wrapped after a single day of testimony. Circuit Judge David Frank ordered both sides to submit proposed rulings by Friday and said he expects to issue a decision by 5 p.m. The ruling could determine whether Fishback remains on the Aug. Read more about the hearing.Florida's current governor, meanwhile, spent the week leading a state business-development mission through England and Scotland.Gov. Ron DeSantis opened Florida's pavilion at the Farnborough International Airshow and announced that Relativity Space plans to expand its operations at Cape Canaveral. The company plans an additional production facility for its Terran R rocket, along with expanded testing and launch infrastructure at Kennedy Space Center and Cape Canaveral Space Force Station.State officials say the project could create thousands of jobs by 2034. Relativity Space is also eligible for up to $134 million through Florida's Spaceport Improvement Program. DeSantis separately oversaw a cooperation agreement between Space Florida and the U.K. Space Agency aimed at research, innovation and commercial development. Space Florida outlined the expansion here.In London, DeSantis and Florida Insurance Commissioner Mike Yaworsky met with leaders from Lloyd's of London and other insurance and reinsurance firms. The trip comes as Florida officials continue trying to attract additional private capital to the state's property-insurance market. Officials said the meetings also explored a potential research partnership between Florida and the Lloyd's Lab insurance-technology program.The mission also produced new academic agreements. Florida International University and Scotland's Heriot-Watt University agreed to pursue cooperation centered on free markets, political economy and the work of Adam Smith. The University of Florida and the University of St. Andrews established a broader framework for joint research and faculty and student exchanges in fields including quantum, marine and physical sciences.Back in Florida, a new poll showed the state's proposed property-tax amendment may be popular enough to pass — depending on how it is described to voters.The proposal would raise the homestead exemption for non-school property taxes from $50,000 to $150,000 in 2027 and then to $250,000 in 2028. It would also lower the annual assessment-growth cap for non-homestead properties from 10% to 5% and restrict how local governments spend remaining property-tax revenue.The UNF survey initially found 61% support after respondents were told the amendment would reserve property-tax revenue for core public services. That is narrowly above the 60% approval required for a constitutional amendment.Support fell 16 points, however, after respondents were told the proposal is estimated to create an approximately $11.8 billion municipal budget shortfall over two years. With that information, 45% supported the amendment and 47% opposed it.The poll surveyed 848 likely midterm voters from July 8 through July 17.Those results add significance to three lawsuits challenging the amendment's ballot title and summary. Plaintiffs argue phrases promising to "protect small businesses," "ensure fairness" and preserve core services amount to political advertising instead of a neutral description of the proposal.The challengers are not asking a judge to remove the amendment from the November ballot. If the language is found defective, state law would require Attorney General James Uthmeier to rewrite what voters see.A hearing on the ballot-language challenges is scheduled for July 29 in Leon County. The cases could be consolidated ahead of that hearing.

cards.headline: Byron Donalds pushes bill requiring AI data centers to supply their own power and water
cards.teaser: Florida Republican U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds introduced legislation requiring hyperscale AI data centers to provide their own power generation and water resources instead of relying on public utilities.
cards.body:
AI data centers could soon face new federal requirements under legislation backed by Florida Republican U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds that aims to prevent rising electricity demand from increasing utility bills for everyday customers. The proposal comes as the rapid expansion of hyperscale AI data centers raises concerns nationwide about strain on the power grid and water resources. The Electric Power Research Institute estimates data centers could consume up to 9 percent of all U.S. electricity generation by 2030, a sharp increase from current levels.

Donalds introduced H.R. 9777, known as the Protecting Ratepayers Act, which would require hyperscale AI data centers to provide their own power generation and water resources instead of relying on public utilities. Supporters of the proposal say it could help shield customers in Florida and across the country from future utility rate increases tied to growing energy demand from artificial intelligence infrastructure. The legislation comes as companies race to build AI infrastructure capable of supporting growing demand for generative AI systems and cloud computing.

The Trump administration recently announced the Ratepayer Protection Pledge, a voluntary agreement involving major technology companies, utilities and state leaders intended to keep the cost of powering new AI facilities from being passed on to residential and commercial utility customers. The pledge has been signed by several major technology companies, including Amazon, Google, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, Oracle and xAI. Utilities and state leaders have also joined the initiative, according to the administration.

Byron is legislating and leading on this issue, while Democrat David Jolly is reacting with cheap talk like the washed up MSNBC analyst he is ,” said communications director Gates McGavick.”The legislation comes as companies race to build AI infrastructure capable of supporting growing demand for generative AI systems and cloud computing.The Trump administration’s voluntary Ratepayer Protection Pledge has been signed by several major technology companies, including Amazon, Google, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, Oracle and xAI.Utilities and state leaders have also joined the initiative, according to the administration.The pledge is designed to reassure customers that the expansion of AI-related infrastructure will not automatically lead to higher electricity costs for households and small businesses.Mehran Basiratmand, director of innovations and programs at Florida Atlantic University, said the proposed legislation could address some of the biggest public concerns surrounding AI data centers.Basiratmand previously served as chairperson of the policy board for what he described as the state’s largest data center.“I think it’s clearly a move in the right direction,” Basiratmand told WPTV's Michael Hoffman.He said requiring companies to generate their own power could encourage investment in alternative energy solutions rather than placing added pressure on public infrastructure.“I think as we set up the threshold, law is clearly going to force companies to look at alternative sources,” Basiratmand said. “I do not think it’s going to shift companies to go overseas because we already see significant pushback in many countries on that as well.”Basiratmand added that the proposal could ultimately benefit communities beyond the United States by encouraging more sustainable approaches to powering AI technology.AI companies are rapidly expanding data center construction nationwide as demand grows for artificial intelligence tools, cloud computing and digital services. cards.headline: Poll shows Florida property tax amendment support depends on how voters are informed
cards.teaser: A University of North Florida poll found 61 percent support for Florida's proposed property tax amendment initially, but support fell to 45 percent after voters learned of an estimated $11.8 billion municipal budget shortfall.
cards.body:
A new poll showed Florida's proposed property tax amendment may be popular enough to pass depending on how it is described to voters. The proposal would raise the homestead exemption for non-school property taxes from $50,000 to $150,000 in 2027 and then to $250,000 in 2028. It would also lower the annual assessment growth cap for non-homestead properties from 10 percent to 5 percent and restrict how local governments spend remaining property tax revenue.

The UNF survey initially found 61 percent support after respondents were told the amendment would reserve property tax revenue for core public services. That is narrowly above the 60 percent approval required for a constitutional amendment. Support fell 16 points, however, after respondents were told the proposal is estimated to create an approximately $11.8 billion municipal budget shortfall over two years. With that information, 45 percent supported the amendment and 47 percent opposed it. The poll surveyed 848 likely midterm voters from July 8 through July 17.

Those results add significance to three lawsuits challenging the amendment's ballot title and summary. Plaintiffs argue phrases promising to protect small businesses, ensure fairness and preserve core services amount to political advertising instead of a neutral description of the proposal. The challengers are not asking a judge to remove the amendment from the November ballot. If the language is found defective, state law would require Attorney General James Uthmeier to rewrite what voters see. cards.headline: Palm Beach County families say Florida Medicaid abruptly cut autism therapy for children
cards.teaser: Palm Beach County parents say their children lost access to Applied Behavioral Analysis therapy after Medicaid abruptly stopped covering it. Florida's health agency has not explained why.
cards.body:
Palm Beach County parents say their children lost access to a critical autism therapy after Medicaid abruptly stopped covering it and Florida's health agency has not explained why. The therapy at the center of the dispute is Applied Behavioral Analysis, or ABA. The Cleveland Clinic describes it as a research-based behavior therapy for people with autism and other developmental disorders, adding that many studies have proven the effectiveness of ABA. Families connected to Reflection Services ABA Therapy in Lake Worth say they received notice that Medicaid would no longer cover their children's treatment.

Daura Mabel Sanchez Cano de Fundora said her son David is classified by his neurologist as level one on the autism spectrum. She described the progress he had made through ABA, saying his vocabulary have been increasingly amazing and he can understand what is happening. Myrian Suarez, a mother of two boys with autism, said ABA gave her son tools to manage his emotions. Since the therapy stopped, Talia Quiroz said she has experienced dangerous regressions in her daughter's behavior. Suarez described similar physical consequences, saying she has bruised arms from one of her son's pinching.

Reports of Medicaid cuts to ABA therapy have surfaced in states across the country. The Health and Human Services Office of the Inspector General audited Medicaid spending on ABA in Maine, Michigan, Wisconsin, and Colorado. Its findings identified roughly $200 million in what it considers improper payments among the four states. A separate audit in Nebraska found yearly Medicaid spending on ABA therapy multiplied 18 times over, across a five-year period. Questions were sent to Florida's Agency for Healthcare Administration, which runs the state's Medicaid program.
cards.article_text: Palm Beach County parents say their children lost access to a critical autism therapy after Medicaid abruptly stopped covering it — and Florida's health agency has not explained why.WATCH BELOW:The therapy at the center of the dispute is Applied Behavioral Analysis, or ABA. The Cleveland Clinic describes it as "a research-based behavior therapy for people with autism and other developmental disorders," adding that "many studies have proven the effectiveness of ABA."Families connected to Reflection Services ABA Therapy in Lake Worth say they received notice that Medicaid would no longer cover their children's treatment. For many, the loss has been immediate and painful."It's like a dark hole. Like you don't know what to do," Daura Mabel Sanchez Cano de Fundora said.Her son David, she said, is classified by his neurologist as level one on the autism spectrum. She described the progress he had made through ABA."His vocabulary have been increasingly amazing. He can understand what is happening," Sanchez Cano de Fundora said. "How you can deny a service that can decide the life of those children and those parents?"Myrian Suarez, a mother of two boys with autism, described the daily demands of caring for her children without adequate support."I have to do everything for them: feed them, bathe them, help them get dressed, comb their hair — everything, everything, everything," Suarez said.She said ABA gave her son tools to manage his emotions."His therapist gives him tools so he can channel the frustration he feels," Suarez said.Talia Quiroz said her daughter Salma was diagnosed with autism at 2 and a half years old. She described the progress Salma made through ABA therapy."She can learn. In fact, things that years before we're not thinking that will be possible," Quiroz said.Since the therapy stopped, Quiroz said she has experienced dangerous regressions in her daughter's behavior."I cannot show, but I have bites all over me," Quiroz said.Suarez described similar physical consequences."I have bruised arms from (one of my son's) pinching," Suarez said.She also described the role ABA support plays in her son's school day."The ABA registered behavior technician at school helps Dagito stay seated and complete his tasks, but she is also protecting Dagito from other children who are like him and protecting the other children from how Dagito is," Suarez said."It just hurts-- not just as a family, but it hurts thinking in the future," Quiroz said. The chance to be able to grow up and be part of this society."Reports of Medicaid cuts to ABA therapy have surfaced in states across the country.The Health and Human Services Office of the Inspector General audited Medicaid spending on ABA in Maine, Michigan, Wisconsin, and Colorado. Its findings identified roughly $200 million — specifically $197.9 million — in what it considers improper payments among the four states.A separate audit in Nebraska found yearly Medicaid spending on ABA therapy multiplied 18 times over, across a five-year period.The Trump administration has said it is targeting waste, fraud, and abuse in government healthcare spending."We are not sending Medicaid and Medicare dollars out the door until we have confidence that they are being spent lawfully and appropriately," U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert Kennedy Jr. said during a news conference last week.Florida has not been officially audited, so it's not immediately clear how much its Medicaid program spends on ABA.Melissa Moran, a registered behavior technician at Reflection Services ABA Therapy, acknowledged the cost of the services but said the consequences of cutting them must be weighed carefully."We know that the services are expensive," Moran said. "(But) the things that may happen in society if they don't have ABA — those are really important. So those are things that we need to take into account when cutting funds."Moran warned of the societal repercussions of families losing access to ABA, as forcing some parents to supervise their children around the clock."So the parents may not go to work, so that affects the economy of this country," Moran said. "Sometimes (the kids) have unsafe behaviors-- physical aggression. They have self-injurious behaviors. All of these kind of behaviors that may put themselves, the other kids, at risk too. So that's something that may affect the rhythm of the class that's at school and in the community.Questions were sent to Florida's Agency for Healthcare Administration, which runs the state's Medicaid program. The agency has not responded.A public records request was also filed asking for a detailed breakdown of Medicaid spending on ABA, or any documents that could help explain why the state is no longer paying for the therapy. cards.headline: Gov. DeSantis announces Relativity Space expansion at Cape Canaveral during UK trade mission
cards.teaser: Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis announced that Relativity Space plans to expand its operations at Cape Canaveral during a state business development mission through England and Scotland.
cards.body:
Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis led a state business development mission through England and Scotland, opening Florida's pavilion at the Farnborough International Airshow and announcing that Relativity Space plans to expand its operations at Cape Canaveral. The company plans an additional production facility for its Terran R rocket, along with expanded testing and launch infrastructure at Kennedy Space Center and Cape Canaveral Space Force Station. State officials say the project could create thousands of jobs by 2034. Relativity Space is also eligible for up to $134 million through Florida's Spaceport Improvement Program.

DeSantis separately oversaw a cooperation agreement between Space Florida and the U.K. Space Agency aimed at research, innovation and commercial development. In London, DeSantis and Florida Insurance Commissioner Mike Yaworsky met with leaders from Lloyd's of London and other insurance and reinsurance firms. The trip comes as Florida officials continue trying to attract additional private capital to the state's property insurance market. Officials said the meetings also explored a potential research partnership between Florida and the Lloyd's Lab insurance technology program.

The mission also produced new academic agreements. Florida International University and Scotland's Heriot-Watt University agreed to pursue cooperation centered on free markets, political economy and the work of Adam Smith. The University of Florida and the University of St. Andrews established a broader framework for joint research and faculty and student exchanges in fields including quantum, marine and physical sciences.

cards.headline: Boston cyclist begins 2,600-mile ride from Key West to Maine to honor friend lost to colorectal cancer
cards.teaser: Jay Weedall traveled to South Florida to begin a 2,600-mile bike ride from Key West to Maine with a goal of raising $50,000 for young-onset colorectal cancer research.
cards.body:
A Boston cyclist is turning heartbreak into hope. After losing a close friend to young-onset colorectal cancer, Jay Weedall traveled to South Florida to begin a 2,600-mile bike ride from Key West to Maine, with a goal of raising $50,000 for research while honoring his friend's memory. The death of his friend, who was also named Jay, inspired Weedall to honor his memory by riding his bike across the country. His goal is to raise $50,000 for the Young Onset Colorectal Cancer Research Center in honor of the friend he lost to the disease.

To prepare, Weedall trained 200 to 300 miles a week, mapped out his route, and planned for the long journey ahead. Weedall began his journey in Key West, pedaling 155 miles to Miami on day one. He set off on his second leg a 163-mile ride to Vero Beach. Weedall is riding roughly 150 miles a day along the coast through nearly every state all the way to the Pan Mass Challenge. He will do the Pan Mass Challenge across Massachusetts on August 2 and continue to the Canadian border in Maine.

By avoiding highways, Weedall says the route offers something unexpected, allowing him to experience little coastal towns along those inlets. When riding hundreds of miles alone, Weedall says he has plenty of time to think. He said that even when his legs are hurting, even when the traffic is big or even when he is a little anxious about what is going on around him, he is largely just thinking about his friend who does not get the opportunity to do this with him anymore. Fans can follow Weedall's journey on the cycling app Strava.

hero.headline: Indiantown Council rejects pause on data center applications despite resident pressure
hero.body:
A pair of Indiantown Village Council members failed to gain support Monday for a 90-day pause on data center applications, with village officials citing concerns about violating state law and risking millions in state funding. Councilwoman Karen Onsager proposed an administrative pause on accepting, processing and approving new applications for large-load data center development projects. The motion came after civic activist Melissa Hague renewed her request from June, telling the Council that not pausing to review land development regulations would be negligent.

Village Attorney Wade Vose said the pause would violate Senate Bills 180 and 484, repeating his legal opinion from June that such a move would put Indiantown at risk of lawsuits from property owners and developers. Vose told the Council he received an email that same afternoon from a local land use attorney representing multiple developers within the village, warning that SB 180 would prohibit any regulation that would inhibit the process of applications for development. Village Manager Taryn Kryzda confirmed that industrially zoned lands within the village allow data centers as a permitted use.

Councilwoman Vernestine Palmer supported the concept but wanted a longer timeframe of 12 to 18 months rather than 90 days. Onsager said she chose 90 days specifically to avoid running afoul of state law and because the village is in the middle of an election cycle. Mayor Carmine Dipaolo warned against offending state officials who have given Indiantown over $120 million in funding. Kryzda added that when local government goes against the state or federal government, the first thing they look to do is withhold funding.

No council member seconded Onsager's motion, causing it to die. The proposal followed the withdrawal in April of a data center application submitted by Nelson Ferreira, which had drawn protests from scores of local residents. Kryzda confirmed that the community meeting Onsager requested will be scheduled for Saturday, August 2, and will include technical experts, representatives from the South Florida Water Management District, utility providers and relevant staff.

Hague repeated her request during the July 13 budget workshop. “I’m coming back asking for an administrative pause on data centers,” she said. “It’s already been admitted on media that we don’t know what we’re dealing with. If we don’t know, not having an administrative pause to go through the motions of finding out and looking at land development regulations is negligent. I know there’s pressure behind the scenes not to have that happen, but the people want it to happen, and that’s who you represent.” A few minutes later, Councilwoman Karen Onsager – who’d supported Hague’s request the previous month – again broached the topic, this time couching it in the milder terminology of a “pause.” “I’ve asked for an informative community meeting,” she said. “In light of that meeting, I move that the Village of Indiantown establish a 90-day administrative pause on the acceptance, processing and approval of all new applications for large-load data center development projects. During the 90-day period, I request the Village staff proceed with the informational meeting I requested, including technical experts, representatives from the South Florida Water Management District, utility providers and relevant staff so that the Council and our residents can better understand the current and projected demands on our water and electrical infrastructure.” Councilwoman Onsager emphasized more than once that her proposed pause was intended to provide the Council additional time to gather facts, evaluate data and consider potential solutions to community concerns while putting off any potential Board decisions on such applications until after the current election cycle. “To be clear, I am not proposing any amendments to our land development regulations nor am I seeking to impose additional restrictions or requirements on the application process at this time,” she added in a nod to the aforementioned legislation. “I am simply requesting sufficient time for the Council to conduct due-diligence and make informed decisions regarding future industrial development applications based on a thorough understanding of the facts and the infrastructure implications.” Rather than offering a second to Onsager’s motion, however, Councilwoman Vernestine Palmer wanted to negotiate the length of that pause with her colleague. “I think the administrative pause should be more than 90 days,” she said. “I think we should have at least a 12-to-18-month administrative pause so we can get all the information concerning it. No one is saying we’re against it or for it; we just want to know what’s going on so we can make an informed decision and [ensure] the LDRs have some safeguards in it for us.” That failed to sway Onsager, who knew her motion was already going against Vose’s prior legal advice. “I asked for a 90-day pause because a 90-day pause does give us time to collect information, have the meeting, get some important data and not necessarily bring down problems for our community,” she explained. “We can’t afford to be sued for doing things wrong –12 to 18 months is restrictive. hero.headline: Port St. Lucie opens $28.8 million police training facility
hero.teaser: Port St. Lucie cut the ribbon on a 54,283-square-foot police training center on the City Hall grounds, featuring a 20-lane indoor firearms range, tactical shoot house, and virtual simulation technology.
hero.body:
Port St. Lucie officially opened its 54,283-square-foot, $28.8 million police training center on July 24 on the grounds of City Hall, just northwest of the police department. Mayor Shannon Martin and Chief Leo Niemczyk cut the ribbon for the facility after four years of construction. The three-story building includes a 20-lane, 9,508-square-foot indoor firearms range with an integrated MILO live-fire scenario system, a 2,848-square-foot tactical shoot house with configurable rooms, and a MILO Virtual Simulation Theater for decision-making and de-escalation exercises.

The facility also features a defensive tactics training room equipped with Axon VR technology, a multi-purpose training room, and three floors of office space supporting the Training Division and Criminal Investigations Division. The offices include 19 individual offices and 86 workstations. Officer Brittany McNally said that for years, officers traveled to Indian River State College in Fort Pierce for extensive training, and the new facility will reduce those recurring costs while allowing more efficient training.

The facility was designed by ADG Architecture and constructed by HJ High. Police personnel immediately began moving into the new facility after the ribbon cutting. The facility is not open to the general public because of safety and confidentiality concerns. Port St. Lucie has a population of more than 260,000 and a police department with 455 employees, including 360 sworn officers.

cards.headline: Three arrested after 3-month-old dies from dehydration and malnutrition in Fort Pierce home
cards.body:
Three people face charges of aggravated manslaughter of a child and aggravated child abuse after a 3-month-old died from dehydration and malnutrition in a Fort Pierce mobile home, the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office announced Monday. Nicole Maxwell, the infant's mother, her father Robert Maxwell, and his girlfriend Vikki Koon were arrested nearly a year after investigators responded to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital in August 2025 when the child was brought in deceased.

The medical examiner determined the child died from dehydration and malnutrition and ruled the death a homicide. Court documents describe the infant's ribs as more prominent than its stomach. Detective Jennifer Diaz said the child lived primarily with Robert Maxwell and Koon while Nicole Maxwell lived at her boyfriend's home. Koon told investigators she primarily fed the infant only twice a day and admitted that when she ran out of formula, she fed the child watered-down milk with bay cereal mixed in. The child's father lived in Virginia.

Investigators found the mobile home in Fort Pierce had windows boarded shut, exposed electrical wiring, and live and dead cockroaches throughout. Detective Diaz described the house as extremely hot with a bug infestation and unsafe for walking. A neighbor named Suzan said she witnessed the conditions firsthand and would often see the other children walking around the neighborhood asking for water. Suzan said the children wore the same clothes every day and were not bathed. Nicole Maxwell's other children who were living inside the mobile home are now in foster care.

Detective Diaz, who has 20 years in law enforcement, called this one of the worst cases she has ever worked. The Department of Children and Families had been involved with the family before. Sheriff Richard Del Toro urged the public to report any signs of child abuse or neglect, stating that one phone call can be the difference between a child receiving help and a life being saved. The case required outside medical expertise and months of additional testing before charges could be filed.

cards.headline: Armed robbery at Fort Pierce Wells Fargo ATM forces victim to withdraw cash
cards.teaser: Two men forced a victim to withdraw cash at a Wells Fargo ATM in Fort Pierce on Sunday evening, with one suspect displaying a gun concealed in his waistband.
cards.body:
A man using a Wells Fargo ATM in Fort Pierce became the victim of an armed robbery Sunday at about 8:38 p.m. when two men forced him to pull out cash before fleeing on foot. One of the suspects displayed a gun concealed in his waistband before forcing the victim to withdraw an unknown amount of cash, the Fort Pierce Police Department said.

Officers responded to the scene, established a perimeter, and used a K-9 and drone to search for the suspects. The suspects were not located. Police described them as two men in their early 20s, about 5 feet 10 inches tall and weighing about 170 pounds. The armed suspect was last seen wearing jeans and a gray hooded sweatshirt.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie police arrest two after high-speed chase, find suspect hiding on roof
cards.teaser: A suspected drunk driver fled Port St. Lucie police at nearly 80 mph before he and his passenger abandoned their car and ran, with one suspect found hiding on the roof of an occupied home.
cards.body:
Joseph Gary Harris, 42, and Bryan Shawn Baker, 46, were arrested after fleeing Port St. Lucie police at nearly 80 mph in a 45 mph zone on Southwest Becker Road. Officers attempted to stop a white Acura after observing multiple traffic violations and signs of impaired driving, but the driver accelerated and weaved in and out of traffic, ignoring traffic signs and signals.

The driver and passenger abandoned the vehicle in a residential driveway near Southwest Idol Avenue before fleeing on foot. A nearby resident called 911 after seeing the two men run from the scene. Police deployed a K-9 and a drone while officers established a perimeter. Both suspects were located, including one who was found hiding on the roof of an occupied home.

Harris was charged with fleeing and eluding law enforcement, burglary of an occupied dwelling, resisting an officer without violence, and loitering or prowling. Baker was charged with resisting an officer without violence and loitering or prowling.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie cuts property tax rate for 11th straight year
cards.teaser: Port St. Lucie City Council lowered the city's millage rate to 4.8750 for fiscal year 2026-27, down from 4.9750, continuing an 11-year trend of property tax reductions.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie City Council agreed to lower the city's property tax millage rate for the 11th consecutive year at the annual Summer Workshop held July 22-23. The Council approved a millage rate of 4.8750 for fiscal year 2026-27, a decrease from 4.9750 in fiscal year 2025-26. The budget will be adopted by City Council in September, with public hearings taking place Sept. 4 and Sept. 18, and goes into effect Oct. 1.

Since 2016, the city has reduced its millage rate by 25 percent, saving the average homeowner nearly $2,000 over a 10-year period. Port St. Lucie has the third lowest municipal tax rate out of Florida's 20 largest cities. The property tax reduction maintains Port St. Lucie's record of steadily reducing its millage rate while managing historic population growth, investing in essential infrastructure and improving public safety.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County could lose $63 million if property tax amendment passes
cards.teaser: Port St. Lucie is preparing for a potential $48 million revenue loss over two years if voters approve a property tax amendment in November, already canceling projects and freezing 184 positions.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie reviewed its budget Thursday at the Port St. Lucie Community Center as city leaders prepare for a potential $48 million loss in property tax revenue over the next two years if Amendment 3 passes in November. City Manager Jesus Merejo told the City Council the city won't fund 184 requested positions worth $28.3 million, including 25 new police officers and parks staff planned for Torino Regional Park and the new BMX facility at Tradition Regional Park.

City employees will not receive a cost-of-living raise in the coming budget. The city canceled $7.8 million in projects, including a study for a new interchange connecting Marshall Parkway to I-95, an inclusive playground at McChesney Park, and parking improvements at Riverland Paseo Park, along with construction on a new City Hall and parking garage. Police Chief Leo Niemczyk said the department may have to reduce staff size as costs rise.

Amendment 3, headed to Florida voters on the November 3, 2026 ballot, would raise the state's homestead exemption from $50,000 to $150,000 starting in January 2027 and to $250,000 in January 2028. The constitutional amendment needs at least 60 percent approval from voters to pass. Scott Samples with the city said the council will reconvene shortly after the November 3 election to determine next steps.
cards.article_text: Lucie review the upcoming city budget as some city council members worry about lost revenue if property taxes go away. Lucie hosted the summer budget workshop at the Port St. Lucie Community Center Thursday morning. During the workshop, City Manager Jesus Merejo told the City Council the city would lose over $48 million in property taxes over the next two years if the item passes in November. To prepare for the potential hit, the city isn't just deferring projects it's also holding the line on hiring. Lucie says it won't fund 184 requested positions, worth $28.3 million, including 25 new police officers and parks staff the city had already planned to add this year to keep up with growth at Torino Regional Park and the new BMX facility at Tradition Regional Park. Well, our costs continually rise just like everybody else. So, the only place that we can take that from is personnel. So, we'll have to reduce the size of the place, said Police Chief Leo Niemczyk when asked how this budget will impact the department. See also: Funeral held for Belle Glade father, two sons killed when pickup overturned into canal City employees also won't get a cost-of-living raise in the coming budget. On the capital side, the $7.8 million in canceled projects includes a study for a new interchange connecting Marshall Parkway to I-95, an inclusive playground at McChesney Park, and parking improvements at Riverland Paseo Park, along with construction on a new City Hall and parking garage Despite parks and recreation receiving an extra $1.34 million, most of that money is tied to new developments, such as the Torino Regional Park and the BMX facility at Tradition Regional Park. Parks and recreation officials told city councilors what a lack of new staff to keep these parks going will look like. I dare say the dirty words of deferred maintenance. But that's the reality when you don't have the people in the parks to maintain them at the level that we've been accustomed to doing, said Brad Keen, the director of the parks and recreation department. Not everything is being cut, though. The police department's budget is actually going up nearly 10%, to just under $104 million, driven mostly by a 5% contractual raise for sworn officers along with new equipment, training and technology upgrades. But the number of officers isn't growing; staffing stays flat at just over 468 positions, meaning the department is spending more to keep the officers it already has, not to add more. City leaders have flagged public safety, police, code enforcement, and emergency management as the areas most exposed if deeper cuts are eventually needed, since they already eat up 56% of the city's general fund. This is the reality of what the future is for, not just our city, but all this needs for safety if we're not able to be competitive and keep our officers, said Vice Mayor Jolien Caraballo. The proposal, known as Amendment 3, is headed to Florida voters on the November 3, 2026 ballot after the Legislature passed it during a June special session. If approved, it would raise the state's homestead exemption from $50,000 to $150,000 starting in January 2027, and to $250,000 in January 2028, while also directing lawmakers to come up with a plan to eliminate non-school property taxes on homesteaded properties eventually. Because it's a constitutional amendment, it needs at least 60% approval from voters to pass. Economists have estimated the change could cut local government revenue statewide by billions of dollars a year, which is why cities and counties across Florida, including Port St. Lucie, are already building the potential loss into their budget planning. Lucie County homeowners currently pay the highest property tax in the state, according to Florida tax data. Scott Samples with the city said the council will reconvene shortly after the November 3rd election to determine next steps, whether the proposal is passed or fails.

cards.headline: P1 Motor Club building private racetrack resort in St. Lucie County
cards.teaser: A 650-acre private racetrack resort community is under construction off Okeechobee Road, featuring 10 miles of racing circuits and opening its first track in October.
cards.body:
P1 Motor Club is being built on 650 acres off Okeechobee Road in St. Lucie County, featuring 10 miles of racing circuits designed for street cars, race cars and go-karts. The club is designed for drivers of all ages and skill levels, with children as young as 8 years old driving go-karts. Chris DuPlessis, Director of Fun for P1 Motor Club, described it as a high-end golf resort with a racetrack instead of a golf course.

The first track under construction is the 3-mile Treasure Coast Track, set to open in October. Over the next six months, crews will continue work on additional circuits, including the flagship 4.5-mile P1 International Circuit. Membership comes with a $192,000 initiation fee and $12,000 in yearly dues. The club already has 260 members.

Construction on a clubhouse and homes for up to 125 residents is scheduled to begin in 2027. The development will also include condos and customizable garages with living spaces situated directly along the tracks. Developers plan to preserve the character of the region by planting trees, creating lakes, and incorporating natural landscaping throughout the property. P1 Motor Club is expected to be fully completed by 2028.

hero.headline: Indian River County firefighter Geoffrey Lang dies following personal tragedy in Sebastian
hero.body:
Indian River County Fire Rescue is mourning the loss of Firefighter/Paramedic Geoffrey Lang, who died Saturday following what officials described as a personal tragedy at his Sebastian home. Lang, 35, joined Indian River County Fire Rescue in 2015 and worked out of Station 9 at 13550 Roseland Road in Sebastian. He is survived by his wife, two children and his parents.

County officials said Lang was known for his professionalism, compassion and dedication to serving others. Fire Chief David Johnson said Lang faithfully served the community for more than a decade and his absence will be deeply felt throughout the department. County Administrator John A. said the county's thoughts are with Lang's family, friends and fellow firefighters during this difficult time.

County Commission Chairman Deryl Loar extended condolences on behalf of the Board of County Commissioners and emphasized the county's commitment to supporting the mental health and well-being of first responders and their families. Multiple agencies including the Sebastian Police Department, Vero Beach Police Department and Indian River County Sheriff's Office expressed condolences following Lang's death.

Indian River County Fire Rescue asked the public to respect the privacy of Lang's family, friends and colleagues as they grieve. Officials said memorial service information will be released when it becomes available.

cards.headline: Boston cyclist passes through Vero Beach on 2,600-mile ride to honor friend lost to cancer
cards.teaser: Jay Weedall is riding his bike from Key West to Maine to raise $50,000 for young-onset colorectal cancer research after losing a close friend to the disease.
cards.body:
Jay Weedall, a Boston cyclist, began a 2,600-mile bike ride from Key West to Maine after losing a close friend named Jay to young-onset colorectal cancer. Weedall is raising $50,000 for the Young Onset Colorectal Cancer Research Center in honor of his friend. He trained 200 to 300 miles a week before beginning his journey.

Weedall rode 155 miles from Key West to Miami on day one, then continued with a 163-mile ride to Vero Beach on day two. He is riding roughly 150 miles per day up the coast through multiple states, planning to reach the Canadian border in Maine and participate in the Pan Mass Challenge across Massachusetts on August 2.

By avoiding highways, Weedall gets to experience small coastal towns along the inlets. He said even when his legs hurt or traffic gets heavy, he thinks about his friend who no longer has the opportunity to ride with him. Fans can follow Weedall's journey on the cycling app Strava.

hero.headline: 3 arrested in St. Lucie County after 3-month-old dies from dehydration and malnutrition in Fort Pierce
hero.body:
Three people face charges of aggravated manslaughter of a child and aggravated child abuse after a 3-month-old infant died from dehydration and malnutrition in Fort Pierce. The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office arrested Nicole Maxwell, the infant's mother, Robert Maxwell, the grandfather, and Vikki Koon, the grandfather's girlfriend, nearly a year after the baby's death in August 2025.

The investigation began when Robert Maxwell and Koon brought the deceased infant to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital. The medical examiner determined the child died from dehydration and malnutrition, with court documents describing the infant's ribs as more prominent than its stomach. Detective Jennifer Diaz said in her 20 years of law enforcement, this is one of the worst cases she has ever worked. The baby lived primarily with Robert Maxwell and Koon in a Fort Pierce mobile home while Nicole Maxwell lived with her boyfriend in Vero Beach.

Koon admitted to investigators that she fed the infant only twice a day and when she ran out of formula, she fed the child watered-down milk with baby cereal mixed in. The mobile home had windows boarded shut, exposed electrical wiring and live and dead cockroaches throughout. A neighbor named Suzan said she witnessed the conditions firsthand and described the home as unlivable. She said other children living in the home would come to her door asking for water and wore the same clothes every day.

The Department of Children and Families had been involved with the family before the infant's death. Nicole Maxwell's other children who were living inside the mobile home are now in foster care. Sheriff Richard Del Toro said protecting children is a responsibility the community shares and urged anyone who sees signs that a child may be neglected, abused or living in unsafe conditions to report it. Detectives said the case required outside expertise and months of additional testing before they could move forward with charges.

cards.body:
A man using a Wells Fargo ATM in Fort Pierce became the victim of an armed robbery on Sunday at about 8:38 p.m. Two men approached the victim, and one of them displayed a gun concealed in his waistband before forcing the victim to withdraw an unknown amount of cash.

Officers with the Fort Pierce Police Department responded to the scene, established a perimeter, and used a K-9 and drone to search for the suspects. The suspects were not located. Police described the suspects as two men in their early 20s, about 5 feet 10 inches tall and weighing about 170 pounds. The armed suspect was last seen wearing jeans and a gray hooded sweatshirt.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie police find suspect hiding on roof after high-speed chase on Southwest Becker Road
cards.teaser: A suspected drunk driver fled Port St. Lucie police at nearly 80 mph in a 45 mph zone before he and his passenger abandoned their car and ran, with one suspect later found hiding on the roof of an occupied home.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie police attempted to stop a white Acura after observing multiple traffic violations and signs of impaired driving. The driver accelerated to nearly 80 mph in a 45 mph zone on Southwest Becker Road. The driver and passenger weaved in and out of traffic, ignored traffic signs and signals, then abandoned the vehicle in a residential driveway near Southwest Idol Avenue before fleeing on foot.

A nearby resident called 911 after seeing the two men run from the scene. Police deployed a K-9 and a drone while officers established a perimeter. Both suspects were located, including one who was found hiding on the roof of an occupied home. The suspects were identified as Joseph Gary Harris, 42, and Bryan Shawn Baker, 46. Harris was charged with fleeing and eluding law enforcement, burglary of an occupied dwelling, resisting an officer without violence, and loitering or prowling. Baker was charged with resisting an officer without violence and loitering or prowling.
